One of the reasons that it took several hundred years for us to get from Newtonian mechanics to general relativity is that the dramatic relativistic effects predicted by Albert Einstein’s equations only manifest noticeably at significant fractions of the speed of light—and the speed of light is very, very fast. In everyday life, the only thing that moves anywhere near as fast as light is, well, light, so we simply don’t notice the infinitesimal differences between the predictions of Einstein’s theory and those of Newton’s. To be clear, those differences can and do affect our lives—famously, for instance, GPS wouldn’t work if we didn’t take relativity into account. But for the most part, we move through our lives without noticing things like time dilation or the relativistic Doppler effect. But what if c—the speed of light—was slower? What if instead of 299,792,458 meters per second, it was… say, 1.38 meters per second? That’s exactly 5 km (3.11 miles) per hour, and it’s the value chosen by developer Dmitry Brant for a project he’s called Relativity Park. The project simulates walking around an environment where the speed of light is slow enough for relativistic effects to become noticeable the moment you begin moving. The simulation defaults to setting c at 5 km/h—a value Brant chose because it is, as he puts it, a “brisk walking speed”— but you can increase it as far as 40 km/h or drop it right down to 1 km/h, which is faster than a sloth, but not much else. Whatever value you choose for c, you’ll find that your own speed can never reach that value—that’s the nature of our universe, after all. The first thing you’ll notice as soon as you begin to move is that the lighting of the scene changes. This is because of an optical version of the Doppler effect. If you move forwards, you’ll start catching up to the light ahead of you. From your perspective, this will result in the light’s wavelength being compressed and the light appearing to be shifted toward the blue end of the spectrum, in the same way that an ambulance’s siren sounds higher as it approaches you. If you move backward, the opposite is true; light ahead of you now has trouble catching up with you, making its wavelength appear stretched and its color more red. Both effects become more extreme as your speed gets closer and closer to c. As you accelerate, you’ll also notice other visual distortion—while you’re accelerating, you don’t actually seem to move toward the objects in the distance. It’s not until you stop accelerating and coast that you actually appear to be moving. This is due to length contraction, a phenomenon whereby objects traveling at significant proportions of the speed of light appear to be contracted to inertial observers, while to those traveling at relativistic speeds, the opposite is true. (There are excellent explanations of this to be found at Minute Physics and The Science Asylum.) Finally, the bottom right corner of the screen provides two clocks: your own, and a “world clock” that functions as the perspective of someone observing you from an inertial frame of reference. These demonstrate perhaps the most famous relativistic effect: time dilation. You’ll notice that as you move faster and faster, there’s an increasing discrepancy between your clock and the world clock; from your perspective, time continues to pass at its “normal” speed, but the observer’s clock ticks faster and faster. If you book it to, say, the train tracks in the distance then turn around and travel at the same speed back again, you’ll find that significantly more time has passed on the world clock than on yours. (As an aside: is it fascinating that our brains can see similar sorts of effects on psychedelics? Why yes. Yes, indeed it is.) Relativity Park isn’t the first project to play with this idea; in 2012, MIT’s Game Lab released a game called A Slower Speed of Light based around the same concept. Brant acknowledge the influence of this project, but explains that he wanted to “make something much more lightweight: plain javascript and WebGL, usable in a web app.” And because this is 2026, the project is largely vibe coded—but if you’re going to use Claude for something, well, you could do worse than an accessible demonstration of one of the crown jewels of the human intellect.

item.title: Bitcoin’s Network Hashrate Is 50% Below Trend as Miners Shift to AI
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 6.32
Over the past year, the bitcoin mining industry has undergone a massive shift toward artificial intelligence. In an effort to secure reliable revenue streams without relying entirely on the price of bitcoin, operators have begun repurposing their infrastructure, with some having sold off their bitcoin holdings and mining hardware to transition entirely into high-performance computing. Meanwhile, others have opted to simply diversify their data centers, selling off all or part of their bitcoin reserves while also reallocating power capacity to maintain the overall health of their businesses. This diversification into AI has allowed bitcoin miners to land lucrative deals, such as TeraWulf’s 20-year data-center lease with Anthropic, which could potentially generate upwards of $19 billion in revenue. As more operators decide to shut down their mining rigs in search of AI profits, Bitcoin’s network hashrate has fallen well below its prior growth path. However, despite the diversification of miners into the AI industry, the long-term prospects of the bitcoin mining industry and the crypto asset itself remain strong. Historic, But Not Unprecedented According to a second-quarter bitcoin mining report from digital asset manager CoinShares, the total processing power of the Bitcoin network, known as the hashrate, is currently sitting roughly 50% below its expected growth trend. While significant, the report also noted that these sorts of post-halving contractions align with normal patterns seen at this point in past halving cycles. That said, this most recent drop represents the longest sustained decline in network hashrate since China banned bitcoin mining in 2021. Despite a reduction in competition caused by miners taking their hardware offline, production costs remain elevated across the sector. Luke Nolan, Senior Ethereum Research Associate at CoinShares, noted in the report that the weighted average ex-tax cash cost to produce one bitcoin among listed miners reached approximately $75,500 during the second quarter. In fact, some operators faced production costs exceeding $100,000 per bitcoin when the asset was trading below $60,000 at the end of June. However, the asset has since mounted a significant recovery and rebounded sharply in recent weeks, climbing back up near $78,000 amidst concerns around U.S. Treasury Department buyback policies and increased sanctions that highlight U.S. dominance over the global financial system. The Premium on Existing Datacenters A major catalyst driving the AI pivot is the growing difficulty of constructing new data infrastructure. “A new constraint has emerged in the US that we believe is fundamentally repricing the asset base of listed miners: it is becoming increasingly difficult to build new data centres at all,” Nolan wrote in the report. “The market has responded by placing a substantial premium on capacity that already exists.” That premium has pushed some companies to abandon mining commitments altogether. For example, Core Scientific paid $41.9 million to cancel its agreement with Block’s Proto division, walking away from roughly 15 EH/s of next-generation 3nm mining chip deliveries to prioritize AI infrastructure instead. A Bitcoin Bull Market Could Reverse This Trend Despite the recent dip in processing power, Nolan emphasized that the shift does not signal systemic failure for Bitcoin. Instead, public miners are simply pivoting toward a “lucrative and seemingly secular tailwind” in artificial intelligence. With network hashrate already bouncing back from earlier 2026 lows, it’s clear plenty of operators still view bitcoin mining as economically viable, which suggests the network could begin its next typical growth cycle ahead of the next halving event in 2028. Alongside the AI compute rush, the CoinShares report attributes the hashrate drop to rising Texas energy costs seen at the beginning of the year. According to the report, high-performance computing currently generates roughly $1.5 million per megawatt annually compared to just $500,000 for Bitcoin mining. “A sustained rise in the bitcoin price could alter this calculus dramatically, however, and prompt some miners to recommit capacity to mining,” the report added. Of course, those who have already completely pivoted and gone all-in on AI would find it much more difficult to return to bitcoin mining in a scenario where the crypto asset’s price appears headed for new all-time highs once again.

item.title: Kalshi’s AI Compute Price Tracker Reportedly Pulled Over National Security Concerns
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 5.68
The Trump administration reportedly shut down part of Kalshi’s effort to establish a futures market for AI compute. Citing people familiar with the matter, Semafor reported on Tuesday that the U.S. Commerce Department ordered Kalshi last month to take down a product tracking the future price of AI compute. According to Semafor, Commerce officials cited national security concerns when they told Kalshi to remove what the company called its compute forward curves. Kalshi launched the forward curves in July for Nvidia’s B200, H200, and A100 chips. The charts were designed to serve as benchmarks showing the market’s implied future price for renting one hour of a particular GPU. The curves themselves were not tradable. Instead, they were built using data from Kalshi’s underlying markets on weekly and monthly GPU rental prices. Kalshi pitched the benchmarks as a reference for neoclouds, data centers, hyperscalers, and AI labs negotiating compute deals. Companies could also use the underlying markets to hedge against future changes in compute prices, similar to how companies and traders already use commodity futures to manage the risk of rising or falling oil prices. “Compute is the new oil. Like every commodity before it, it needs a real derivatives market,” said Kalshi CEO Tarek Mansour in a press release at the time. “Demand for AI is only going to increase. Kalshi intends to be the exchange where all future buyers and sellers manage their risk.” Semafor reported that Kalshi quietly complied with Commerce’s request, although many of the underlying markets that allow users to trade on future compute prices remain open. It’s not entirely clear why the Commerce Department is worried about the benchmarks. But market participants told Semafor that one concern is that the thinly traded compute market could be manipulated to make it look like prices for older chips are falling, potentially affecting AI stocks and the industry overall. Semafor separately reported that the Commerce Department also pushed the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) to freeze approval of new compute derivatives contracts for 60 days. Around the same time, the CFTC announced in August that it was opening a 60-day public comment period on compute derivatives. “America cannot win the AI race without a robust derivatives market for compute,” said CFTC Chairman Michael S. Selig. “Just as American markets helped establish the gold standard for trading the commodities that powered the industrial economy, we will do the same for the commodity that will power the intelligence economy. This request for comment is the first step toward establishing clear rules of the road for American compute markets.” Kalshi declined to comment. Meanwhile, the Commerce Department did not immediately respond to Gizmodo’s request for comment. However, a department spokesperson told Semafor that the story was false and that Commerce “has never once asked Kalshi to take down this market or any other markets.”

item.title: Polar Ice Sheets Have Lost 11 Trillion Tons of Ice—and ‘Speeding’ Glaciers Are Driving the Loss
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 5.62
As greenhouse gas emissions push Earth’s temperature to new heights, polar ice sheets are rapidly melting away. Numerous studies have sought to estimate ice loss from Greenland and Antarctica, but one team of researchers may have just produced the most comprehensive analysis to date. A study published today in the journal Scientific Data presents the longest satellite record of polar ice loss ever assembled. The findings reveal that the Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets have lost an enormous amount of mass over the last 50 years and have become key drivers of sea level rise, and that’s just the tip of the iceberg. “What’s really interesting is that we can see that there’s a long-term trend that glaciers are flowing faster, and so you have more and more ice discharge,” lead author Inès Otosaka, an assistant professor at Northumbria University who also works at the U.K. Centre for Polar Observation and Monitoring, told Gizmodo. 11 trillion tons of ice lost There are dozens of satellites that observe Greenland and Antarctica, and scientists around the world use these observations to track polar ice loss. According to Otosaka, there are about 50 published estimates of mass loss from these two ice sheets, but they are based on different satellite datasets that have been processed in slightly different ways. “What we really wanted to do is to produce a very comprehensive and robust estimate,” Otosaka said. “By combining all of those different independent estimates, we can then come up with one dataset and assessment of how the ice sheets have evolved over the past five decades.” To that end, she and her colleagues compared and combined 42 independent estimates of ice sheet mass balance (the net difference between the total mass gained and the total mass lost) derived from satellite observations of ice sheet flow, volume, and gravitational attraction over time. This allowed them to estimate how much mass Greenland and Antarctica’s ice sheets have lost since the 1970s. The researchers found that the two ice sheets lost a combined 11.3 trillion tons of ice between 1979 and 2023. “It is a huge number,” Otosaka said. “If you put that into context, it’s about enough ice to fill a cube that would be 23 kilometers [14 miles] in height.” Her team estimates that this ice loss has raised global average sea levels by about 1 inch (3 centimeters). That may not sound like much, but it shows that Greenland and Antarctica have become key drivers of sea level rise in recent years, according to Otosaka. Early in the satellite record, the ice sheets contributed relatively little to sea level rise. Now, they are responsible for about one-quarter of the global average increase. Discharge is the main driver The mechanism behind this ice loss is perhaps even more surprising than the scale. Ice sheets gain mass only through snowfall accumulation, but they can lose mass through two different processes: surface melting (driven by atmospheric temperatures) and outflow (driven by ocean temperatures). “Here we really found that the main cause of ice loss from the ice sheets is the latter, where you have glaciers that are flowing faster into the ocean,” Otosaka explained. Indeed, she and her colleagues found that 84% of the combined ice loss from Greenland and Antarctica stemmed from glaciers pouring more ice into the ocean, with just 16% due to surface melting. Looking at each ice sheet separately reveals some differences. Ice loss from both Greenland and Antarctica has accelerated significantly since the 1990s, but Greenland saw its biggest losses in the 2010s, when several extreme summer melt events occurred. Surface melting remains a major driver of Greenland’s ice loss, accounting for about one-third of the total. The remaining two-thirds comes from ice discharge, according to Otosaka. Antarctica’s melt rate also surged in the 2010s, but its net mass loss was entirely due to ocean-driven melting of its outlet glaciers. In fact, the speed of outflow from West Antarctica, driven by Pine Island and Thwaites glaciers, has risen in every decade of the satellite record. Between 2020 and 2023, record snowfall over East Antarctica and milder Greenland summers led to a temporary slowdown of mass loss from both ice sheets. Still, Otosaka emphasizes that the record shows a clear trend of glaciers flowing faster, so while snowfall and atmospheric temperatures can mitigate or exacerbate ice mass loss, discharge remains the long-term driver. Overall, the findings highlight polar ice sheets as a growing contributor to global sea level rise and help scientists better understand what’s driving their mass loss. Next, Otosaka’s team plans to estimate Greenland and Antarctica’s ice loss on a regional scale, “because we know that some parts of the ice sheets are responding differently,” she said.

item.title: Earth May Be Hoarding a Secret Water Stash 1,800 Miles Beneath Our Feet
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 5.17
Water is fundamental to life on Earth. Yet for all its importance, scientists still do not have a complete picture of where Earth’s water came from in the first place. Now, a new study suggests that the planet’s mantle could be hiding an ancient water reservoir, potentially preserving some of the water that dates back to Earth’s formation billions of years. A team of scientists identified two previously unknown iron compounds capable of storing water under the extreme pressures and temperatures found deep inside Earth. The findings, published in Nature Geoscience, offer new clues to our understanding of Earth’s water cycle and interior structure. Hidden reservoir Water plays a surprisingly important role deep inside Earth; it affects the movement of tectonic plates, helps drive volcanism, and changes how rocks behave. It isn’t necessarily there as liquid water. Instead, much of it is chemically bound inside minerals in the crust and mantle. Until now, however, scientists weren’t sure which minerals can store water over long periods under the extreme conditions of the deep mantle. To help solve the mystery of Earth’s stored water, the scientists behind the new study recreated the extreme pressure and temperature conditions found deep within the Earth’s interior in the lab. The researchers compressed tiny samples between two diamonds and heated them with lasers, reaching pressures around two million times the atmospheric pressure at Earth’s surface and temperatures of about 4,500 Fahrenheit (2,500 degrees Celsius). Those conditions are similar to ones found around 1,800 miles (2,900 kilometers) below the surface. Under these extreme conditions, two previously unknown iron oxyhydroxides—Fe5O12Hx and Fe7O12Hx—had formed. The new compounds formed not only from water-rich starting materials but also from samples containing almost no water. “It appears that even very small amounts of hydrogen are sufficient for these water-rich iron compounds to form,” Leonid Dubrovinsky, a researcher at the Bavarian Research Institute of Experimental Geochemistry and Geophysics (BGI) at the University of Bayreuth and one of the authors of the new study, said in a statement. Ancient clues The iron oxyhydroxides are capable of capturing and retaining water across a wide range of lower-mantle conditions and can host both primordial and recycled water, according to the study. “These minerals could also store water that is transported deep into Earth by the movement of tectonic plates. Because the compounds are very dense, they would likely remain near the core-mantle boundary and retain water there over geological timescales,” Man Lianjie, a former doctoral student at BGI and one of the authors of the study, said in a statement. While the recent experiment suggests the new compounds are ideal candidates for storing water deep within Earth’s mantle, it doesn’t necessarily demonstrate that they occur naturally in our planet’s interior. Still, the findings offer new clues as to where Earth’s ancient water may be hiding.

item.title: This Bouncy Castle Spread a Dangerous Superbug to 47 Kids in a Single Afternoon
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 5.07
As anyone who’s spent time inside one can tell you, bouncy castles are supposed to be a source of joy. Unfortunately, for one large party of kids in the Republic of Ireland, their bouncy experience led them to contract a dangerous, drug-resistant bacterial infection. Irish health officials detailed the world’s worst party in a report earlier this month. Dozens of children and teens were infected by a strain of meticillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, or MRSA, with nearly all cases directly linked to playing inside a bounce house. Though several children were hospitalized as a result, none died. “This was an unusual and complex community outbreak of MRSA SSTI in children and adolescents following a social event in eastern Ireland, linked to bouncy castle play,” the authors wrote in their report, published last week in the journal Eurosurveillance. Bouncy MRSA MRSA is one of the most infamous and worrisome examples of antibiotic resistance. These bacteria usually cause skin or soft tissue infections, and they can shrug off the most common drugs used to treat staph. Some strains have acquired even more resistance to the few remaining last-resort options available. Like many superbugs, MRSA cases are typically found in hospitals or other healthcare facilities, but we’re starting to see it appear more often elsewhere in the greater community. According to the report, this particular outbreak occurred sometime in the fall of 2025. The Department of Public Health for the Health Service Executive Dublin and Midlands region was alerted to the case of a 12-year-old boy who had been hospitalized with MRSA. The boy recounted that he had been to a party nine days earlier. Officials then reached out to the children and families who had attended the party. Ultimately, officials uncovered 22 confirmed and 26 probable cases of MRSA among partygoers, none of whom were adults. The children experienced various symptoms of a skin infection, including spots, pustules, redness, and blisters; some also developed a fever, nausea, and vomiting. Four children were hospitalized, though none suffered severe complications. All but one case spent time playing in the bouncy castle set up at the party, while the other remaining case had close contact with one of the latter children. Most fell sick within a day or two after the party, though one child only became ill 17 days later. An unprecedented outbreak This outbreak was noteworthy for several reasons. For starters, it’s the largest ever outbreak of community-acquired MRSA ever reported in Ireland, according to the authors, and it seems to be the first outbreak of this size ever linked to a bounce house. Officials opted not to test the bouncy castle equipment for signs of the bacteria, fearing too much time had passed to collect a viable sample. But given the proximity and timing of cases, they concluded that it was almost certainly the primary vector of transmission. It’s likely one or more people with a symptomatic infection who played in the bounce house contaminated the equipment, which then infected others, they determined. The infection’s spread was also probably aided by the warm, humid, and occasionally rainy weather that day and by the fact that many children spent hours playing inside the bouncy castle (at least 24 kids reported spending three or more hours playing). The outbreak was successfully contained through contact tracing and support of the affected cases, the officials say, which included notifying the local primary school about the need to temporarily keep infected cases at home. The company that provided the bouncy castle was also advised to not reuse their equipment again until it was adequately disinfected. Though this outbreak was corralled, it’s perhaps a sign that superbugs like MRSA are making their presence more felt in the community. And while a bounce house may not be the most obvious place to get such infections, it’s one that people should know about, the authors say. “Public health practitioners should be aware of the risk of CA-MRSA outbreaks in contexts involving prolonged, close physical contact, such as play activities and contact sport,” they wrote.

item.title: New Humanoid Worker Bot Seems to Cower When It Encounters Humans
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 5.01
I live in a neighborhood with a lot of delivery bots, and I can’t stand having to move even one inch out of the way to let one pass. If robots must be around, I would ideally like them to avoid making their presence known at all. With that in mind, the folks at Agility Robotics are on the right track with their new Digit 5 humanoid robot, perhaps the first humanoid robot programed to strenuously avoid getting in the way of human beings. Watch how it ducks down low in what may not be, but nonetheless looks like, a display of deep respect for humanity: Speaking to Ars Technica, Agility’s chief technology officer, Pras Velagapudi, said Digit 5 “was designed with a complex safe motion system that can take a variety of different mitigations depending on exactly what sort of human presence is detected.” According to Agility’s September 15 press release for Digit 5, the robot makes use of “proprietary AI algorithms and multiple sensor technologies to continuously monitor for people and take appropriate action by autonomously avoiding, stopping or assuming a seated position.” It’s clear from the release, which boasts about “65,000 hours of operation and commercial deployments,” that Agility wants its devices to be perceived as ready for normal workplaces, and it frequently name checks the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) in marketing materials. In November of last year, an earlier version of Digit—one you might remember for it’s unsettlingly satyr-like backwards knees—was subjected to a safety test touted by a company release as “OSHA-recognized.” It apparently passed that inspection. As humanoid robots have come to prominence—particularly those Unitree robots that dazzle audiences with pre-programmed dancing and martial arts movements—it’s become common to see clips on social media of humanoids hurting people. If they’re going to be legitimately useful for companies like Hyundai who say they plan to mingle humans and humanoid robots in workplaces, the companies (and their insurers) really do need to be confident that the robots won’t be an OSHA nightmare. Agility’s release quotes CEO Peggy Johnson as saying her company is “removing a major barrier to scaling humanoid robots in industrial environments.” And the robot itself is not just designed to duck when a human gets near. The release makes it sound ready to work, with a 90-minute battery life, and the ability to lift 50-pounds and reach shelves up to 7.2 feet high. Currently, it’s not uncommon for robots in workplaces to be sequestered in cages with elaborate, multi-step locking and shutdown procedures. Judging from the elaborate safety maneuvers on display from Digit 5, it’s taking an awful lot to convince companies that it’s okay to free the humanoid robots from their cages.

item.title: Rumored Round of Funding Could Make OpenAI More Valuable Than Anthropic Again. Perhaps Briefly
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 4.90
Insiders are claiming that OpenAI may soon receive a funding round valuing it at $1.2 trillion, according to the Financial Times. The intriguingly timed round could give OpenAI a higher valuation than its rival Anthropic once again, though it could also come around the same time as Anthropic’s IPO. The decision to give OpenAI this capital injection “will hinge on exactly when OpenAI decides to go public,” the Financial Times writes. In an interview published in Fortune this past weekend, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said the company would not go public in 2026. Altman cited safety concerns as a cause, saying his company has “a lot of stuff to do” as it tackles model alignment, and that sorting out such nagging issues is easier as a private company. OpenAI declined to comment to the Financial Times. OpenAI was once the clear leader in frontier AI. The release of OpenAI’s ChatGPT in 2022 made AI the focus of the tech industry. But Anthropic’s valuation surged past OpenAI’s over the past year, as business and productivity became the focus of the frontier AI companies, as opposed to scrapped projects like OpenAI’s video generator Sora. Viewed as a horserace measured in dollar amounts, the OpenAI-Anthropic rivalry breaks down like this: - Toward the beginning of last year, OpenAI was way, way ahead. March funding rounds valued OpenAI at $300 billion and Anthropic at $61.5 billion. - In September of last year, another money injection came along, placing Anthropic at $183 billion. The next month, an OpenAI funding round gave it a proportionally less dramatic valuation spike to $500 billion—though it kept its authoritative lead. - In February of this year—notably after the rise of the agentic platform OpenClaw—Anthropic stepped on the gas, getting itself valued at $380 billion. The following month, upon receiving an astonishing commitment of $122 billion, OpenAI’s valuation ascended to $852 billion. - But then in May, Anthropic exploded past OpenAI with a funding round valuing it at $965 billion. So if OpenAI’s rumored funding round succeeds, and values the company at $1.2 trillion, it might—perhaps only briefly—retake the top spot. I say “briefly” because anonymously sourced reports on Anthropic’s IPO say that investors are targeting a $2 billion valuation once it’s a public company. According to anonymous insiders who spoke to Reuters, the IPO is expected in the middle of next month.

item.title: 71% of Americans Say They’re Completely Exhausted
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 4.88
If you’ve felt a complete sense of exhaustion lately, join the club. New research from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention shows that fatigue is running rampant in the good ol’ U.S. of A. CDC scientists examined nationally representative data of Americans across the country. Nearly three-quarters of people over 18 reported they felt fatigued in the past three months, they found, while over 15% felt fatigued most or all of the time. People with frequent fatigue were also substantially more likely to have other health problems, including depression. “This report provides a unique look at the prevalence and distribution of fatigue symptoms that are not condition-specific in the general U.S. population,” the authors wrote in their paper, published this month by the CDC’s National Center for Health Statistics. The fatigued states of America Though everyone feels tired from time to time, fatigue is a state of extreme exhaustion that doesn’t necessarily improve with rest or sleep. It can be the primary sign of a persistent medical issue, as with myalgic encephalomyelitis (also known as chronic fatigue syndrome), or a symptom of acute, self-limiting illnesses like the flu. According to the CDC researchers, studies looking at the prevalence of fatigue have typically focused on smaller groups of people with specific medical conditions, such as cancer. For this study, the researchers wanted to measure fatigue more broadly in the general public. To do so, they turned to data from the 2024 version of the National Health Interview Survey, a long-running survey of Americans’ reported medical conditions, health care use, and other health-related behaviors conducted by the U.S. Census Bureau. The researchers defined fatigue in this study as people saying yes when asked if they had felt “very tired or exhausted.” In 2024, a total of 71.5% of respondents said they were fatigued in the preceding three months. Of these, 54.9% said they had fatigue some days, 10.7% said it was most days, and 5.9% felt it every day. A majority of people with frequent fatigue said they felt it most (34.5%) or all of the day (20.2%). Based on the overall U.S. adult population, that would amount to about 190 million people who have recently experienced at least some fatigue. As often the case with health problems, the risk of fatigue wasn’t evenly distributed in the population. Women were more likely to report frequent fatigue than men (20% compared to 13%), for instance, as were the youngest adults (roughly 19% of people ages 18 to 34 compared to 13% of people over 65). Indigenous populations had the highest rates of frequent fatigue compared to other racial demographics; people in the southern U.S. had the highest regional rates; the poorest Americans had the highest rates compared to other wealth groups; and people in rural areas had higher rates than those living in large and medium-sized cities. The burden of fatigue Unfortunately, people with frequent fatigue often face other challenges, the authors note. Nearly 90% reported having trouble in at least one out of nine areas related to healthy functioning, for instance, such as difficulty concentrating, being unable to take care of their basic needs like washing or dressing themselves, or mental health symptoms like depression and anxiety. More than half said they had trouble in three or more of these areas, compared to about 17% of adults without frequent fatigue who said the same. About 29% of frequent fatigue sufferers also reported having limitations participating in social activities, and 36% reported having workplace limitations. The findings are based on people’s self-reported feelings of fatigue, which can be subjective. Also, this study is cross-sectional, meaning it only looked at a snapshot of people’s current health. As such, it’s not possible to tell which factors might be contributing to people’s fatigue, or vice versa. Some people’s fatigue might worsen their pre-existing depression symptoms, for instance, or a separate condition might be responsible for a person’s fatigue and their other issues (the authors cite the example of a person recovering from a stroke). What this study does show is that fatigue is a widespread problem among Americans and that frequent fatigue can be especially disruptive to a person’s life.

item.title: Kids of 2026 Make Futuristic Predictions That Are Very Similar to the Kids of 50 Years Ago
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 4.62
When American kids of the mid-1970s were asked what the year 2000 might look like, a quarter century into the future, it was a bizarre mix of ideas. There were the optimistic predictions, like robot servants, living in undersea habitats, and bionic limbs. But there were also the incredibly pessimistic predictions, including worries about World War III, shortages of consumer goods, and people thrown out of work. Does this strange mix sound familiar? It should to anyone who’s talked with a child recently. The New York Times recently asked a handful of 10-year-olds to predict what life might look like in 2050, 24 years from now. Their hopes and fears sound remarkably similar to those expressed by kids in the 1970s. Below, I’ve put together some of the predictions from 10-year-olds today next to predictions that I’ve compiled over the years from kids in 1976 and 1977. It was a common time for predictions, given the U.S. Bicentennial, and these predictions were published in newspapers across the country as well as in a time capsule called the Tricentennial Report. For example, the illustration above showing a mushroom cloud that presumably kicked off World War III was drawn in 1976 by a high school kid in New York. Bionic limbs The idea of supplementing the human body with robotic parts has a long history, dating to at least the 1920s. By the 1970s, the TV show The Six Million Dollar Man was more likely to be the inspiration for kids about what the future might look like. (1976) Cindy Wade of Texas: In the year 2000, your doctors might discover a way to make bionic arms and legs so that if you have an accident and you lose an arm, or a leg the doctors can replace it with a new one. (2026) Grant VanHooser of Napa Valley, California: People will have the choice to have robot body parts. Bionic limbs have advanced tremendously in recent years, with some now able to provide neural feedback. In many respects, the future imagined by those kids in 1976 has already arrived. World War III Kids growing up in the 1970s were well aware of the devastation wrought by the Vietnam War. Some projected those anxieties into the future with visions of space war to come. (1976) Billy McPherson of Texas: Our space and areo-space divisions are ready for World War III coming soon. Naturally, the kids of 2026 are viewing the Iran War similarly, though the kid who spoke with the New York Times didn’t imagine the war would make it to space. (2026) Riley Grunch, Gainesville, Georgia: There’s bound to be a war. The war against Iran right now is bound to spark a couple more wars. I really hope it doesn’t start World War III. The U.S. military confirmed for the first time on Monday that it’s deployed weapons in space. The 1970s kids may have been on to something. Robot servants The idea of building your own robotic servant predates not just Rosey from The Jetsons but even the word “robot” itself, which was coined in the 1920s. The kids of the 1970s believed that students of the future would have robot teachers, and yes, robot maids. (1976) Mary Bohen of Steubenville, Ohio: In the year 2000, we will have all round buildings. We will have a robot teacher, a robot maid, and all workers will be robots, too. We will have a pocket computer that has everything you can name. We will even be able to push a button to get anything you want! Kids of the 2020s are growing up in a world where AI dominates the conversation, so it’s only natural that you’d see any discussion of robots include that element heavily. (2026) Amani Green of Denver, Colorado: Higher-class citizens will start owning robot butlers. But I feel like with the rise of robot butlers, humans will start to lose competence and basic everyday skills. The caveat that “higher-class citizens” would own robot butlers brings an interesting nuance to the discussion. Whereas kids of the 20th century largely thought everyone would have robots by the year 2000, kids of 2026 perhaps understand that the future will not be evenly distributed, as sci-fi author William Gibson pointed out. Living Under the Ocean The kids of 1976 seemed to believe that humans would be able to live in the ocean thanks to underwater habitats, which became a popular idea in futuristic kids’ books of the 1960s. The TV show The Undersea World of Jacques Cousteau premiered in 1968 and ran through 1976, which no doubt contributed to a broader interest in the future of the ocean. (1976) Elida Buenrosta of Texas: How are you? Fine? 2000 might be living under the ocean. What might be happening in the year of 2000. Maybe they have horses instead of cars, trucks and airplanes. They might ride horses to the groceries and by me food for them. They might have spaceships over there. What else might be happening in the year 2000. There is something else happening there than that. They might ride horses to work and go to restaurants over there when they are at. They might even have carts to go with horses. (2026) Sarah Fink of Denver, Colorado: I want to live in the ocean, honestly. I want to be an architect, designing homes underwater — coral-friendly hotels and apartments and homes. They’ll have underwater taxis, too. Or you could swim. That would be like walking. Work in the future The rise of AI has devastated the younger generations that are looking for work. And at least one kid from 1977 predicted youth unemployment would skyrocket in the future. (1977) Pietro Sincropi, Steubenville, Ohio: I think by the year 2000 we will be riding bikes or driving solar-energized cars. By then more younger people will be unemployed. The price of gas will go up and so will the price of coal, silver, gold and oil. The kids of today are perhaps more in tune with the anger that comes with that. (2026) Amani Green of Denver, Colorado: New York Times: What’s life going to be like in 2050? Companies will start using A.I. instead of human workers. That’s probably going to cause a pretty big job shortage. Times: What kinds of jobs will A.I. take? People are already starting to hire an A.I. actress for movies. So people are going to be like, “That’s making so much money, I should do that!” That’ll make a lot of actors pretty mad. Times: What will happen to people who lose jobs to A.I.? Lots of anger. Probably protests. Just lots of outrage. Travel to the Moon and Mars The predictions from the 1970s and 2020s are anecdotes rather than a scientifically designed poll. But they still provide insights into what kids are thinking about. Perhaps most interestingly, none of the kids the Times spoke with here in 2026 seemed to volunteer the idea that they’d be traveling to the Moon or Mars. That was a much more common idea in the 1970s. One child of today, Liam Kwon from Queens, talked about what people might do in space, but only after he was prompted by the interviewer at the New York Times: New York Times: Will people go to space? In the old days, they paid Americans to go to the West. They might pay people to go to space, because the population is so big that there might not be enough room. The kids of the 1970s not only talked about traveling in spaceships; they specifically mentioned women becoming astronauts. Tim Villies of Ohio wrote in 1977: The year 2000 may send ladies to the moon to explore and look and see if there are people living on the moon. And when you work you will push buttons and robots will come out and do the work for you. In 1963, Soviet cosmonaut Valentina Tereshkova became the first woman in space, but Sally Ride wouldn’t become the first American female astronaut until 1983. NASA has received criticism for the planned Artemis III mission, which launches next year and will include only men. Similar challenges The 1970s posed unique challenges for kids who were imagining what the future might look like compared to the generations of Americans that had come before them. U.S. troops left Vietnam for good in 1975 after a prolonged and costly war where Americans ultimately lost. President Richard Nixon had resigned in 1974, and cynicism about politics was naturally becoming the norm. There was also the prospect of nuclear war between the U.S. and the Soviet Union that hung over kids of the 1970s. The corruption of Richard Nixon almost seems quaint for those of us living through the Trump era. Our current president has put his own face on money, plastered his name on government-owned buildings, and enriched himself by at least $2.2 billion last year. There is no U.S. precedent for what we’re living through but you can still see how kids of the 1970s were struggling in similar ways. Oil was at the center of American problems in the 1970s, and many of the predictions expected that life would get worse unless humanity could move on from fossil fuels. While the use of alternative energy has exploded in popularity, the world is still largely dependent on the oil that’s currently sitting on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz. Every generation faces unique challenges. But it’s rather striking to see how many similarities there are when we compare the kids of the 2020s to the kids of fifty years ago. One small difference may be catastrophizing about terrorism against U.S. targets, not just dying in a nuclear war. The kids of 2026 don’t remember the terror attacks of 9/11 because they weren’t born yet, but they’re well aware of terrorism, even if it’s just because of the school shooter drills they’re forced to do. Young Mary Foster of New Jersey told the New York Times that “I think Mount Rushmore is going to fall down,” because “Someone’s going to bomb it or something.”

item.title: Meta’s Next Pair of Smart Glasses May Drastically Tone Down the Creep Factor
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 4.54
Meta’s smart glasses are controversial for an increasing number of reasons at this point, but the biggest reason is easily the cameras. Cameras on your face, as it turns out, can be used for all sorts of unsavory stuff, but there is one way to prevent that, and it’s by removing them from the equation entirely. According to a report from The Information, that’s exactly what Meta is planning to do with a new generation of smart glasses codenamed Luna that might launch next week during Meta Connect, the company’s annual hardware showcase. Luna, The Information reports, do not have cameras, but they do have microphones, which act as a pathway to Meta’s AI. Using a voice assistant, anyone wearing Meta’s new camera-less smart glasses would reportedly be able to interface with Muse, Meta’s new AI model that lives on its current line of first-party and Ray-Ban-branded smart glasses. In addition to AI features, Luna will also have speakers, which separates them from other camera-less smart glasses like those made by Even Realities. With the exclusion of a camera, Luna might also be a bit smaller, with slimmer arms, presenting more as a regular pair of glasses, which is, again, similar to Even Realities, though unlike the Even G2, Luna doesn’t appear to have any screen inside. If Luna is truly in the works, it’s clear that Meta is taking a blanket approach to its smart glasses offerings, which makes a lot of sense. As desirable as having a camera on a pair of smart glasses is to some, it’s also a major liability. Camera glasses are getting banned in all sorts of places, including courts, popular restaurants and bars, and even in some public spaces. There’s also the perception problem. While some people may not mind the idea of walking around with cameras on people’s faces, the idea viscerally offends others. One quick way to circumvent any potential backlash is by getting rid of the one thing that people know to look for and hate on principle. According to The Information, there’s a chance that Luna may be announced next week at Meta Connect with a hard launch in October, so if the company does indeed have camera-less smart glasses in the hopper, I’ll be there to show you exactly what they can and cannot do.

item.title: ‘The Last of Us’ Season 3 Is Now Likely to Be the Show’s End
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 4.50
There was always a question of how much Last of Us we would be getting. Before even a single episode of the show aired, co-creator Craig Mazin was being asked about how many seasons were planned and whether it could go above and beyond the story of the video games. Later, he even floated the idea of a season four, though season two’s structure seemed to suggest a potential end. And now, one of the people who would definitely know has weighed in. Speaking to Deadline after the Emmys, HBO CEO Casey Bloys said that The Last of Us season three is coming at some point in 2027 and that “I think [showrunner] Craig [Mazin] has planned it as the final season.” Which, of course, is not a definitive statement, but it’s worth noting that Bloys was not as certain of Mazin’s plans as recently as earlier this year. Plus, if Mazin’s boss is under the impression season three is the end, it’s probably the end. If that is indeed the case, it makes sense on several levels. Season two of The Last of Us adapted the first half of The Last of Us Part II video game and season three is set to do the second half. That game, and the show, split its story between two characters, Ellie (Bella Ramsey) in this season and Abby (Kaitlyn Dever) in the upcoming season. That’s where the game series ends, at least for now. And with game and series creator Neil Druckmann no longer working on the show, adapting that second half of his game seems like a nice way to keep him involved in spirit. There’s also the simple fact that season two of The Last of Us didn’t light up the world in the way season one did. In large part, that’s probably due to the fact that season one starred one of the biggest movie stars out there, Pedro Pascal, and season two killed him off in an early episode. But Pascal probably wouldn’t have even done The Last of Us at all had that not been built into the DNA of the story. So he giveth and taketh away. Nevertheless, The Last of Us Part II video game is a hugely satisfying conclusion to the series (which is rumored to continue with a new game at some point), so if Mazin can capture that with season three, it’s better to go out on top. The last thing any of us want is five seasons of wheel-spinning. Three and out feels right. Want more io9 news? Check out the best movies and TV shows to stream this month and all the upcoming sci-fi, fantasy, and horror books that should be on your radar.

item.title: It’s a Long Shot, but Here’s How the Steam Frame Could Save VR
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 4.48
Valve’s Steam Frame is one of the last of a dying breed, an honest-to-god interesting example of gaming-focused headset tech in what’s become a slow drought of virtual reality. To save VR, Valve will have to pull out all the stops, and its saving grace may have something in common with many of the celebrities at the Emmys: accessories, accessories, accessories. The Steam Frame is built for wireless VR play, even though that’s diminished by its limited battery life when playing both 2D and virtual reality titles natively. It’s also an awkward device for any AR (augmented reality) content with its monochromatic IR passthrough cameras. However, we may be only scratching the surface of what we can do with the Steam Frame. Valve’s headset is secretly incredibly modular, and not just because it’s effectively a Linux PC you can wear on your face. At launch, the makers of Steam promoted a $150 plug-in accessory made by Arcturus that adds RGB color passthrough and 3D video capture capabilities. This extra doohickey is plugged into the front of the headset through its PCI-E expansion slot. You can see for yourself in hands-on videos how this accessory could allow for more mixed reality game options. More than that, it’s a device that allows for developers to expand what’s possible with Valve’s headset. The PCI-E slot means we could see even more third-party expansions to Steam Frame hardware, though we’ll have to hope somebody comes up with more interesting gear. Still, there are more independent makers thinking outside the box. While the Steam Frame doesn’t require any infrared “base stations” to track the headset or controllers, indie company Soulart is designing hardware-agnostic base stations it promised would be compatible with Valve’s headset. This is probably more suited for people keen on VRChat if you really need full-body tracking for your avatar’s fursuit (no hate to the VRChat denizens out there). At least, it proves there are other possibilities that show there’s still progress to be made for virtual reality. Valve itself has indicated it’s working on a separate expansion kit. The company told PCGamer it was going to craft a new headstrap with a hot-swappable battery and higher-end speakers, akin to what it had inside its Index headset from 2019. What’s important about all this modularity is that both players and developers may not have to keep waiting for next-gen headsets to arrive to find more interesting VR tech. No, this won’t finally make VR gaming truly mainstream, but it may help keep the flame alive for a few more years. Valve certainly has its legion of fans, but that $1,060 price tag is still going to stymie the Steam Frame from becoming anywhere as big as the Meta Quest was just a few years ago. Not to mention, the Steam Frame arrives just when multiple big companies seem to be losing all interest in VR. Sony seems to have all but given up on its PlayStation VR2 just three years after its launch. PCGuide was first to point out that practically all major online retailers, including PlayStation Direct, list the PSVR2 as out of stock or only available used or refurbished. Due in large part to the ongoing RAMpocalypse, VR hardware has languished with ever-expanding prices and fewer new games to play. The week before Valve could debut its $1,060 headset, longtime VR game developer Polyarc, creator of the beloved platformers Moss and Moss II, shut its doors. In prior months, Vertigo Games’ Amsterdam-based team—the developers behind the Metro Awakening VR title—also met its end due to how the “VR market remains a challenging space.” Meta may be crafting a new “Project Pheonix” glasses/headset hybrid that it could reveal at its Meta Connect conference Sept. 23. We have doubts that the device will be explicitly built with play in mind, and neither will Google and XReal’s Project Aura XR glasses. Valve won’t have an easy time keeping gaming VR going, but at this point, the Steam Frame may be virtual reality gamers’ best hope.

item.title: The US Put Weapons in Space. What Could Possibly Go Wrong?
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 3.88
Oh good, space has weapons now. The U.S. has publicly acknowledged for the first time that it has weapons in orbit, a decidedly less sci-fi development than it might sound. The admission comes as the Space Force gears up for a future in which satellites and other systems in orbit could face increasingly serious threats—and the decision to say it out loud may itself be part of the strategy. On Monday, U.S. Air Force Secretary Troy Meink confirmed that the U.S. deployed weapons to space to be prepared against existing threats. “The United States now has on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the joint force against hostile adversary action,” Meink said during a speech at the 2026 Air and Space Cyber Conference. The unusually candid statement comes as a surprise, with the U.S. military previously remaining vague when it comes to sharing information regarding its defense capabilities. While the purpose of the sudden admission remains unclear, the statement has already prompted a response from China warning against orbital warfare. Space wars In the past few years, U.S. officials have increasingly talked about offensive space capabilities and space-based interceptors. The recent admission, however, was far more explicit and seemingly more deliberate than any previous statement. Although the details of the on-orbit space weapons were not clear, Meink doubled down on his statement when asked about it later. “That phrase was very well thought out,” Meink said, according to SpaceNews. “So whatever I said before is what I say again.” Meink’s statement is an apparent transition from decades of proposals and official advocacy to an explicit public acknowledgment that the U.S. has operational weapons in orbit. Last year, President Donald Trump signed an executive order emphasizing the Space Force’s role not just in defense but as an active attacking and space-control force. In July, the Space Force deployed an electromagnetic warfare device designed to “detect, deny, disrupt, and degrade adversary capabilities” to create a so-called silence zone. As part of its Tactically Responsive Space (TacRS) program, the Space Force also pitted two satellites against each other in a simulated orbital threat scenario. Orbital threats The U.S. has become increasingly concerned about the growing space capabilities of nations like Russia and China, with officials warning of systems designed to disrupt, disable, or destroy satellites and other orbital assets. The surprising admission to having weapons of its own has prompted a response from the country’s rivals. “We urge the US side to stop expanding its military capabilities and preparing for war in outer space,” China’s foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun told a news briefing, according to AFP. Russia also called for space to be kept weapon-free. “We are counting on broad international consolidation to continue working toward the complete demilitarization of space,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on Tuesday. While talks of the militarization of space are nothing new, the U.S. has generally kept its arsenal under wraps. That’s why the recent move to publicly admit to having space weapons comes as a surprise. “I don’t think any US government official has ever said that before,” Victoria Samson, the Secure World Foundation’s chief director of space security and stability, told Defense One. “The US also now has to accept the Chinese and Russians doing/saying the same. I don’t think that this is going to be in the interest of US national security.” To be clear, the U.S. does not appear to be violating international agreements by developing conventional weapons for use in space (assuming these are conventional weapons). The 1967 Outer Space Treaty bans placing nuclear weapons and other weapons of mass destruction in orbit, but it does not ban all weapons in space.

item.title: Doctors Scanned This Man’s Chest and Found a Sewing Needle in His Heart
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 3.73
A 35-year-old man’s bloody urine turned out to have an explanation no one could have seen coming: sewing needles jammed into his body. Doctors in China described the unusual injury in a case report earlier this month. The man, who was intellectually disabled, had multiple needles inside his body, all likely self-inserted. The doctors were able to remove the one closest to his heart, and the man recovered. “Cardiac foreign bodies associated with presumed self insertion behaviors can be clinically occult and diagnostically challenging, particularly when a definitive history is difficult to obtain,” the authors wrote in their paper, published last week in BMC Cardiovascular Disorders. A needle surprise According to the report, the man visited doctors two weeks into having urinary pain and blood in his urine. Though he seemed fine otherwise, an initial imaging test revealed a shadow near his heart. Additional CT scans then uncovered the presence of multiple “needle-like metallic foreign bodies” throughout his body, including his abdominal wall, pelvis, bladder, and penis. One needle, about 1.4 inches long (36 millimeters), had pierced the pericardium, the fluid-filled sac that protects the heart; it was inside the left ventricle cavity and was found to be moving in sync with the heart chamber. The man was legally under the care of his father, who gave the doctors written informed consent to discuss the case. Neither the patient nor his family could confirm where the needles had come from, the doctors wrote. Two years earlier, the man visited another hospital, where doctors removed two needle-like objects from his abdomen; however, the medical records from this visit were not available. Despite the missing information, the doctors say the man had likely inserted all these needles himself. Though rare, people with intellectual disabilities are known to be at higher risk of engaging in this type of behavior, which can also include swallowing foreign objects. The man’s fate Though the man had many needles inside his body, some were in locations that carried a high risk of serious complications if doctors tried to surgically remove them. Ultimately, the team only decided to remove the most life-threatening needle near the heart, while planning to keep a close eye on the others for possible removal in the future. The surgery went well without any major problems, with the doctors removing an intact and black metallic sewing needle. Remarkably, they noted, the man’s chest wall showed no signs of an entry wound or scars, while the needle itself was corroded, both of which suggest that it had been inside the man’s heart cavity for quite a long time. The man’s heart function did drop significantly after the surgery, likely as a result of the needle’s damage to his body as well as the strain of the surgery. However, he did eventually improve and was discharged safely from the hospital. At a nine-month follow-up visit, the man appeared to be clinically stable. The doctors say these sorts of cases tend to be very complex, both due to the fact that patients with cognitive impairment might not be able to communicate their medical history well and the fact that such injuries aren’t necessarily easy to outwardly spot. Detecting these cases tends to require a “multimodal imaging strategy,” the doctors wrote. Needle heart cases in particular are also very rare. A 2024 review uncovered only 34 other cases in the medical literature dating back to the 1960s of people deliberately inserting sewing needles in their heart.

item.title: Apple Home’s AI Security Camera Features Are Opt-In, if You Can Afford Them
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 3.68
Apple has finally launched its big Siri AI upgrade for its entire software ecosystem, and for Apple Home users, that means big, AI-powered changes for how their security cameras might work. Happily, the company isn’t raising prices on the existing subscriptions that enable these features and thereby forcing customers who don’t want them to pay up anyway. But for those who do want to open their wallets, it’ll get expensive, fast. The new Apple Intelligence-powered security camera capabilities will only work for HomeKit Secure Video-compatible devices—recent examples include Aqara’s Camera Hub G350 and Doorbell Camera G400—and not those that only support live streaming through Apple Home, like those offered by Arlo. Happily, the features are opt-in, so those who want them will need to explicitly turn them on, either via a splash screen that may appear in the Home app after you update your 2nd-gen-or-later Apple TV 4K and/or HomePods to tvOS 27 or HomePod Software Version 27 (it didn’t, for me), or in the app’s Home Settings menu. After you update, you’ll get a new Apple Intelligence option in the Home Settings that contains a “Summarize Videos” toggle. Flip that on—then visit a sub-menu to pick which cameras you want it to work for—and you’ll get features like natural language search of footage and descriptive notification summaries that tell you what happened when a camera detected something. These descriptions are a lot more specific than before. I haven’t tested extensively yet, but a screenshotted summary from a story from The Verge about the update shows one description: “A cat walked by and walked through the yard. Birds walked around the yard. Chickens walked around the yard.” I don’t think I care about how many birds visited my yard, but I definitely like the idea of being able to search videos to find out if and when a package was delivered. The sting, if you’re interested in the AI security camera features, is in the pricing. You’ll need to pay for at least a $10-per-month, 2TB iCloud+ plan, which only covers a single camera. The price quickly skyrockets if you want to add more cameras. Apple charges $30 per month for a two-camera, 6TB iCloud+ plan and $60 for a 12TB subscription that includes up to five cameras. That’s a lot when compared to, say, the Google Home Premium Advanced plan, which is just $20 a month for similar features and carries no limit to the number of cameras it covers. It’s nice that Apple isn’t just cramming its AI features into its lower-tier plans and raising prices, the way Google did at first for its Google Home Premium plans. But unless you need all the extra iCloud storage and iCloud+ features like Private Relay and Hide My Email, those prices are hard pills to swallow. Still, rolling them into existing subscriptions and pricing tiers as optional features seems smart, considering the generative AI propensity for misinterpreting events or confidently presenting false information. I know I don’t want to specifically pay for a feature that might lie to me. All of this is subject to change. As Apple notes in a support page on its site, “Supported camera counts and other iCloud+ plan features may change over time.” The company doesn’t say whether the counts will go up or down, but based on the undefined limits in a separate Apple Intelligence Usage Terms page, it feels like the company is hedging against the potential for rising costs of generative AI affecting how much it’s willing to offer. iOS 27 and its related operating systems are all available now. To update your HomePods to HomePod Software Version 27, make sure your iPhone or iPad is already on iOS 27/iPadOS 27, then open the Apple Home app, tap a given HomePod, and look for an “Update” button at the top of the screen. For the Apple TV 4K, go to Settings > System > Software Updates and click “Update Software.”

item.title: Laika’s Final ‘Wildwood’ Trailer Is Filled With Pure Adventure
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 3.66
Again and again we’ve gone over just how incredible Laika’s new movie, Wildwood, looks. The visuals would be stunning in any medium, but the fact that they’re done in stop-motion animation almost doesn’t make sense. It all looks too beautiful for words. And yet, if those looks don’t advance an emotional story, it will all be for nothing. The final trailer for Wildwood was just released, and it sure looks like everything is coming together. Director Travis Knight (Kubo and the Two Strings, Masters of the Universe) has put together a stunning voice cast to help breathe life into this magical world. And here, in the final trailer, we see that world through the eyes of the characters as they go on the adventure of a lifetime. “After her baby brother is abducted by a murder of crows, headstrong teenager Prue McKeel (Peyton Elizabeth Lee) launches a desperate rescue mission into the Impassable Wilderness—an enchanted forest hidden just beyond Portland, Oregon,” Laika’s official description reads. “Joined by her hapless but loyal classmate Curtis Mehlberg (Jacob Tremblay), Prue navigates a world of talking animals, bandits, and powerful figures driven by grief and ambition. As the pair is drawn into a conflict threatening the balance of the forest itself, Prue must find a way to save her brother while confronting forces that could determine Wildwood’s future.” So who are behind some of those “talking animals, bandits, and powerful figures”? Well, there’s Carey Mulligan, Angela Bassett, Mahershala Ali, Richard E. Grant, Awkwafina, Amandla Stenberg, Tom Waits, Charlie Day, Blythe Danner, Maya Erskine, Jake Johnson, Rob Delaney, Jemaine Clement, Ólafur Darri Ólafsson, and many, many more. Not too bad. The trailer also announces that tickets are now on sale for the film, which is coming to theaters on October 23. Head to wildwoodmovie.com for more on that, and check io9 later today for your exclusive first look at some of the film’s upcoming collectibles. Want more io9 news? Check out the best movies and TV shows to stream this month and all the upcoming sci-fi, fantasy, and horror books that should be on your radar.

item.title: iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max Review: Apple Is Just Flexing Hard Now
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 3.53
How do you top the iPhone 17 Pro and 17 Pro Max, Apple’s two best—from a features standpoint—smartphones ever made? The iPhones that I called “practical perfection” with ”no compromises” because they put function before form? Not with one specific new feature, but with a bunch that really add up to an even better “Pro” iPhone experience. Somehow, Apple has added even longer battery life for both the iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max, with the smaller model now lasting nearly as long as last year’s biggest iPhone 17 Pro Max and the new larger phone almost impossible to deplete even with two full days of moderate use. Both new iPhones also have a new “variable aperture” main camera lens for more creative control and better low-light shooting, along with several camera settings, including manual-shooting controls and processing, that do not feel gimmicky. Performance from the A20 chip is monstrous, easily lapping flagship Android phones in speed and responsiveness, and without throttling or getting hot thanks to a larger vapor chamber than ever before. Not to mention, the iPhone 18 Pros have a smaller Dynamic Island. And three new colors, including the classy Burgundy, sleek Black, and relaxed Glacier, all with color-matched glass backs this time. It also comes in Silver, but it’s so basic. And if you’ve got the money to spend, you can pony up for a 2TB storage option, which is now available for both models, not just the Pro Max. iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max As far as I'm concerned, Apple's iPhone 18 and 18 Pro Max are its "Ultra" phones. Pros - Monstrous performance - Larger vapor chamber - Incredibly long battery life - Terrific overall cameras - Variable aperture on the main camera is legit - Manual camera controls - Smaller Dynamic Island - Classy Black and Burgundy colors Cons - Same easily bruisable aluminum - Camera Control doesn't support any of the new manual camera settings As I have done every September for the past 16 years, I spent a week testing the new iPhones. Are they worth spending $1,199 for the iPhone 18 Pro and $1,299 for the 18 Pro Max, respectively? Do all of the new features justify the $100 markup over the iPhone 17 Pros? The answer is unequivocally “yes,” and it would be even with half as many new features. Not even Siri AI can ruin the iPhone 18 Pros, because the LLM-powered assistant is actually good now. Unmistakably ‘pro’ As far as touchscreen bar-style phones go, the iPhone 18 Pros are very metal and very slabby. That is to say, they look nearly identical to the iPhone 17 Pros they’re replacing. The body is made of unibody aluminum with a raised camera “plateau” for the triple 48-megapixel camera system and also has a satin-glass cutout made of Ceramic Shield for wireless charging. On paper, the iPhone 18 Pro is 5g heavier than the 17 Pro and the 18 Pro Max is 16g heavier than the 17 Pro Max. I’m typically sensitive to the slab in my pocket getting heavier, but Apple balanced the weight increase across the devices so well that it doesn’t feel like you’re gripping an ever-heavier brick in your hand all day long. This is why specs don’t tell you everything, and hand-feel still matters. The displays—6.3 inches on the iPhone 18 Pro and 6.9 inches on the 18 Pro Max—are as bright, sharp, vibrant, and responsive as ever. Other flagship phones tout higher peak brightness, but I don’t think anyone will look at the screens here and say they’re not bright enough. The big change to the screens is the smaller Dynamic Island, the oval cutout at the top. It’s now about 25% smaller and can display three Live Activities at once. Apple achieved this by moving the Face ID infrared sensor to under the display in the upper left corner. It’s nearly invisible to the eye unless you press your nose up against the pixels and doesn’t impact viewing in my experience. What’s even more interesting to me is how Apple is clearly laying the groundwork for hiding all sensors and cameras on the display to get closer to a true “all-screen” front without any Dynamic Islands or notches. (Might such a screen launch for the rumored 20th anniversary iPhone next year?) The matching glass back cutouts and aluminum look better than the previous two-tone design. As I said last year, in a non-clear case, nobody will ever notice. Black is my favorite new color because it’s actually black and not another variant of Apple’s favorite “Space Gray.” It’s a stealthy throwback to the black iPhone 7. I can only wonder what a “Jet Black” version, with the same polished finish as the iPhone 7 model, of the iPhone 18 Pros could have looked like. That was my favorite black-colored iPhone of all time. Burgundy quickly grew on me after a few days because of how it looks under different lighting. It can appear darker or lighter. Both colors have a downside, though: they pick up fingerprints very easily and wiping them off will require a quality microfiber cloth and some elbow grease. Glacier and Silver have no long-lasting impression on me—they’re mid. Fight me in the comments! Maybe the only thing I wanted to see improved on the iPhone 18 Pros was the durability of the aluminum. While the metal is great for spreading heat away from the A20 chip, it bruises more easily compared to titanium or stainless steel. I confirmed with Apple that the iPhone 18 Pros use the same 7000-series aluminum as the 17 Pros, which means drops will likely sustain the same visible chips, dents, and any other physical damage as before. In the two years that I have used my personal iPhone 16 Pro, I’ve dropped it more times than I could count, and the titanium has barely any scratches or scuffs, despite being caseless. Get a case if you’re worried about damage, especially if you’re purchasing through Apple Upgrade, which is a lease that doesn’t include Apple Care. As usual, Apple sent me a few of its official cases to try (a TechWoven case for the iPhone 18 Pro and a silicone and clear case for the 18 Pro Max); Casetify also sent me its Impact and Ultra Impact cases. They all add some extra heft, but you will get protection for the corners, which are the most common place for bruising. The best camera in your pocket Best is subjective. What makes the camera in a specific phone the best? Is it the sharpest image quality? Having the biggest image sensors with the most megapixels? The longest zoom? All the AI enhancement and Gemini-powered camera modes in the Pixel 11 phones? As much as I like certain features and aspects about the cameras on Android phones, the iPhone has always been my “best” phone camera for a very simple reason: Apple stays true to photography. On the iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max, Apple has added a “variable aperture” to the main 48-megapixel lens. For non-photography geeks, this means the lens has individual blades that mechanically widen to let in more light or narrow to reduce light. With a variable aperture and the lens wide open, you can take better photos and videos in low light and also not have to hold your hand steady as long for Night Mode shots. A variable aperture gives you more control over depth of field in a photo; set it wide open and you’ll get more background blur (bokeh) or closed to its smallest for less. Yes, Samsung had a variable aperture on its Galaxy S9, Note 9, and S10 series phones. But the combination of small image sensors and two-aperture settings meant the photo results were negligible. Apple’s version comes eight years later, but it’s better implemented in every way, with four aperture settings (measured as “f-stops” as f/1.48, f/1.8, f/2.8, and f/4.0) where you can actually see a difference in bokeh between each. Not only that, but the blades of the aperture as you close them down (higher f-stop) also create star-shaped lens flares around lights, reminiscent of what you might get from traditional camera lenses. Apple brought real properties of traditional DSLR and mirrorless cameras to the iPhone. By default, the variable aperture is set to auto mode, and the camera app will choose the best aperture for a scene. If you know nothing about photography or have no interest in learning about it, you don’t need to do anything but point and shoot. Auto is supposed to detect when and by how much to open and close the aperture based on a scene or how close you are to a subject. In my testing, I found that the camera preferred to shoot at f/1.8 for close-up photos or f/1.48 in low light; it rarely selected f/2.8 or f/4.0 for these scenarios. For example, in a close-up shot of several figurines, I wanted them all to be in focus, which would have meant shooting with a narrower aperture (higher f-stop). Instead, the iPhone 18 Pro chose the second widest f/1.8 aperture, focusing on the closest figurine while blurring out all the ones in the back. Below are the four photos of the figurines, where I manually set the aperture to f/1.48, f/1.8, f/2.8, and f/4.0 (clockwise from top left): This is where, as easy as auto mode is, it cannot 100% make creative decisions for a photo exactly the way you envision it. For that, you’ll have to switch to manual mode and set the aperture yourself. Fortunately, access to the “lens aperture” settings is a tap away. Furthermore, the iPhone 18 Pros also have “Pro controls” that let you adjust shutter speed, white balance, and exposure with swipes. I also really like that you can toggle a histogram on and off to easily see if a scene is over or underexposed. And you can customize your camera app by adding buttons for the manual settings that you use the most. Third-party camera apps like Halide II and Moment Pro Camera II have long offered these advanced camera settings, but they’re all built into the camera app now and don’t cost extra. I had a blast taking “light trail” photos, long-exposure shots of cars and buses driving down the street, like this one: The variable aperture’s widest opening (f/1.48) also improves low-light and night photography, letting in 50 percent more light, according to Apple. I can’t say I noticed any major difference between night photos taken with the iPhone 17 Pros versus the iPhone 18 Pros, unless I pixel-peeped. Below, a night photo comparison between the iPhone 18 Pro shot at f/1.48 aperture (left) and iPhone 17 Pro shot at f/1.78 aperture (right): Viewed side by side, the iPhone 18 Pro’s night photos appear to have greater dynamic range and better-preserved highlights. The larger f/1.48 aperture does make shooting night photos easier; Night Mode doesn’t kick in as much as on previous iPhones, meaning you won’t need to hold your hand still as often. The variable aperture also works for video recording from the main lens (1x to 3.9x zoom). Once you switch to the 4x telephoto zoom, the camera switches to its non-variable f/2.8 aperture. Most people will probably never need or want to fiddle with the variable aperture, but it’s great that the ability to manually control the aperture and other camera settings is there if you want it. It makes the iPhone 18 Pros not only a better camera for professionals and content creators who have been begging for manual controls but also for people who want to take more creative shots without needing to buy a traditional camera. Weirdly, none of the manual camera settings can be controlled with Camera Control, the capacitive camera app launch button that also lets you adjust settings. At this point, Camera Control feels like a neglected and forgotten feature, much like the Touch Bar was on old MacBook Pros. There are several other features exclusive to the iPhone 18 Pros that make their camera systems even more versatile. You can shoot video and then apply a “cinematic effect” that blurs the background after capture. It’s not as good compared to shooting a video at f/1.48 and getting a very shallow depth of field, but it does work, even when you’re panning and dollying. I was surprised to see the blur effect applied pretty well to my colleague even when he was moving his arms in all directions. Smart focus tracking also works; double-tapping a subject keeps it in focus even when they move. It enjoyed using it to track my two cats, Lemons and Kiwi, running around my apartment. Parents will love it for recording their kids. The iPhone 18 Pros also have Photographic Styles 3. This lets you add “texture,” including “soft skin,” “glow,” “film,” and “grain” to either make skin appear smoother or images look less processed. You can adjust how much of each texture you want to apply.
