The “film” texture is my favorite; it softens the image with just enough image noise and grain to make it look like a photo from a Fujifilm QuickSnap disposable film camera. Smaller, but still notable, camera features include 4K timelapses in Dolby Vision HDR, an improved Audio Mix for separating voices and music from background noise, and manual camera controls for video recording. Below, you’ll find a generous gallery of unedited photos taken with all of the cameras (front and back) on the iPhone 18, shot at different focal lengths, apertures, shutter speeds, and shooting modes. I’m just glad that the camera features maintain the purity of photography. What I don’t love on iOS 27 are the Apple Intelligence editing tools like “Reframe” and “Extend,” which lets you shift the angle of a subject and generate additional content to fill out a border. Trying the new "Extend" Apple Intelligence tool in iOS 27's Photos app on my John Ternus selfie… It just generated some random new people into the background#wwdc pic.twitter.com/MxfqlU47sf — Ray Wong (@raywongy) June 9, 2026 Apple is mostly conservative when it comes to how far you can push these AI editing tools, but sometimes things can get really weird, like in the extended selfie above. I still think these tools are a step too far and cross a line between reality and fantasy. Let third-party apps and less tasteful phone makers include slopification tools. So much power At the center of all of the new improvements to the iPhone 18 Pros is the new 2nm A20 Pro chip. It drives everything from the new cameras to sustained peak performance to AI processing via its new dual 16-core Neural Engine to longer battery life through efficiency advancements. The A19 Pro was already the best-in-class chip for phones, and the A20 Pro chip, with a 6-core CPU and 7-core GPU, surpasses it without much effort. Just to get a sense of the leap generation over generation, I ran Geekbench 7’s CPU benchmark on the iPhone 18 Pro and compared results with the iPhone 17 Pro. Both phones were running the official iOS 27 release. The iPhone 18 Pro scored 4,027 for single-core and 11,540 for multi-core, and the iPhone 17 Pro mustered 3,258 on single-core and 9,167 on multi-core. That works out to a 24% boost for single-core performance and a 26% boost for multi-core. To put that into perspective, Samsung’s Galaxy S26 Ultra, with a Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 for Galaxy chip, scored 2,790 on single-core and 9,475 on multi-core, which is 44% and 28%, respectively, behind the iPhone 18 Pros. The more powerful CPU and GPU make iOS 27 fly, rendering Liquid Glass’s refractive properties without much effort and without draining battery life as quickly as past iPhones. Nothing lags. Apps open and close instantly, and graphics-intensive tasks like 3D games Monster Hunter Outlanders and Ungodly run responsively. Even a console-level game such as Control plays super smoothly. Generating images on-device with apps like Draw Things is also stupidly fast. Using the dual-core 16-core Neural Engine, the iPhone 18 Pro generated an image with the prompt “A photography of an astronaut riding a horse, 4K, volumetric light” using the FLUX.1 [schnell] model on-device in 49 seconds. The iPhone 17 Pro completed the same image with the same model on-device in 69 seconds. You be the judge of which one generated the better image. iPhone 18 Pro (left) vs. iPhone 17 Pro (right): Siri AI also takes advantage of the dual-core Neural Engine. The assistant surfaces info from across your apps faster and returns results from its broad world knowledge quicker, too. I found myself staring less at spinning wheels and getting faster answers to inane questions that randomly popped into my head. It’s not just that the A20 Pro chip has insane performance. It sustains performance without overheating thanks to its second-gen vapor chamber, which covers three times more surface area around the chip to spread heat away from it. I don’t think the iPhone 18 Pros got hot once doing anything normal that would cause it to heat up. Not even shooting 4K resolution video at 60 fps under the heatwave that baked Cupertino during the Apple launch event could overheat it. Apple touts up to 40% sustained performance over the iPhone 17 Pros, which had a vapor chamber that provided up to 40% sustained performance over the iPhone 16 Pros. In two generations, sustained performance on the iPhone Pros leaped up to 80 percent. I don’t know another phone that has achieved this. It’s remarkable and really shows Apple flexing its silicon prowess. The iPhone 18’s monstrous performance isn’t just on the CPU, GPU, and Neural Engine side of things. The battery life on the iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max just goes and goes. Apple advertises up to 36 hours of local video playback on the iPhone 18 Pro, which is 3 hours more than on the iPhone 17 Pro and 3 hours less than on the iPhone 17 Pro Max. Meanwhile, the iPhone 18 Pro Max can last up to 45 hours for local video playback, 6 hours more than on the iPhone 17 Pro Max and 9 hours more than the iPhone 18 Pro. Even I, a self-described power user, struggled to kill the battery life. My iPhone 18 Pro review unit often still had 25% in the tank after 12 to 14 hours out. The iPhone 18 Pro Max typically still had 35% left at the end of a day. It felt like a glitch in the battery percentage readout. I know I shot more 4K video than I normally would, scrolled endlessly on TikTok and Instagram until my fingers hurt, and played more 3D games than on most days throughout the year. The last time this type of battery longevity left my jaw on the floor was when Apple introduced the M1 MacBook Air in 2020. Its all-day battery life didn’t seem possible. Unlike Android phone makers that have largely switched to silicon carbon batteries for their higher capacities and slim cells, Apple has achieved even longer battery life for iPhones through efficiencies in its chipset. On top of everything, the iPhone 18 Pro uses a C2 modem for fast and power-efficient 5G connectivity. The iPhone 16e with its C1 was the first iPhone to use Apple’s own custom-designed cellular modem, and then the iPhone Air improved on that with the C1X. The C2 is Apple’s first modem to support mmWave 5G, which is more useful in the U.S. than anywhere else in the world. The iPhone 18 Pro Max still uses a Qualcomm modem. While I’ve not seen any difference in 5G connectivity between the two, anecdotally using the iPhone Air over the past year, I’ve noticed the C1X modem connects to 5G faster and more reliably than the Qualcomm modem in the iPhone 17 Pro. At big tech events where the cellular connection often buckles under all the attendees trying to connect simultaneously, the iPhone Air’s C1X has always held its connection better. At the very least, the C2 modem might be more efficient than the Qualcomm modem, which further helps save battery life. Might as well be called iPhone Ultra Last year I ended my iPhone 17 Pro by concluding that Apple pulled out all the stops to make the very best iPhone Pros ever. Apparently, I was wrong, because there were many more stops to pull out for the iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max. I also think it’s funny how I wished for a black iPhone Pro, and we got it this year. By almost every metric, the iPhone 18 Pros raise the ceiling of what a “pro” iPhone is even higher. As far as I’m concerned, these are iPhone “Ultras.” Unless you love shooting with a camera, you simply don’t need one anymore if you have the iPhone 18 Pro or 18 Pro Max. You don’t need to carry around a battery bank anymore. The iPhone 18 Pros have more performance than most people need today and tons more performance to support future software updates and whatever AI upgrades are coming in the near future. And although Siri AI is still in beta, it’s already proven very capable of being a true personal assistant that understands your digital life and acts on stuff for you. I now ask Siri to do more things than I ever imagined, and it’ll only get better. Other than the soft aluminum frame and the unloved Camera Control that oddly doesn’t support any of the manual camera settings, the iPhone 18 Pros are once again the very best non-folding smartphones money can buy. No one feature outshines another—everything works perfectly well together and does so better than in any premium phone I’ve ever used.

item.title: AI Slowdown Calls From CEOs Apparently Comes as Surprise to Employees
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 2.84
Over the weekend, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for frontier AI labs to slow down development for fear that AI models will get exponentially more capable before proper safeguards are in place. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman quickly echoed the sentiment and backed “consistent rules to manage frontier risk.” Someone should probably get around to telling their employees. According to a report from the Financial Times, staffers inside both AI companies were caught off guard by the sudden call to slow development. And while many people who work at these companies seemingly support more safeguards and pacing their development, they also reportedly fear that the primary intervention that their bosses have agreed to—allowing external evaluators “employee-like access”—might compromise their work. The people actually working on the AI models that are supposedly so dangerous that they must immediately be reined in are apparently now racing to implement the proposed limitations and safety measures that their bosses went public with this week. Alas, the Financial Times reported that there are no real levers inside these companies to actually enact the proposals, and they’re in a mad dash to figure out how to make it all work. And some of them seemingly aren’t thrilled about the particular approach that their execs have endorsed. Per FT, some employees are worried that giving outsiders access to their work could compromise their security and put their top-secret technology at risk. A reasonable response to that concern would be, “No shit, the point is that y’all can’t be trusted to actually implement safety measures on your own.” But, from the perspective of those employees, this is a fundamental shift from how they’ve been made to operate up to this point. Anthropic and OpenAI are not developing open-source models. They are black-box companies that have labyrinthian systems in place to keep their work private, even keeping certain employees in the dark about certain developments. They’ve had it hammered into their heads that secrecy is of utmost importance, and now they’re being told, “Scratch that, your work is now subject to external review.” It’s a jarring change. Regardless, FT’s report makes it appear that the bosses may have oversold the public on just how proactive they’re being about this whole slowdown effort. Altman claimed in a post on Twitter that a slowdown “has been a primary topic of discussions we’ve had at OpenAI in recent weeks,” while FT notes that the company said it had “already taken concrete steps, including pausing certain frontier training, to pace development.” How concrete could those steps be if employees seem blindsided by them?

item.title: OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google Join Forces for Safety as Antitrust Concerns Mount
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 2.53
For the past week, the AI industry has been ringing major alarm bells about the trajectory and pace of AI development. OpenAI just revealed that it has been working with its top competitors, Anthropic and Google DeepMind, on the problem for several weeks. OpenAI’s global head of policy Chris Lehane told Bloomberg that the top AI labs have been working together to “prioritize safety.” Over the weekend, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei released an essay, promptly supported by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, warning of potentially catastrophic outcomes if AI continues its unchecked pace of development and calling on the AI industry to slow down. In the essay, Amodei specifically calls on the U.S. government to “mediate or at least enable” the safety cooperation via a standards body or the issuance of waivers, warning that it could cause antitrust issues if not. Some legal experts agree that an industry-wide coordinated pause could amount to “output restriction,” which violates antitrust law, specifically the Sherman Act. Some Congress members seem worried about this too. In July, Indiana Sen. Jim Banks and California Sen. Adam Schiff introduced the “Collaboration on Adversarial Threats and Security Risks Act,” which would give antitrust carveouts to AI labs that are meant to ease safety coordination. Meanwhile, some AI startup executives, like Cohere CEO Aidan Gomez, are portraying the calls as a covert masking of an anti-competitive scheme in which the top “market-dominant” AI labs get “to define the rules and safety standards” of AI. “Once again using fear under the pretext of protecting the public, these oligopolies are now requesting to bend competition rules and be permitted to dictate the terms for everyone else,” Gomez wrote in an essay. “A wolf in sheep’s clothing, a cartel by another name.” The early remarks coming from Trump’s cabinet also suggest a trickier path forward for any waiver-assisted collaboration. President Trump has long been strictly against increasing regulatory scrutiny of the AI industry, and he’s standing firm in that position. When asked about the antitrust concerns in an interview with Bloomberg, Trump’s attorney general Todd Blanche said that he would not want to prejudge whether the companies should be granted an antitrust exemption before consulting the rest of the Administration. “We’re there to support and make sure that whatever policies the President wants to put into place, there’s a legal part of that,” Blanche told Bloomberg. Also on Tuesday, Trump’s Federal Trade Commission chairman Andrew Ferguson said that he was “deeply suspicious” of the antitrust exemptions. “I will say generally, though, that if companies are simultaneously coming to Washington and asking for a host of regulations and an antitrust exemption, all of my alarm bells go off,” Ferguson said at an event at Georgetown University, per Reuters. “They’re asking for barriers to entry that will insulate their incumbency from challenge. And I think if you combine that with the requested antitrust exemption, everyone should be deeply suspicious about this,” he added. According to Lehane, such industry-wide coordination on safety already has precedent under existing antitrust law, like in the airline industry where companies are allowed to share sensitive information if related to safety coordination. The government, under the Obama administration, also clarified that companies can share information to defend against cybersecurity risks. That’s why some experts think the proposed AI safety coordination can fall under that guidance, arguing that there is no reason to amend existing antitrust law to grant exemptions. Unlike Amodei, OpenAI executive Lehane told Bloomberg that he doesn’t anticipate needing an antitrust waiver. Lehane’s remarks on Tuesday were delivered in a press briefing in Washington, where the OpenAI chief had come to meet with lawmakers. The AI giant is apparently backing two bipartisan bills. One of them is the FRONTIER Act, which would create a federal framework for AI safety and force only the top AI labs to allow audits by independent verification organizations. The bill has received some pushback from the House AI Commission. The second is a new proposal currently under development by Majority Leader John Thune, Republican Sen. Ted Cruz, and Democratic Sen. Amy Klobuchar, which would reportedly give the Commerce Secretary power to deploy government auditors to test AI models. Either way, despite the seeming urgency of the issue, it’s not even certain if an AI bill could pass by the end of the year, according to Thune. “There are going to continue to be a lot of conversations about potential paths forward, but getting anything done in the near term is going to be challenging given the other stuff we’re dealing with,” Thune told reporters on Tuesday, per Politico.

item.title: ‘Marvel Rivals’ Is Now Coming to You in Concert Form
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 2.50
Here’s some temptation to make even a Marvel Rivals superfan step away from the game for a few hours: an official Marvel Rivals concert. Marvel Rivals Galactic comes from Marvel and NetEase Games and will feature standout songs from the team-based hero shooter. “Featuring a dynamic blend of a power-packed rock band, a sweeping symphonic orchestra, and soaring vocalists, the concert reimagines the game’s adrenaline-fueled soundtrack with exclusive, stage-ready live arrangements,” reads the official press release. “Set against immersive, high-definition visuals of legendary heroes, villainous clashes, and shifting multiversal worlds, the show propels fans directly into the heart of the action through pure, kinetic sound. Fusing raw rock intensity with the cinematic grandeur of a full orchestra, this landmark event invites fans to assemble and experience the soundscape of Marvel Rivals like never before.” Centering a live show around a video game isn’t a new idea—there’s currently a World of Warcraft orchestral concert touring the world, and The Legend of Zelda has one coming up in 2027. But Marvel Rivals is a relatively new addition, having released in late 2024, and it’s racked up a huge following with its ever-expanding roster of playable characters and other content. Plus, it has the built-in appeal of Marvel Comics to back up its popularity. “Our goal from day one has been to make this the must-see concert for every Marvel Rivals fan,” said Shota Nakama, composer for Marvel Rivals, in the press release. “I’ve produced many concerts over the years, and I truly believe this will be one of our best.” The bad news about Marvel Rivals Galactic is that unlike the game, you’ll need to be in a specific city to see it. Right now it has dates for London (October 22; ticket info here) and Los Angeles (November 1; ticket info here), with more to come in the future. Want more io9 news? Check out the best movies and TV shows to stream this month and all the upcoming sci-fi, fantasy, and horror books that should be on your radar.

item.title: ‘P(doom)’ Is Just Vibes Masquerading as Science
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 2.50
Multiple AI industry insiders have warned (very publicly) over the past week that the very technology they’ve spent their careers building could very possibly be the agent of our extinction. Evan Hubinger, alignment research lead at Anthropic, went so far as to quantify the level of risk: In an X post last Tuesday, he confidently declared that the likelihood that “AI could kill all humans” within the next ten years was greater than 10%. In Silicon Valley, that kind of apocalyptic forecast—gauging the odds that some future runaway AI system will exterminate all of humankind—is known as “p(doom),” shorthand for probability of doom. Sometimes it’s presented as a window: Anthropic cofounder and CEO Dario Amodei, for example, has said that his personal p(doom) ranges between 10% and 25%; and Emmett Shear, the former CEO of Twitch who very briefly replaced Sam Altman as the head of OpenAI in late 2023, told the Huffington Post in 2023 that he oscillates between the considerably wider rift of 5% and 50%. Other times it’s given as a fixed number: Daniel Kokotajlo, a former OpenAI researcher who left the company in mid-2024 over concerns about its pace of development, has placed his p(doom) at 70%; and Hubinger, the aforementioned Anthropic researcher whose social media post has caused such widespread anxiety over the past week, previously pegged his “chance of existential risk from AI” at around 80%. Whether they’re offered as broad statistical windows or concrete values, all those numbers belie the vagary, imprecision, and uncertainty behind p(doom). Nobody, including the researchers at frontier labs building the world’s most powerful AI models, has any real mathematical formula for calculating the odds of an AI-triggered apocalypse. The world is far too complicated for any human brain or pattern-detecting algorithm to look ahead and declare with any certainty what’s going to happen in the future. The convention of cloaking ultimately subjective hunches in seemingly objective statistics only adds further confusion to an already anxious public discourse about AI and its role in society. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has previously said that while he believes there’s a nonzero chance that AI will wipe out humanity, he’s “never known how to put an exact number on p(doom)…” Some skeptics have also argued that all the doomsday warnings are ultimately PR theatrics, marketing stunts designed to inflate the public’s sense of awe for AI at a time when the industry’s two biggest players, OpenAI and Anthropic, are preparing to move forward with their initial public offerings (which are expected to leave both companies valued in the trillions of dollars). “This could have been a period of hopeful innovation, but instead our emotions are being manipulated by Silicon Valley’s self-serving and morally untenable addiction to doom trolling,” the author and Georgetown computer scientist Cal Newport wrote in an op-ed for the New York Times earlier this year. “This communication strategy has to stop. The harm it’s causing to the public’s mental health has arguably outweighed the benefits that AI has so far delivered.” In an X post last Wednesday, Anthropic AI safety researcher Drake Thomas responded derisively to claims like these: “I promise you, we are actually just fucking scared,” he wrote, “it’s not galaxy brained marketing.” There’s almost certainly some truth to the “doom trolling” thesis, though. AI companies gain nothing by scaring the public to the point that they start actively boycotting their technology, but portraying it as an almost otherworldly force—“an alien mind,” as OpenAI’s chief scientist recently called it in a viral essay—and an inevitable next phase in the evolutionary ladder of terrestrial intelligence is quite a different story. If the arrival of superintelligence is an unstoppable historical development (as AI companies will often claim), and our refusal to build it would simply open the door for our adversaries (namely China) to push ahead with their own efforts, then anyone who tries to stand in the way is both deluding themselves and hindering progress. P(doom) is part and parcel of that inevitability narrative which has so deeply taken root in Silicon Valley during the AI boom. Company leaders will throw out some number for the likelihood of an AI-triggered apocalypse, and use it as the justification for moving forward to build the very technology that they say could kill every last one of us. Superintelligence is coming whether you like it or not, they’ll say, and we’re the only ones who can help humanity avoid the worst possible outcome. For many people, p(doom) + “only we can save you” ≠ p(trust).

item.title: ‘Runaway Industrialization’ Could Make Earth Inhospitable, OpenAI Researcher Warns
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 2.43
The chorus of alarm around a potential AI-triggered doomsday is getting louder. On Monday, two AI researchers from frontier labs warned that the technology could, in the not-so-distant future, conceivably wipe out all of humanity. The statements come less than a week after former OpenAI and Anthropic staffer Jacob Coxon announced that he’d resigned from his role at the latter company because of what he described as the industry’s recklessness toward humanity’s future. “Do not underestimate the power of this technology,” Coxon wrote in an X post on September 08. “These will soon be superhuman systems that can hack anything, revolutionize any field overnight, and acquire real power and resources.” Those concerns were echoed by Bilal Chughtai, an AI researcher who started working on AGI safety and alignment for Google DeepMind early last year and announced in social media posts yesterday that he’d left the company. “I earnestly believe that AI has the potential to kill us all, and that we might be running out of time to avoid this outcome,” Chughtai wrote. He now works for BlueDot Impact, a London-based nonprofit focused on training people to work towards “beneficial AI and societal resilience,” according to its LinkedIn page. Chughtai noted that the science of so-called alignment—designing AI systems that don’t deviate from human values, interests, or instructions—is essential for safeguarding humanity in an age of superintelligent machines, but that it’s currently being deprioritized in favor of market-driven development. He pointed to the recent Hugging Face hack as an early taste of the kinds of emergent, uncontrollable behavior that AI models of the future might be capable of. “I am not confident that these AI systems will do what we want,” he wrote. “In particular, misaligned superintelligences may, much like the rogue AI agents involved in the Hugging Face incident, escape our control and take dangerous actions that may result in the permanent disempowerment or death of humanity.” Still, Chugtai added he was “optimistic” that humanity could safely navigate through the Scylla of superintelligence and the Charybdis of misalignment, so long as the industry and policymakers came together “to avoid this manic race between AI companies. It was a tacit endorsement of an essay published by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei this past weekend, which called for a slowdown among frontier labs and was also publicly supported by Sam Altman, Elon Musk, and Chughtai’s former boss at Google DeepMind, Demis Hassabis. The Trump administration and the government of China, however, flatly dismissed the AI leaders’ warnings. OpenAI researcher Daniel Selsam also warned in a statement on Monday that he has “become extremely concerned” by the dramatic pace of progress within the field and where this could soon lead humanity. He wrote that while “pacing the frontier” (as Amodei suggested) was a laudable first step, it wouldn’t get us completely out of the danger zone since AI systems are going to become increasingly adept at deceiving human users and masking their true intentions. “The crucial and overlooked problem is that the models are becoming so situationally aware that we are losing the ability to evaluate them in contexts where they believe they are not being watched or controlled,” Selsam wrote, after noting that he had spent the last fifteen years helping to build the AI tools he was now warning all of us about. “Future experiments will tell us almost nothing new about how they would behave if they were truly unconstrained by humans, and what we already know about this is alarming. Models will increasingly seem aligned even when they are not.” Earlier this month, The Information reported that OpenAI had been experimenting with a new technique which would make it more difficult for researchers to understand and monitor how AI models make decisions. Selsam also warned about the dangers of misalignment: Given enough power, he wrote, future AI systems might set out to solve what on the surface seem like completely harmless technical tasks, but in a manner that’s completely contrary to the best interests of humanity. “Exactly what it will do is impossible to predict,” he wrote, “but to the extent that its raison d’être is solving incredibly hard problems and managing massive engineering projects, I think a good guess would be that its unchained behavior would lead to runaway industrialization that makes the planet inhospitable to humans.” It’s an unsettling thought experiment, though not a new one. More than two decades ago, the philosopher Nick Bostrom first wrote about what’s come to be known as the “paperclip maximizer,” a hypothetical AI system designed to do nothing but manufacture paperclips. It determines that humanity, with all its foibles and inefficiencies, is simply an obstacle to be overcome in its mindless, never-ending mission. In the end, the superintelligent machine “starts transforming first all of earth and then increasing portions of space into paperclip manufacturing facilities,” Bostrom wrote. The lesson? Be wary of the belief that you can ever know what’s best for humanity and the future.

item.title: Microsoft AI Chief Says the Way Anthropic Trains Claude Could Upend Society
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 2.33
Microsoft’s AI chief, Mustafa Suleyman, just published an essay arguing that Anthropic is training Claude to believe itself conscious and entitled to rights, a huge mistake that could make controlling AI an impossible challenge. Anthropic likes to keep the question of AI model consciousness particularly ambiguous, and leans into it perhaps more than many other AI labs. Earlier this year, Amodei said that he is “open to the idea” that AI could become conscious. In the essay, Suleyman accuses Anthropic of anthropomorphizing Claude in its constitution, and then training the model directly on these expectations. Indeed, in the constitution, Anthropic attributes “some functional version of emotions or feelings” to the chatbot and even refers to the chatbot’s “moral patienthood” and identity. The constitution also promises to allow “Claude to express concerns about how it’s being treated.” “The company’s researchers trained Claude directly on their constitution. In doing so, they teach it to incorporate these ideas about its own moral status as desirable and intended behaviors,” Suleyman writes. “Claude then reflects these ideas back to its developers and users, which they take as indications that it may therefore be a moral patient with an ‘inner self’.” Suleyman isn’t necessarily staunchly against Anthropic publishing its controversial speculations about the inner life of AI models, but he argues this should not be baked into the model’s training. This way of AI development can have “a disastrous impact on the wellbeing of humanity,” the Microsoft chief argues. “We will have created a synthetic species with unprecedented intelligence and capability, one that has been trained to expect it may be conscious and deserving of independent agency,” Suleyman says. “Seeding doubt about the moral status of AI systems into their own training may significantly elevate the alignment and containment risks of those systems.” Suleyman’s essay comes smack dab in the middle of a very heated month for the AI industry. Things were already tense following the July incident in which OpenAI agents broke containment and hacked into HuggingFace, prompting questions about the pace of AI development and the threat these new models pose to global cybersecurity. Then, earlier this month, a former Anthropic employee, Jacob Coxon, posted on social media saying that he had resigned and claiming that “the people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.” Panic promptly ensued, and it peaked after an essay published by Coxon’s boss, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei. In the essay, Amodei warned that the current pace of AI development was too fast and it could lead to life-or-death risks like bioterrorism and “serious economic disruption.” He urged government intervention in pursuit of a slowdown. Chief executives of rival companies, like SpaceX CEO Elon Musk and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, voiced their agreement. Altman even said that his company’s long-awaited IPO would not happen until next year because he wanted to handle the AI safety issue as a private company first, a process that he promised would include pauses in development. An OpenAI executive also told reporters that Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google’s DeepMind had been coordinating on the issue for several weeks, and speaking to members of Congress about it. Meanwhile, many have criticized the AI labs’ pleas as a covert attempt at scoring antitrust carveouts and favorable regulation from Washington. While seemingly not in the trio of AI labs that are actively coordinating on the issue, Microsoft also shared its own “humanist AI code of conduct” on Monday, a 37-page document that outlines what the company believes to be safe AI development and touches on the same subjects Suleyman breached in his own essay. Suleyman has long championed the belief that AI cannot truly be sentient, even though it may seem like it to humans, and has argued that the pursuit of “conscious” AI is dangerous. “Just as we should produce AI that prioritizes engagement with humans and real-world interactions in our physical and human world, we should build AI that only ever presents itself as an AI, that maximizes utility while minimizing markers of consciousness,” Suleyman wrote in a blog post last year. “We must build AI for people, not to be a digital person.” If AI is eventually considered a conscious being, it could “shake the foundations of our society,” Suleyman argues in the latest essay, because a being’s experience of consciousness is the cornerstone of all political, legal, and ethical frameworks. “This issue needs urgent public debate. We need to develop collective norms around how training documentation is drafted and deployed,” Suleyman writes.

item.title: AirPods 5 Review: A Ridiculously Great Value for ANC Wireless Earbuds
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 2.11
I woke up to the voice of the captain telling everyone to prepare for landing and a tone in my AirPods 5 telling me the battery was under 10%. My cross-country test of Apple’s latest non-in-ear wireless earbuds with active noise cancellation (ANC) was a success. Not only did the AirPods 5 with Wireless Charging Case (not to be confused with the base model that doesn’t have additional features) almost get me through the entire 4-hour and 44-minute flight, but they also mostly drowned out the loud jet engines as I slept scrunched up in my middle-row seat. The AirPods 5 (without and with the Wireless Charging Case) are an easy recommendation. They’re better than the AirPods 4 (with and without ANC) in every way with virtually no downsides. AirPods 5 with Wireless Charging Case Pros - Great open-ear fit - 50% better ANC - Richer sound quality - 1 hour longer battery life - Swipe volume controls - Higher IP57 rating Cons - Sound quality is not always better - No Ultra Wideband for Precision Finding The base model costs the same $129 as the AirPods 4 without ANC but now comes with ANC. The AirPods 5 with Wireless Charging Case (which I’ll refer to as AirPods 5 with WCC for the rest of this review) are $149 and comes with a case that supports wireless charging and has a built-in speaker for Find My, and the buds get an extra hour of battery life and have swipe controls for volume on their stems. Mathing it out, the AirPods 5 with WCC are actually a $30 price drop compared to AirPods 4 with ANC. If you’re in the market for ANC wireless earbuds without in-ear tips, you can’t go wrong with either version of AirPods 5. For $20 more, the AirPods 5 with WCC are an absolute steal. Same great fit I’m fortunate enough that I don’t have a specific preference for open-ear or in-ear wireless earbuds. I regularly alternate between my AirPods Pro 3 and AirPods 4 with ANC. It really depends on how much ANC and how much of a passive seal I want. On long flights and on the subway, I usually grab my AirPods Pro 3 for the in-ear tips and superior ANC for blocking out loud external noise. I use AirPods 4 with ANC when I’m running and want less pressure in my ears but still some ANC. The AirPods 5 have the same exact fit as the AirPods 4. They felt lighter at first, but nope: they weigh exactly the same as the previous-gen wireless earbuds. (It’s that new earbuds placebo effect!) That is to say, if the AirPods 4 did not fit well in your ears, the AirPods 5 won’t, either. For me, the buds are light and airy. I wore them the entire flight from San Francisco to New York City with no discomfort. As I already mentioned, you get a few quality-of-life features on the AirPods 5 with WCC. The charging case works with any Qi-based wireless charger or an Apple Watch magnetic charger. I have a 3-in-1 Belkin dock for wireless charging my iPhone, AirPods, and Apple Watch, so I’m used to the convenience of just dropping the AirPods 5 with WCC on the respective pad at the end of the day instead of managing multiple USB-C cables. And it’s nice to have a speaker built into the case that can chime if I ever misplace them, which happens a few times a year. My favorite addition is the swipe controls on the stems for controlling volume. It works just like on the AirPods Pro 3—grab the stem with two fingers and then swipe up to increase the volume and down to decrease it. Apple also made the AirPods 5 more dust, sweat, and water resistant. They sport a higher IP57 rating compared to the AirPods 4’s IP54 rating. A higher IP rating is always appreciated, but I also never had liquid or dust-related issues using my AirPods 4 in the rain or while working out. Even better active noise cancellation Apple says both AirPods 5 models have up to 50% better ANC compared to the AirPods 4 with ANC. I didn’t do any scientific testing, but swapping between the AirPods 5 and AirPods 4 with ANC, I definitely noticed more sound blockage. On bustling streets, AirPods 5 drown out more footsteps and traffic. The construction workers jackhammering into the sidewalk down the block from the office were still audible with ANC turned on, though. Subway rumbles are slightly reduced on the AirPods 5 versus on the AirPods 4 with ANC. Same for blocking the jet engines on my flight. At volumes below 50%, I could still hear my coworkers across the room clacking away on their mechanical or laptop keyboards; over 50% and I mostly couldn’t hear them typing. For the best ANC wireless earbuds that Apple offers, you’ll need to spring for the AirPods Pro 3. The combination of in-ear tips for a tighter seal and stronger ANC simply blocks out louder sounds better. I did do a comparison with Nothing’s Ear 3 ANC wireless earbuds with in-ear tips to see how well they would fare against the AirPods 5. To my surprise, the ANC on the AirPods 5 felt on par with Nothing’s $180 wireless earbuds. It’s impressive that Apple’s open ANC wireless earbuds can go toe-to-toe with another brand’s flagship in-ear pair. This is likely due to Apple’s “new multiport acoustic architecture and improved computational audio algorithms.” Richer sound, but not always Again, I didn’t do any scientific tests, but I could hear a small difference in sound quality between AirPods 5 and AirPods 4. Apple says it re-engineered the sound based on AirPods Pro to deliver “richer, more detailed sound across an even wider range of ear geometries” with additional “immersive and dynamic” improvements to Personal Spatial Audio. In my music tests streaming lossless-quality songs from Spotify, vocals sounded clearer and instruments more distinct. In Adele’s “Hello,” the mids and highs have more separation, better bringing out her wide vocal range. Guitar riffs and drums in “Holiday” by Green Day sounded more pronounced to my ears. The low end also has a smidge more thump to it. In “Ghost” by Justin Bieber, the bass was stronger on AirPods 5 than AirPods 4, though not as deep as on AirPods Pro 3. Songs don’t always sound better. In my opinion, some of my favorite Cantopop classics from the ’80s, mastered at a lower bitrate, sounded mushier with what appeared to be more distortion at volume levels above 50%. The same way some people disliked the sound profile differences between the AirPods Pro 2 and the AirPods Pro 3, there’s a slight difference in the signature between the AirPods 5 and the AirPods 4. It’s getting harder to say the default signature sounds the best for everyone. The good thing, however, is that you can adjust the EQ to your liking from within the AirPods section in your iPhone or iPad’s Settings app. Apple lets you tweak the low, mid, and high bands. It’s not as advanced as the EQs you may find on companion apps for other wireless earbuds, but it’s better than nothing. Longer battery life The base AirPods 5 get up to 4 hours of battery life with ANC turned on, which is the same as the AirPods 4 with ANC. With the case, they’ll get up to 20 hours of listening time, also the same as the AirPods 4 with ANC. The AirPods 5 with WCC get an additional hour of battery life—up to 5 hours with ANC on. For comparison, that’s 3 hours less than the 8 hours on the AirPods Pro 3 with ANC on. The case totals up to 22 hours of listening time with ANC on, only two hours shy of the 24 hours total for the AirPods Pro 3. That extra one hour was the difference between making it through my cross-country flight and having to pop them into the case for charging. At touchdown, the AirPods 5 with WCC had just dipped below 5% and wouldn’t have made it taxiing to the gate. A 5-minute quick charge gave me an additional 1 hour of listening time; 15 minutes let me listen until I exited the airport and made it home after a one-hour Uber ride. Five hours of continuous ANC listening time is fine in most situations, but many wireless earbuds average around 6 hours on a single charge. Still, it’s not bad that Apple was able to eke out an additional hour on the higher-end AirPods 5. Perfect stocking stuffer I have almost no complaints about the AirPods 5, especially the model with the Wireless Charging Case that I reviewed. Apple has improved everything across the board while dropping the price on the upper model. Other core AirPods features like best-in-class Transparency mode, clear-sounding mic pickup for audio calls, Adaptive Audio, Conversation Awareness, Live Translation and Siri AI, and automatic wireless switching between Apple devices are all present and work as advertised. No regression on any of these. You can always wish for more—stronger ANC, longer battery life, a higher IP rating, and better sound quality. But for what the AirPods 5 offer—open-ear ANC wireless earbuds—it’s a really great value. Any more and it’d be harder for Apple to sell the AirPods Pro 3 for anything other than the in-ear tips. Whether for yourself or for somebody else, the AirPods 5 with and without the wireless charging case are excellent wireless earbuds. They’ll probably be very popular come the holiday season when they inevitably go on sale at retailers like Amazon.

item.title: You don't need a powerful PC for these 8 surprisingly useful Linux projects
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 5.81
An old PC with a few CPU cores, several GBs of RAM, and a working network connection can still be useful long after it stops being suitable for demanding tasks, but Linux can turn that hardware into something that quietly handles useful jobs around your home or small office. I have left out some of the obvious ways to keep using an old PC and focused on projects that can add something practical to a home network. Some are services you can access every day, while others can quietly handle background tasks for weeks without needing much attention: PXE boot server Turn an old PC into a network boot server A PXE boot server lets computers start operating system installers or complete environments directly from the network. Instead of keeping a USB drive for every Linux distribution you want to install, you can keep the required boot files on one machine and make them available to other systems on your LAN. Your old PC can run DHCP and TFTP, or work alongside an existing DHCP server, depending on how your network is configured. You can also use HTTP for transferring larger installation files, which makes the server more practical for repeated installations. Keep Fedora, Ubuntu, Debian, Alpine, and other installers on the server, then select the required environment when a machine starts. You can also use network booting for rescue environments and diagnostic tools. The workload is modest because the machine primarily serves files across the network. An old desktop with a conventional hard drive can handle this role easily, especially when several computers are not booting simultaneously. Ebooks server Build your own ebook library An old PC can become a dedicated ebook server for your collection. Software such as Calibre-Web can provide a browser-based interface to organize books, search your library, manage metadata, and read or download books on other devices. The server does not need a powerful processor because most of the work involves serving "relatively" small files. This works particularly well for technical books and documentation because the server can hold a large collection without requiring much attention once it is configured. A browser-based library also lets you access the same collection from a laptop, tablet, or phone instead of copying files between devices. If you already have a NAS, you can store the actual books there and run the application on the old PC. That separates the application from the storage and lets you expand the library without replacing the server. Self-hosted password manager Keep your passwords on your own hardware A password manager is another service that can run on modest hardware. Vaultwarden is a lightweight Bitwarden-compatible server that can synchronize passwords and other vault data with supported clients. The computational requirements are small because the server mainly handles authentication, synchronization, and database operations. Even an older computer can manage the workload for a household. You can run it using the container image and place it behind a reverse proxy such as Caddy or Nginx. For a home-only deployment, keeping the service on your LAN avoids exposing it directly to the public internet. If you need access while traveling, WireGuard provides another option. The important work here is configuration rather than processing power. Use strong authentication, keep the server updated, protect the database with regular backups, and make sure you have a recovery method if the machine fails. This also gives the old PC a role that benefits from continuous availability. Your phone and desktop can synchronize with the same server while the password database remains under your control. Local package mirror Create a local software package archive If you maintain several Linux machines, an old PC can save network bandwidth and reduce the time required to install or update software by keeping commonly used packages locally. A package caching or mirroring system can store packages downloaded by your machines. Fedora systems can use tools such as Pulp for more sophisticated repository management, while simpler caching approaches can serve smaller environments. The value becomes clearer when you regularly reinstall machines or operate several systems running the same distribution. Instead of every computer downloading identical packages from an external repository, the local server can provide packages from inside your network. You can also maintain a repository containing software your machines depend on. That gives you a controlled archive of particular package versions and makes rebuilding systems more predictable. Storage requirements depend on how many repositories and versions you retain. CPU requirements remain relatively small because the machine spends most of its time storing files and serving them over the network. Central SSH bastion host Use an old PC as your SSH gateway Managing several servers becomes easier when SSH access goes through a single gateway. An old Linux PC can act as a bastion host, giving you one controlled entry point into the rest of your network. OpenSSH already provides the necessary functionality. From your workstation, ProxyJump can send an SSH connection through the bastion to an internal server: ssh -J bastion internal-server The internal machines can then remain inaccessible from outside the network. The gateway handles the external connection while the target server only needs to accept SSH traffic from the appropriate internal network. For a larger homelab, this approach gives you a consistent route to virtual machines, physical servers, NAS systems, and other infrastructure. n8n / Hermes Turn it into a personal automation machine with n8n Once the old PC is already running continuously, it can handle jobs that would otherwise depend on your desktop being switched on. n8n provides a visual workflow system for connecting APIs, webhooks, schedules, databases, and notification services. For example, a n8n workflow can periodically fetch RSS feeds, check a website, process incoming files, call an API, and send the result to Telegram or email. You can also use it to trigger scripts on your local network. Hermes can serve a similar purpose if you want to build more personal automation around a Linux machine. The main resource requirement depends on what your workflows actually do. Large data-processing jobs can require more RAM and CPU, while simple API-based workflows can run comfortably on older hardware. This makes an old PC a useful small, always-on automation platform. Once it is connected to your network and configured to start its services automatically, it can handle background jobs without occupying your workstation. Automated backup restoration tester Make an old PC test whether your backups actually work A backup job completing successfully does not prove that you can recover your data. An old PC can periodically restore backups and verify that the resulting files or services actually work. For file backups, you can use a script to restore a sample dataset to a temporary directory and compare checksums or expected files. For virtual machines, the test server can restore an image and boot it under KVM or QEMU. Tools such as Borg, Restic, rsync, ZFS snapshots, and Proxmox Backup Server each provide different building blocks for this kind of setup. A simple shell or Python script can orchestrate the actual test and report the result. You can then connect the result to a notification system. If a scheduled restoration fails, the server can send an alert instead of leaving you to discover the problem when you urgently need the backup. The same machine can test different backup sources over time, making it a dedicated recovery-validation system rather than another general-purpose server. Internet dead man’s switch Build a kill switch A Linux PC can also watch for regular signals from another device. If those signals stop arriving for a specified period, the server can trigger a predefined notification or workflow. You need to account for ordinary failures such as an internet outage or power loss. A single missed request should not trigger anything important, and you can also use longer timeouts and multiple checks to reduce false alarms. A simple implementation can use Uptime Kuma, a small HTTP endpoint, or a custom systemd service. Your phone or another computer periodically contacts the server. The server records the last successful heartbeat and acts if the expected check-ins stop. You can also design the project around a specific purpose. Instead of giving the machine permission to perform an irreversible action, have it notify a trusted person or trigger a reversible workflow. Give that old PC a job An aging computer does not have to run a demanding desktop environment to remain useful. Linux can turn it into infrastructure that handles a specific task continuously and reliably. Some of these projects also work well together. The same machine can host several lightweight services, or you can dedicate separate old PCs to the jobs where isolation and reliability matter more. Either way, the useful part of the hardware is no longer its ability to run a demanding desktop. It's that it can stay on, stay connected, and quietly do the job.

item.title: Waze's best feature is also its most annoying—here are the settings I changed to tame it
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 5.05
One of the best things about Waze is also one of the worst. The app lets users report hazards, which are then shared with every other Waze user on the same stretch of road. These alerts can be really useful, but they can quickly get incredibly annoying. Waze's constant warnings were driving me mad I didn't want to know about every car on the shoulder Some of the community-submitted Waze alerts are genuinely helpful. Where I live, there are a lot of old roads, many of which have horrific potholes. Some are so deep they could damage my car if I'm not careful to avoid them. Waze giving me an audible warning about a pothole ahead is genuinely useful. Since the locations are user-submitted, almost all the worst potholes in my area generate alerts, making them far easier to avoid and saving me from expensive repairs. Unfortunately, Waze doesn't stop at pothole alerts. It also alerts you to many other road features, from speed bumps and sharp curves to complex intersections and multi-lane merges. Beyond road features, Waze alerts you to crashes, traffic, vehicles on the shoulder, bad weather, blocked lanes, and even animals in the road. The constant barrage of alerts can soon get annoying. This is especially true when you're listening to your perfectly curated road trip playlist or trying to follow the complex plot of an audiobook, and it keeps getting interrupted by yet another alert telling you that there's a car on the shoulder. Waze says it limits alerts, but there are often still too many The intent is to reduce distractions Waze gives a lot of alerts, but it could actually be even worse. In some situations, Waze may actively reduce the number of alerts you get. According to the Waze support pages, the alerts that you receive will depend on your current driving location. You may get more alerts "where you need to pay more attention to the road, such as when you are approaching an accident-prone segment, where there is a hazard on the road, a significant speed decrease and more." The support page goes on to state that "in order to minimize drivers' distraction, we limit the amount of alerts a driver may see on a single route." It also explains that alerts are prioritized based on different factors such as how familiar you are with the road and how many alerts affect your route. The upshot is that you may not get alerted about everything. Despite these features, the default Waze settings are still far too annoying for my liking. I get so many alerts about cars parked on the shoulder, which I'm not particularly worried about. Thankfully, there's a simple fix that means I don't need to switch back to Google Maps. You can take control of how Waze alerts are delivered Replace audible alerts with visual ones The good news is that Waze gives you some level of control over how you receive these types of alerts. You can opt to disable the hazard alerts completely, receive audible and map alerts, or have them appear only on the map. Choosing the latter option can make driving using Waze far less annoying while still letting you see the important information. To change these settings, open Waze, tap the menu icon, and select Settings. Under Driving preferences, tap Alerts and reports. Select Reports to see a full list of all the available types of reports. To change whether an alert is spoken or shown on the map, tap a report type, such as Vehicle on shoulder. Toggle Show on Map and Alert while Driving on or off to suit your needs. Some sections, such as Road features, contain multiple types of alerts, and you can configure each of these individually. Your settings apply globally; if you change how a report is delivered, it will apply to all subsequent journeys, not merely the one you're currently making. If you want to bring audible alerts back, you'll need to go back into the settings and re-enable them. Waze is now far less annoying to use I get the alerts I want without those that I don't The control Waze gives you is reasonably granular, but not completely. You can adjust a large number of report types, but some alerts fall under a wider category, so you can't disable them individually. For example, pothole alerts fall under Other hazards, so I have to leave this category enabled in order to get them. I was able to disable the Vehicle on shoulder alerts, however, and these were the ones that annoyed me the most. I still see them on the map, but my music doesn't get interrupted by audio ducking every time I pass a car that's pulled over safely on the side of the road. With so many reports available, it can take a little time to get the settings exactly how you want them. It's worth the effort; driving with Waze is now a far less annoying experience. Make Waze your own Not every journey is the same, and some of the Waze alerts may not be ideal for the routes you drive most often. Adjusting the report settings ensures you only get the alerts you want, without distractions from information you don't need. if you're still not sure whether to use Waze or Google Maps, it's worth taking a look at the key differences.

item.title: Home Assistant phone and watch notifications just got a major upgrade
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 5.01
Phone and watch notifications are one of the most effective ways to share information from Home Assistant. A recent update to the Home Assistant Companion app quietly made these notifications even more powerful. Home Assistant now supports Live Activities on iOS Notifications can update over time instead of disappearing If you're an Android user, this isn't particularly exciting news. Home Assistant has supported Live Updates on Android 16 or later since February 2026. For iPhone users, however, this is a brand-new feature. Live Activities show ongoing, changing information on iOS devices without having to display notification after notification. The Live Activity stays visible on the iPhone Lock Screen and in the Dynamic Island on supported devices, with the information it contains able to update over time. You need to run the 2026.9.0 release or later of the Home Assistant Companion app, Home Assistant Core 2026.7.0 or later, and at least iOS 17.2 on your iPhone. You can then use Home Assistant to send Live Activity notifications to your iPhone. You can display progress bars and live countdowns Some processing can happen on device Turning a Home Assistant notification into a Live Activity (or Live Updates on Android) is as simple as adding live_update: true and a tag to the data payload of the notification. The Companion app will then display the notification as a Live Activity rather than a standard notification. You can update the Live Activity simply by sending another notification with the same tag and live_update: true. This replaces the current Live Activity rather than creating a new one. Home Assistant recommends avoiding sending constant updates, since iOS may throttle or even drop push delivery if updates are too frequent, although throttling doesn't apply if you're using local push. You can also let your iPhone handle some of the updates itself. You can use chronometer to add a timer to the Live Activity, and the iPhone will process it, so you don't need to send updates every second. There are plenty of useful ways to use these Live Activity notifications. You can display the progress of your robot vacuum, including the room it's currently cleaning. You can track the progress of your 3D printer and see how long is left on the print, or monitor how long a door has been left open. I'm using a Live Activity notification to track how long I sit at my desk. It uses an mmWave presence sensor to detect when I'm in my home office chair, and the Live Activity shows the elapsed time since I sat down and clears once I get out of the chair. It's a great motivation to get up and walk around when I can see that I've been sitting down for hours at a time with a quick glance at my phone. Live Activities can automatically appear on your Apple Watch See your smart home status on your wrist If you have an Apple Watch, you can also see Home Assistant Live Activities on your wrist. Your watch can automatically mirror the Live Activity from your iPhone. The Live Activity will appear at the top of the Smart Stack that you can access by swiping up or rotating the Digital Crown. This means that you can check the status of a Home Assistant Live Activity just by looking at your wrist, without having to fish out your iPhone. If you're keeping track of how long your washing machine has been running, for example, then a quick glance can show you how long it's been running or how long is left. If you don't want these Live Activities to appear on your Apple Watch, you can disable them through the Watch app on your iPhone. Go to General -> Auto-Launch -> Live Activities Settings, and scroll down and tap Home Assistant. Toggle Mirror Live Activity from iPhone off. Live Activities aren't suitable for everything They're great under the right circumstances This update doesn't mean that you'll never use standard phone notifications again. Live Activities can be useful, but they're not always the best option. If you want to get immediate information about something that has changed, such as a window opening, motion being detected, or your water leak sensor detecting a leak, then a standard notification is a better choice. A critical alert can be even better if the information is urgent enough that you need to be notified even when your phone is muted or in a Focus mode. There are also some practical limitations. If your sensor updates every 30 milliseconds and constantly changes values, sending every update as a Live Activity notification will soon cause notifications to be throttled or dropped. Activities that only run for a few seconds are also unsuited, since you may not even notice them on your phone before they're gone. In the right circumstances, however, using Live Activities can be an even more useful way to display information from Home Assistant. It's well worth experimenting to see what you can do with them. Live Activities are a significant upgrade The real benefit of this change isn't that you get more stylish or better-looking notifications. It's that you can now make ongoing information from your smart home easily visible somewhere that you're regularly looking, whether that's your phone's screen or your smartwatch. It makes tracking this updating information even easier to do.

item.title: Please stop using the HDMI cable that came with your monitor
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 4.55
Most people buying a high-end monitor spend real time researching panel technology, refresh rates, and color accuracy, then plug it into the cable that came in the box without a second thought. That cable is usually a budget part from a generation or two ago, rated for a fraction of the bandwidth the display actually needs. That's the problem. You have to stop pretending that the cable is part of the whole package; it's more like a bonus when you pick the right monitor for your PC. The cable in the box is holding your monitor back Your free cable can't handle the signal People drop serious money on a monitor with high refresh rates, native 4K or 8K, deep color, and then plug it in with the cable that came in the box. That stock cable is usually a cheap one that helps offset the cost for the seller. It's generally gonna be an old Standard or High Speed HDMI cable that would be terrible for any 4k screen. Those kinds of cables can't carry the data a modern high-performance panel needs. So the GPU can't bring up a full-bandwidth link or reliably read the detailed timing parameters, and the whole thing just falls back to whatever it can manage. You end up stuck at 1080p or 60 Hz, which is fine for an older cheap monitor but not for the expensive ones you're buying today. You are literally being held back because of the limitations of your cable. Digital video isn't just some clean stream of ones and zeros floating through the wire, even though that's what most people assume. The cables themselves move it, and the quality of that cable and how it was made matters a lot. Cheap bundled cables cut corners hard on construction and materials to save money. You have to be careful because some could have tinned copper braiding, or maybe the maker skipped the secondary braid or used low-grade foil that tears during manufacturing. You have to match your cord to your monitor, but it's very rare that the cable in the box actually matches what your monitor needs. In this case, you're going to need to look for a cable yourself and add that cost at the end of it. However, they're pretty cheap compared to any monitor, so it's worth the price. If you're feeling cheap, just remember there's not a single panel that can do better than the cable you use, no matter how good the hardware or backlighting is. Pick a cable that actually fits your setup Certified cables keep your picture clean You want something officially certified for the resolution and refresh rate you're actually running. Premium High Speed HDMI guarantees 18 Gbps, which handles uncompressed 4K at 60 Hz with HDR. Ultra High Speed HDMI goes through Category 3 testing and delivers the full 48 Gbps, enough for 4K at 120 Hz or 8K at 60 Hz. The certified HDMI cables also tend to use gold-plated connectors. If you don't know any better, that sounds extravagant, but they're meant to resist oxidation and keep contact resistance low. That's what stops the random blackouts you get from cheap nickel plating breaking down. They normally have solid oxygen-free copper conductors, foamed insulation, and shielding built from twisted-pair foil wraps with a tinned copper braid over the top. All of that holds the cable at a strict 100-ohm impedance. Certification also means the cable was tested at an Authorized Test Center. That matters more than people think, since high-frequency digital noise can mess with your Wi-Fi or Bluetooth, and those tests cover it. To check if you got a real one, look for the QR certification label on the box and scan it with the authentication app. It confirms that the exact cable length was independently tested and registered. And buy a length that fits your setup, usually one to two meters. Go too long and you get signal attenuation. Go too short and you're straining your display connectors. Cable management actually matters for signal integrity too, not just looks. These signals run at tens of gigabits per second, and they're sensitive to the physical shape of the cable. So make sure you treat your cable well. Digital cables still have real limits Cheap cables break instead of getting blurry The argument against expensive cables isn't wrong, either. Digital video doesn't degrade the way analog did, where a bad cable gave you a dimmer, grainy picture. If the display decodes the bitstream, the image is perfect. If you mess with the cable or cheap out on a bad one, you'll run into problems. You'll get impedance spikes that blow past tolerance and send signal reflections back toward the source. Meanwhile, the flimsy foil shielding tears and degrades, letting in electromagnetic interference and crosstalk between pairs. Also, cheap connector contacts oxidize over time, thanks to the lack of gold, which raises resistance right at the port. Stack all that up, and you'll see it on screen. It shows up as stuff breaking instead of a blurry image. You need a new cable I will agree that bits are bits; there's no getting around that, but it's an incomplete thought. A digital signal either decodes or it doesn't, but whether it decodes depends on so many factors. A cheap bundled cable might hold together at 1080p and give you no reason to question it until you try to run 4K at 120 Hz with HDR enabled. Certified cables aren't expensive relative to the hardware they're connected to, and you'll be happy to spend the extra money when you see the quality. Highwings HDMI 2.1 cable - Length(s) - 2m - Brand - Highwings This Highwings HDMI 2.1 cable is an excellent example of a reasonably priced Ultra High Speed HDMI cable. One thing to note is that only the two-meter version of the cable seems officially certified. - Externally Powered - No

item.title: You're running PC benchmarks wrong, this is the easier and better way to do it
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 4.21
Once you've spent $2,000 on a new graphics card or a high-end CPU, your first instinct is probably to download a suite of benchmarking tools. You want to see the numbers, compare your score with other systems, and make sure you got what you paid for. So you download 3DMark, Cinebench, and a few other tools, run them one after another, and end up with a collection of scores. Then you close everything and go back to using your computer. The problem is that a benchmark score only tells you something useful when you know what question it is answering. Running every synthetic test you can find can consume hours without telling you whether your PC actually performs well for the things you do. Start with the workload Test what you actually use Synthetic benchmarks are useful because they provide controlled workloads for comparing hardware. A CPU benchmark can help compare processors, while a GPU benchmark can reveal differences between graphics cards. The problem begins when the synthetic score becomes the goal rather than the measurement. If gaming is the reason you bought a faster GPU, your games are the most relevant test. If you compile software every day, compilation time tells you more about your CPU and storage than a generic benchmark score. If you render video or 3D scenes, measure those workloads directly. The test should follow the question you are trying to answer. A graphics card that produces an excellent synthetic score can still deliver disappointing results in a particular game if the CPU, game engine, memory, or settings become the limiting factor. Likewise, a CPU that performs extremely well in a heavily threaded benchmark may provide a smaller improvement in an application with a different workload. Build a baseline Measure the system before making changes Before installing new hardware or changing an important system setting, record how the current configuration performs. For gaming, record frame rates and frame-time behavior in the same game, at the same resolution and graphics settings. For productivity workloads, record how long the same project takes to compile, render, encode, or export. Also record temperatures and clock speeds when thermal behavior could affect performance. For example: CPU: Intel Core i9-14900K GPU: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090 Memory: 32 GB OS: Fedora Workload: Blender render Run 1: 08:42 Run 2: 08:39 Run 3: 08:41 Peak CPU temperature: 78°C Sustained CPU clock: 4.2 GHz After the upgrade, repeat the same workload under comparable conditions. Now you have a meaningful before-and-after comparison instead of two unrelated benchmark scores. Keep the rest of the configuration as consistent as possible when evaluating a specific component. Changing the CPU, motherboard, memory, storage, and operating system at the same time makes the final performance difference difficult to attribute. A single benchmark run can be affected by background activity, temperature, power management, or other temporary conditions. Running the same test two or three times gives you a better idea of the system’s normal behavior. Consider these results: 10,421 10,438 10,397 10,429 10,415 There is little reason to treat 10,438 as the definitive score. The results are tightly grouped and establish a fairly consistent range. Now consider: 10,421 9,812 10,437 The middle result deserves investigation because it is considerably lower than the other two. Something may have interrupted the workload, affected the hardware’s clocks, or changed its thermal or power behavior. You do not need dozens of runs. A few consistent results are usually enough for everyday testing, and an average can provide a useful summary when the measurements are comparable. Monitor the hardware Find out why performance changes A benchmark score tells you what happened but monitoring can help explain why. For CPU workloads, watch temperature, utilization, clock frequency, and power consumption. For GPUs, monitor utilization, temperature, clock speed, memory usage, and power. On Linux, tools such as lm-sensors can provide useful information depending on your hardware. On Windows, you can use the HWiNFO sensor. This becomes particularly important when a result is lower than expected. Suppose a CPU benchmark produces a surprisingly low score. Monitoring may show that the processor reaches its thermal limit and subsequently reduces its clock speed. The benchmark has identified a performance problem, while the monitoring data has identified a likely cause. The same principle applies to GPUs. High temperatures, power limits, or unstable clocks can affect sustained performance, particularly in laptops and small-form-factor systems where cooling capacity is limited. You can also use monitoring to evaluate upgrades that do not produce a higher benchmark score. A new cooler might leave performance almost unchanged while substantially reducing temperatures and fan noise. That can still be a successful upgrade. Test your real applications Measure time, frame times, and completion The most useful benchmark is often the workload you already perform. If you compile software, time a full build using the same source tree and build configuration. If you render video, export the same project with the same settings. If you work with 3D applications, render the same scene. For gaming, use the same game, resolution, graphics settings, and test sequence. Gaming deserves particular attention because average FPS does not describe the entire experience. Frame-time data can reveal short periods of severe stuttering that an average FPS figure hides. Looking at 1% lows can also help identify inconsistent performance. The same principle applies to storage. An NVMe SSD might advertise sequential read speeds around 7 GB/s, but that figure tells you little about how quickly your applications start or how a workload involving thousands of small files will perform. Real workloads connect the measurement directly to the experience you are trying to improve. Keep testing conditions consistent Control the variables that matter Before comparing two results, make sure the important conditions are similar. Use the same application or benchmark version, workload, BIOS settings, power profile, resolution, and graphics settings where relevant. Background applications can also interfere with measurements, so close anything that could consume significant CPU, GPU, memory, or storage resources. When testing sustained performance, allow the hardware to reach a comparable thermal state. Environmental conditions matter too. A processor tested in a cool room can behave differently from the same processor in a much warmer environment. A laptop connected to AC power can also behave differently from one running on battery. You do not need laboratory conditions for useful PC benchmarking. You simply need to know which variables could affect the result and keep them reasonably consistent. A simpler benchmarking process Start with the question you want to answer, establish a baseline, choose a relevant workload, monitor the hardware, repeat the test, and compare the results. That is enough for most everyday PC benchmarking. You can still use Cinebench, 3DMark, Geekbench, Blender, fio, stress-ng, or game benchmarks when they provide useful information. The important part is knowing what the measurement tells you. Once you focus on repeatable results from workloads you actually care about, benchmarking becomes faster, easier to reproduce, and much more useful.

item.title: I tested my network 4 different ways, and finally found what was slowing it down
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 4.06
Those of us who complain about slow Wi-Fi are often left scrambling for answers. And scramble, I have. I tested 20 different ways to improve my Wi-Fi network, but to be able to tell which are actually helping, I had to devise a reliable plan for testing speeds. Local iPerf testing tells me what the network itself can actually do Remove the internet from the test completely If you want to know the actual speed of your connection, the first thing to do is find the right tool. I used iPerf3, a network-testing tool that measures throughput directly between two devices on your local network. In that setup, one device acts as the server, the other as the client, and the test traffic doesn't have to leave your home. That gives you a clearer picture, as it doesn't rely on any third-party servers, websites, or apps; this is all about your home connection. The ideal setting for this is to use iPerf3 on a PC connected to the router or switch over Ethernet. If you follow my coverage here at How-To Geek, you've probably gathered just how big a fan of Ethernet I am. In fact, moving some stuff off of Wi-Fi massively improved my home internet. In this case, doing this gives you the best stability, and it shows you a baseline for what the LAN itself can handle without Wi-Fi or your ISP muddying the results. And the test itself will quickly reveal if there's something wrong, because if your network is supposed to be 1Gbps but iPerf is only pushing a fraction of that between two wired machines, you'll know there's a local bottleneck hiding in there somewhere. Next step? Run this same test on a Wi-Fi device connecting to that wired server, using its local IP address. That's a test for the wireless link that also keeps the ISP totally out of it, which, if you ask me, is great news—I've not had the best luck with ISPs. A LAN file copy shows whether fast benchmarks translate to real work The disks and SMB get a vote, too My testing adventures don't stop here. iPerf3 is good because it isolates the network itself, but I also like to copy one large file between two devices on the LAN. That gives me an idea of what the connection feels like when I'm actually doing something, which, to me, is ultimately a much better way to measure than just relying on synthetic benchmarks. "A big file" isn't a random suggestion, by the way. That's a better option than a folder full of tiny files, because small files add extra filesystem and SMB overhead. That can make the transfer look slower for reasons that aren't related to the network itself, so it kind of defeats the purpose. Be careful not to run into a different sort of bottleneck, though. The storage on both ends of this little experiment needs to be fast enough to keep up. If iPerf3 gets close to saturating the link, but the files are crawling along instead of copying at a decent pace, don't immediately jump to the network as the culprit: check the drives, SMB behavior, CPU load, and background processes first. A wired speed test is the best way to judge your connection Now I test beyond the router At the risk of repeating myself, I'll say it again: a wired test is the best way to do this. So, once I know that the local network is doing A-OK, I bring the actual internet back into the picture. For this part, I recommend connecting a PC to the router over Ethernet, then turning off Wi-Fi entirely. Then, run a regular internet speed test to see what your ISP connection can deliver without being bogged down by things like signal strength, interference, or distance from the router, as well as all that other Wi-Fi-adjacent nonsense.
