This is also where your router's own speed test comes in as a useful point of comparison. Is it better? Is it worse? If it's fairly close to your plan's full speed, the WAN side is most likely doing a good enough job. But if the router looks great and the wired PC is much slower, that means issues that aren't router-related, such as the LAN port, the Ethernet cable, the network adapter, or any other number of local bottlenecks between the router and the device. Wi-Fi has to be tested where you actually use it One result beside the router tells me almost nothing We're circling back to Wi-Fi for this final check, and yes, you should only proceed if the wired side has proven itself to be in top shape. That lets you judge Wi-Fi as a standalone connection in your home, and that can save some trouble, as it isolates potential problems and narrows them down to just the wireless side of things. Coincidentally, this is where a lot of testing goes wrong, because Wi-Fi introduces an inherent element of unpredictability. It has a lot to do with your distance to the router, because getting a good result right next to the device tells you nothing about how well it'll perform once you're a room or two away. For this test to have any meaning whatsoever, I recommend testing a few spots around the home, preferably using the same laptop or phone each time. At each location, compare both the local and the internet-side results, and that means running iPerf3 against the same wired server, then following it up with a regular internet speed test. If a particular location in your home shows a huge drop in the connection while everything else looks fine, you might be dealing with dead zones. The useful number is the one that isolates the problem Speaking as a person who's spent more time fiddling with her internet connection than I can truly recommend, I'll tell you that there's no magic threshold where your internet speed goes from "slow" to "fast." It's more about what's good enough to you and your needs, as well as what exact number you're looking at. The more thorough your testing, the easier it'll be to isolate the bottleneck (and hopefully fix it, too).

item.title: 6 beginner self-hosting projects you can run on any old PC
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 3.87
Your busted laptop from 2019 or that old desktop that has been gathering dust in a closet might not be suitable for use as a "normal" PC, but they have more than enough power to run useful services. You don't need a data center tucked under your desk to get started with self-hosting—almost any PC will do. These are six lightweight apps or services that you can run on almost any PC that'll still boot today without requiring an expensive RAM upgrade. Pi-hole Network-wide ad-block and tracker blocking Pi-hole is a classic self-hosting project because it is useful, easy to set up, and low-stakes if something breaks. A Pi-hole sits between the devices on your network and a DNS server on the internet, where it can effectively prevent specified websites from loading by referencing a blocklist. If you use the right blocklist, you can block ads, trackers, and even some malware. That makes it an especially useful project if you have a lot of smart devices on your network that don't support conventional ad blocking. Additionally, the Pi-hole's dashboard makes it easy to know which device is trying to access the internet, when, and the domain it is trying to connect to. If you're privacy conscious, that allows you to prevent many smart devices from "phoning home" without your permission. You can run a Pi-hole using Docker on almost any major operating system, but I typically install it using the official install script on Linux instead. Once it has been installed, you need to log into your router's admin panel (use the app or the web portal) and point the router's DNS server at the Pi-hole's local IP address. Then all you need to do is select a blocklist that you like. Vaultwarden Store your own passwords securely Bitwarden is an open-source password manager that normally relies on Bitwarden's official servers to store your passwords, but it isn't strictly necessary. If you want, you can host your own password server using Vaultwarden. Vaultwarden is an implementation of the normal Bitwarden Client API written in Rust. Critically, that means that you can use the official Bitwarden app on your phone or desktop—or the browser extension—normally to connect to it. You also get the premium features Bitwarden offers, like time-based one-time-passwords (TOTPs) and attachments at no cost. Vaultwarden only uses a few hundred megabytes of RAM (at most), so it'll run on pretty much anything. However, you're assuming total responsibility for maintaining robust backups of your passwords and making sure that your network is secured against would-be intruders. Syncthing Keep files moving between devices without a cloud account If you don't like using Google Drive or OneDrive every time you need to sync your files from one device to another, you could self-host Syncthing instead. Rather than rely on a cloud-based provider, Syncthing works by creating a continuous, encrypted peer-to-peer sync system between the devices you set up. Those devices could be anything, ranging from phones to personal computers to home servers. When you add an old PC into the mix as an always-on node, it functions a bit like your own personal central cloud server. Say you have three different devices on your network: A, B, and C, where B is your old PC working as an always-on node. If A and C need to sync their files, but they're not always online at the same time, they can both just send the files to be synced to B in the interim. When A comes online, B will send C's files to the A device and vice versa. Syncthing's footprint is pretty small, and usually only consumes a few hundred megabytes of RAM at a time. FreshRSS News and a feed without the algorithm One of my least favorite parts of the modern internet is algorithmically driven feeds. So, I switched to an RSS feed instead. FreshRSS is a simple, lightweight RSS aggregator that you can self-host. It offers a web UI and API support for mobile apps, so you can access it from any modern device. It allows you to follow blogs, subreddits, YouTube channels, and countless other things without a recommendation engine making decisions on your behalf. Uptime Kuma Monitoring everything you host Once your homelab has grown to more than a handful of services, manually keeping track of them all is a pain. Uptime Kuma is a self-hosted service that monitors them for you. If something goes wrong, you can have notifications sent to you via Discord, Telegram, Email, or ntfy. It isn't a system metrics tool, though. If you want an overview of your network's performance, or detailed CPU and RAM usage information, you'll need to look elsewhere. Homepage If you build a homelab, you need a dashboard If you're not running Caddy (or some other service) to give all of your services easily-memorable domain names, then keeping track of your services can get to be pretty tedious. I have more than 20 self-hosted services running on my network these days, and I have no hope of remembering whether Jellyfin or Navidrome live at 192.168.0.111 or 192.168.0.101. Fortunately, I don't have to enter an IP address manually most of the time. Homepage is a dashboard that provides an overview and link to all of the self-hosted services on my network. It integrates neatly with Pi-hole, Uptime Kuma, Proxmox, and Docker to provide tidy widgets that display the status of various services running on your network. The only slight downside is that you handle configuration via YAML files, which are a type of text file. They're human-readable, so you don't need to know C++ or Python to configure Homepage. Self-hosting doesn't need anything special None of the services on this list are especially demanding, and if you use Proxmox or Docker, you could probably run all of them on a single 10-year-old desktop PC with 8GB of RAM as long as you are careful. If you had 16GB of RAM, you'd easily be able to run a dozen lightweight services.

item.title: 4 AirTag features that are still missing from Android trackers
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 3.64
Android trackers used to lag far behind AirTags, but they've closed the gap considerably. Google's Find Hub now supports crowdsourced location finding, tracker sharing, and Ultra Wideband (UWB) precision finding when using compatible phones and trackers. AirTags still do a few things that Android trackers can't when using Google's Find Hub. Getting warned when you leave an item behind AirTags let you know before you even realize something is missing The Find My app can send you a notification when your iPhone becomes separated from an AirTag or other supported Find My item. For example, if you put an AirTag on your keyring and walk out of a coffee shop with your keys still on the table, your iPhone can notify you that the AirTag was left behind. Instead of simply helping you track down lost items, AirTags can actively prevent you from losing them in the first place. This Notify When Left Behind feature is one of the most useful things about AirTags. Currently, Google's Find Hub has no equivalent feature, which is a significant omission. The feature is on the way, however. The Pixel Tag is due to be released in November 2026, and Google has announced that it will support Left Behind alerts when it launches. For now, this is still perhaps the biggest advantage of using AirTags. Finding lost tags in quieter places Find Hub uses aggregated locations by default One of the cleverest features of AirTags is that they can use crowdsourced location finding. An AirTag doesn't have its own mobile network connection, so if it gets separated from your iPhone, you might expect to lose contact with it completely. However, nearby Apple devices can detect the AirTag's Bluetooth signal and share its location using their own network connections, letting you track an AirTag in the wild even when you're miles away. Find Hub uses a similar crowdsourced location system, but there's a significant difference from Apple's setup. Find Hub's default setting is With network in busy places only. This setting means that Find Hub waits for multiple Android devices to detect an item before providing the owner with the aggregated location. In other words, the feature works best in areas with a lot of foot traffic, such as airports or busy pedestrian areas. If you lose your Android tracker on a quiet trail in the woods, and a single person carrying an Android device passes by, this default setting means that you won't immediately be provided with the location of the tracker. This will only happen if the device is set to use the With network everywhere setting. Apple's Find My doesn't have the same aggregation requirements. A single detection can be enough to share the location of your AirTag. Precision Finding with every AirTag Your Android phone and tracker both need UWB Finding the rough location of your device is only the beginning. Once you have a ballpark location, you need to know precisely where to look. Precision Finding with AirTags makes this possible. Precision Finding uses short-range wireless technology called Ultra Wideband (UWB) to accurately determine the distance and direction of your AirTag from your iPhone. You can follow on-screen instructions to the location of the AirTag. UWB isn't exclusive to AirTags. Google's Find Hub now supports a similar kind of precision finding using UWB technology. The difference is that this isn't standard across all Android trackers. Every AirTag includes UWB, with the new AirTag 2 including an upgraded Ultra Wideband chip for expanded Precision Finding range on newer iPhones. As long as your iPhone supports UWB, you can use Precision Finding for all your AirTags. With Android trackers, you need both a supported phone and a supported tracker, and not every tracker will work. Using your smartwatch to find a tracker's precise location You can find an AirTag 2 without using your phone at all While Precision Finding will work for any AirTag with a compatible iPhone, if you're using an AirTag 2, you can skip your phone completely. With an Apple Watch Series 9 or later, or an Apple Watch Ultra 2 or later, you can use Precision Finding for an AirTag 2 directly from your watch. Even if you don't have your iPhone to hand, you can follow the directions on your Apple Watch to lead you to the location of your AirTag 2. While Wear OS can work with an Android tracker to play sounds or give directions to its last location, you can't use a Wear OS watch to find the tracker using precision finding; you still need to use your phone. Google hasn't announced this functionality for the upcoming Pixel Tag, either. While Google has said you will be able to use a Wear OS watch to ring your Pixel Tag from your wrist, it hasn't mentioned precision finding from a watch, despite the Pixel Tag containing UWB tech. Android trackers are catching up AirTags used to have much better features than many Android trackers, but Google has slowly closed the gap. Android trackers still can't match everything an AirTag can do, but that may not be true for much longer.

item.title: 5 VS Code plugins so fundamental they should be built in
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 3.58
Visual Studio Code (VS Code) is arguably one of the most popular text editors and integrated development environments widely used by individual coders and professionals. But the standard setup can make you work harder than necessary for simple tasks. Whether it's catching a syntax error that requires you to squint at the Problems panel at the bottom or scrolling through dozens of lines to find a matching closing tag for your HTML block. These minor friction points silently steal your time, especially if you're new to the platform and everything you look at is your code. So, I found these five extensions, which I believe should have been built-in in the first place, to address these problems, help you catch errors, and save time on repetitive tasks. Error Lens Catch broken syntax and typos without checking the bottom problems tray By default, VS Code indicates syntax errors, compile-time bugs, code warnings, etc., with red, yellow, or orange squiggly lines right beneath the problematic code. To read the compiler or linter diagnostics, you have to stop typing and hover your mouse over the exact error line. Alternatively, you can keep the bottom Problems panel open, which eats up your valuable screen real estate. Error Lens extension by Alexander addresses this friction. Instead of hiding critical errors, it pulls the diagnostic message and prints it directly at the end of the broken line in bright red or yellow text as you type. For example, if I accidentally drop a closing parenthesis on a console.log(phone.model); statement in my JavaScript code, Error Lens instantly highlights the entire line in red and tells me exactly what's missing. This helps me actively debug my code as I type, a real-time safety net that should have been built into the code editor by default. Prettier - Code formatter Stop fixing indentation and trailing commas by hand I deal with JSON files quite often when building AI apps. Working with these raw data exports often results in jagged indentation, inconsistent quotes, and trailing commas that can cause JSON parsing errors. The Prettier extension solves this by automatically formatting your code by standardizing indentation, spacing, and quotes every single time you save the code. It enforces a unified style guide across JavaScript, TypeScript, JSON, HTML, Markdown, and more by parsing your code and reprinting it with its own rules, taking the maximum line length into account and wrapping code when necessary. If you use VS Code's editor.defaultFormatter settings. After installing the extension, you'll need to manually tweak the VS Code settings to make Prettier your default formatter. To do so, go to Settings, and search for "default formatter" and set Editor: Default Formatter to Prettier - Code formatter. Auto Rename Tag For synchronized HTML editing I'm sure you've faced this hassle of keeping nested HTML elements in sync when modifying markup structures or refactoring frontend layouts. Changing an opening HTML tag and forgetting to update its closing tag can create malformed markup and force manual cleanup. The Auto Rename Tag extension by Jun Han removes this friction entirely. It automatically renames paired HTML/XML tags. Running in the background, it mirrors tag edits in real time: updating an opening tag instantly renames its closing tag, and vice versa. This has certainly saved me a lot of time, especially when dealing with complex markup structures. Though VS Code offers a native Editor: Linked Editing setting, it strictly limits out-of-the-box support to HTML and Handlebars. Auto Rename Tag remains essential as it covers everything else — including XML, PHP, and React (.jsx) files — without conflicting with the native setting. GitLens View commit context and authors directly inside the active file The default VS Code source control panel is built to offer you the current source control state but doesn't provide much historical context. Figuring out when the last commit was made, why a specific function was modified, or who touched a broken line requires you to manually dig through terminal logs or the clunky built-in timeline view. The GitLens extension by GitKraken fixes this by offering visual cues about code authorship right next to the line where your cursor is positioned. You'll see faint gray "blame" annotations showing the commit author, date, and commit message, giving you a seamless way to see commit context directly in the editor. As you can the commit hash and my commit note about fixing the syntax error. After installing the GitLens extension, it'll prompt you to create an account during onboarding, but the core inline blame annotations work entirely within the free Community Edition without signing in. Better Comments Transform neglected code comments into color-coded action items Standard code comments use a uniform, muted gray or dark green font. Because they blend into the background, critical warning notes, architecture questions, to-dos, and temporary workarounds can easily get lost in a slew of code lines. The Better Comments extension by Aaron Bond helps you address this issue. It will help you write more human-friendly comments in your code that deserve the right attention. Adding the right annotation tag at the beginning of each comment lets the extension style it with a different color code for instant visual cues. For instance, I've used these annotation tags in my src/index.js file. | Prefix | What it does | |---|---| | // ! | Highlights alerts in red | | // ? | Highlights queries in blue | | // TODO: | Marks pending tasks in orange | | // * | Highlights general technical notes in light green | | // | Can be used to style commented-out code with a strike through | You can also customize the default tags, colors, and text styles or add your own tags through the extension settings. Stop settling for the default VS Code experience One of the best things about VS Code is that it's minimal by default, yet its community extension ecosystem lets you make it exactly as powerful and complex as you need. These lightweight extensions have certainly made my coding life simpler by surfacing errors, git messages, and comments and making my code prettier too. There are many more extensions to explore, but hopefully these five give you a solid starting point.

item.title: I turned my giant Excel formula into something I can actually understand
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 3.42
We all know someone who loves building a ridiculously complicated Excel formula and proudly announcing that it works. I used to be that person. I've been writing Excel formulas for decades, and I loved the satisfaction of making a single formula handle a problem that once seemed impossible. The trouble was, those formulas could become a lot less impressive when I came back to them later. Then along came the LET function. My long Excel formula worked fine—until I had to read it It felt like cracking the Enigma code Take this Excel table as an example. It contains nine columns, four of which feed into the performance score out of 100 for whichever salesperson I select in cell B1. The score combines three measures: 50 points for how much of their sales target they've achieved, 30 points for their profit margin, and 20 points for their average customer rating. Here's the formula I'd enter into cell B2: =MIN(SUMIFS(tblSales[Revenue], tblSales[Salesperson], B1)/MAXIFS(tblSales[Sales Target], tblSales[Salesperson], B1), 1)*50+(SUMIFS(tblSales[Profit], tblSales[Salesperson], B1)/SUMIFS(tblSales[Revenue], tblSales[Salesperson], B1))*30+(AVERAGEIFS(tblSales[Customer Rating], tblSales[Salesperson], B1)/5)*20 There's nothing actually wrong with this formula. Excel understands it perfectly well, and it returns the score I expect. The problem is that if I need to change part of it, explain it to someone else, or come back to it a year later, it can take longer to pick apart than it took to build in the first place. I need to spot that one SUMIFS calculates revenue, that MAXIFS retrieves the sales target, that another SUMIFS calculates profit, and that AVERAGEIFS produces the customer rating. There's also some repetition hiding in there. I'm calculating total revenue twice: once to work out how much of the target the salesperson has achieved, and again to calculate their profit margin. This makes the formula longer and gives me another piece of logic to maintain if I ever need to change it. What I really want to see when I look at the formula is the logic behind it: revenue, target, profit, rating, target score, profit margin, and rating score. I don't want to have to translate a wall of functions, references, and parentheses into those concepts every time I return to the formula. LET lets me give each calculation a name The formula suddenly starts talking my language This is where the LET function—available in Excel for Microsoft 365, Excel 2024 and 2021, and Excel for the web—comes in. I can give each intermediate result a meaningful name, then use those names later in the formula. First, I'll tell Excel that I want to use the name revenue for my first calculation. The name comes first, followed by a comma, then the calculation that produces its value: =LET( revenue, SUMIFS(tblSales[Revenue], tblSales[Salesperson], B1), Next, I'll add the salesperson's target: =LET( revenue, SUMIFS(tblSales[Revenue], tblSales[Salesperson], B1), target, MAXIFS(tblSales[Sales Target], tblSales[Salesperson], B1), I'll do the same thing for profit and the average customer rating: =LET( revenue, SUMIFS(tblSales[Revenue], tblSales[Salesperson], B1), target, MAXIFS(tblSales[Sales Target], tblSales[Salesperson], B1), profit, SUMIFS(tblSales[Profit], tblSales[Salesperson], B1), rating, AVERAGEIFS(tblSales[Customer Rating], tblSales[Salesperson], B1), At this point, I've replaced four chunks of complicated-looking calculations with four names that tell me exactly what each result represents. More importantly, I can now use those names to build the next part of the calculation. The targetScore is the salesperson's revenue divided by their target, capped at 100%. The profitMargin is profit divided by revenue, and the ratingScore is the rating converted from a five-point scale: =LET( revenue, SUMIFS(tblSales[Revenue], tblSales[Salesperson], B1), target, MAXIFS(tblSales[Sales Target], tblSales[Salesperson], B1), profit, SUMIFS(tblSales[Profit], tblSales[Salesperson], B1), rating, AVERAGEIFS(tblSales[Customer Rating], tblSales[Salesperson], B1), targetScore, MIN(revenue/target,1), profitMargin, profit/revenue, ratingScore, rating/5, Finally, I'll combine those three scores using their respective weightings: =LET( revenue, SUMIFS(tblSales[Revenue], tblSales[Salesperson], B1), target, MAXIFS(tblSales[Sales Target], tblSales[Salesperson], B1), profit, SUMIFS(tblSales[Profit], tblSales[Salesperson], B1), rating, AVERAGEIFS(tblSales[Customer Rating], tblSales[Salesperson], B1), targetScore, MIN(revenue/target,1), profitMargin, profit/revenue, ratingScore, rating/5, (targetScore*50)+(profitMargin*30)+(ratingScore*20) ) The underlying calculations haven't changed. I'm still using SUMIFS to calculate revenue and profit, MAXIFS to retrieve the salesperson's sales target, and AVERAGEIFS to calculate the average customer rating. I've simply named those results to reflect what they mean: revenue, target, profit, and rating. These named variables are now clearly listed in the formula, so I can quickly scan them and see the building blocks of the calculation at a glance. I can then use those names to create targetScore, profitMargin, and ratingScore before combining them into the final score calculation. Also, revenue is now calculated only once and then reused in both targetScore and profitMargin. And if I decide to change one of those calculations or its weighting later, I can find the relevant named component much more easily than I could in the original formula. This is the part of LET that appeals to me most. I'm still asking Excel to do the same work, but the formula is easier to understand, and the logic is more visible. Where do helper formulas fit into the equation? It depends on the intermediate calculations I'm a big fan of helper formulas, whether they're added as columns to an existing dataset or gathered together in a separate table. The screenshot above shows the trade-off. The helper table makes every intermediate calculation easy to see and reuse, but it also adds a sizable chunk of spreadsheet structure for a calculation that ultimately produces a single value. I'd choose helper formulas over LET if I wanted to use those intermediate calculations elsewhere, such as in a separate analysis, a chart, or a PivotTable. But the trade-off is that they add extra machinery. Every additional calculation creates another moving part in the workbook, and the more moving parts you have, the more opportunities there are for errors. So when deciding whether to use LET or helper formulas, I generally follow this rule of thumb: if an intermediate calculation is useful on its own, give it a helper formula. If it's simply supporting one final result, LET can keep it contained in a single formula while keeping the logic clear. Yes, I could hide or group the helper calculations, but that adds another layer of spreadsheet structure to navigate and maintain. With LET, I can keep the supporting calculations inside the formula, leave the existing structure intact, and present the final result without adding calculations that most people will never need to see. My formulas don't have to be a mystery anymore Thanks to functions like LET, I no longer have to create long, unreadable formulas that only make sense to me at the time. I can still make Excel do complicated things, but I can also make the logic behind those calculations much easier to understand. And if I want to add even more context, I can tuck in plain-language notes using the N() function trick.

item.title: Stop avoiding the Linux terminal—here's how to actually get comfortable with it
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 2.94
If you're new to Linux, you might wonder whether you really need to use the terminal. While Linux comes with modern desktop environments, you can benefit from knowing the Linux terminal. It's easier than you think. Just a few simple steps, and you'll be a pro in no time. Why care about the terminal? The terminal tames the desktop chaos Modern Linux distributions typically come with attractive and usable desktop environments that rival Windows or macOS. That's also the problem. Unlike in Windows or macOS, where there's one desktop, there are many different environments. The two most common desktops are GNOME and KDE Plasma. Other desktops, such as Xfce, my favorite, are also common on distros intended for older or slower machines. And then there are the minimal window managers for power users. The result of the proliferation of different user interfaces that work in different ways is that Linux has no single graphical interface. If you needed help with macOS or Windows, there would be a setting in the Control Panel or Settings menu that an expert could point you toward. Command-line fixes are so popular in Linux because the command line is a common denominator across different systems. No matter what user interface your distro comes with, you'll be able to execute shell commands. This is an artifact of the way Unix, which Linux has inherited a lot from, was designed in the '60s, '70s, and '80s. It would be nice if novice users could do everything graphically, but that's the reality of using Linux today, and that seems unlikely to change. Another reason to care about the terminal if you're a more technical computer user or aspiring to be, whether you're a first-year computer science student or just a computer enthusiast, is that it'll give you access to a lot of fun and useful tools. Editors, compilers, servers, and more all work from the command line, so if you're serious about computing, working knowledge of the Linux command line is essential Try doing as much as you can in the terminal The only way to learn is to use it Using the Linux shell is like learning a new language. And one of the best ways to learn a new language is to immerse yourself in it. If you wanted to learn French, the best way would be to spend a few days, weeks, or months in Paris going through everyday life and picking up new words. Soon enough, you would feel confident ordering your morning café crème and croissant from your favorite café. It's the same way with the terminal. Find a tutorial on basic terminal commands, and use it to manipulate files and navigate the directory tree. It might seem scary at first, but you'll soon get over it and be able to learn more commands. Look for text-based alternatives to apps you use You can do more with the terminal than you think One way to stay motivated in learning the Linux command line is to do useful things. One thing you'll do frequently in Linux is edit text, whether that's configuration files or your own scripts and programs. You should feel comfortable with a few basic commands in an editor like Nano, Vim, or Emacs to start with. As with other things on Linux, you'll learn as you go. You can do a lot of other things that you would normally do in a graphical program in the terminal. You can surf the web in terminal-based browsers like Lynx. The disadvantage is that you won't be able to see any images. There would be some upsides, too. If you find yourself getting distracted by social media or the web, this might be an invitation to not spend so much time surfing. More practically, you can test the accessibility of a website, since many people who are blind or have low vision can only rely on text via screen readers. You can also use IRC chat and play games, among other things. IRC is still a great way to connect with open-source developers, and sometimes you also just need a break. A lot of terminal-based games hold up today, such as those in the famous BSD games collection. Repeat things you do frequently Do it again, and again, and again... I consider myself a fluent command-line user, though using it for over 20 years, plus cutting my computing teeth on MS-DOS, probably helped. Drilling commands like an athlete will help you get comfortable. This might sound silly, but I like to imagine running the "ls" command in my head whenever I feel stressed. I suppose the command is like an electronic "worry stone." Repeatedly running commands will build up muscle memory so you won't have to think about the basic commands. You'll be able to see patterns and things you can automate in a shell script. Use your terminal as a desk calculator Don't fumble with the mouse! A terminal makes a handy desk calculator, even though your desktop comes with a graphical calculator. The problem is that they emulate handheld calculators too well. I find it tedious to click on all the buttons. Using a keyboard is a lot quicker for me. You can use command-line programs like dc or bc, but my favorite tool is interactive Python with IPython. I can just start a terminal and leave it running, and when I want a calculation, I can just type it in. Plus, I can tap into powerful libraries like NumPy or SymPy. I like having a desk calculator that can do calculus or linear algebra. You might get so good at the terminal that you dream in it The best way to learn to use the terminal is to use the terminal. The Linux command line might seem scary if you're used to desktop and mobile interfaces, but if you stick with it, you could do it in your sleep. I've been doing this for over 20 years, and I've had actual dreams about it, so that isn't hyperbole.

item.title: 4K remasters have an AI problem, and it's destroying the history of film
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 2.39
Most people probably assume that the latest 4K Blu-ray release of a movie is the definitive version with the highest quality. It's the version that you should buy to preserve that title for yourself at the highest quality. Right? For many films, the process of creating that 4K release does more harm than good, meaning you might end up buying an inauthentic presentation of your favorite flick because AI is now entering the chat. A 4K remaster should reveal an old film, not redesign it That belongs in a museum! What is the goal of a 4K remaster anyway? On the surface, it sounds pretty simple. A VHS tape, LaserDisc, DVD, or standard Blu-ray has a fixed amount of lines (for VHS and LaserDisc) or pixels that limit how much detail can be seen on-screen. So the goal is to increase that detail level to what 4K UHD offers. Which is about 8.3 million pixels. Four times that of a standard Blu-ray, and a silly amount of extra detail compared to older formats. Where does the extra detail come from? If the film was originally shot on actual film, then you can rescan the negatives at higher detail levels. 35mm film holds detail roughly equivalent to between 4K and 6K in digital formats. So when you remaster the movie with fresh scans, you can actually now see detail that was invisible in the original cut but was actually captured on-set. The issues arise when the original film was shot digitally. If a movie was shot in 1080p, then 1080p is the only ground-truth level of detail that film will ever have. To make the image appear sharper and more detailed, you need to use some form of upscaling process. AI upscaling has become the most advanced form of this process, but the AI is making up that extra detail from pure digital imagination, which can also sometimes include hallucinations. "True Lies," "Aliens," and shows what happens when AI starts guessing Now the humans look like aliens There's an excellent video by the YouTube channel Nerrel called AI Can Ruin Movies Now, Too - Aliens and True Lies on 4k, which uses those two titles to break down how AI upscalers are absolutely butchering movies, resulting in a 4K commercial release that is objectively worse than other lower-resolution formats. From giving actors uncanny, smooth, and waxlike skin to distorting or even hallucinating entire faces, it's shocking that any professional film editor would sign off on a final cut like this. What makes it even more egregious is that films like Aliens were indeed shot on celluloid. So there was no reason to use upscaling on a 2K intermediate master. However, doing a proper 4K version based on new film scans is expensive and time-consuming. So you're getting the cheapskate, low-effort 4K cut, and I guess they just hope no one notices. Film grain is part of the photograph, not dirt covering it The medium is the message AI is also one of the technologies used to remove film grain, although some people might call that "denoising." The thing is, film grain isn't a defect that has to be removed; it's the original texture of the medium used to make the movie. To me, it's like taking an oil painting and then treating it to look like it was made using an inkjet printer. An oil painting should look like it was made with oil-based paints, right? But even when those who remaster films argue that film grain is visual distortion that gets in the way of what the filmmaker wanted us to see, there's actually a technical reason why it can be a problem. Film grain makes it hard to compress a film because it's random and therefore gets in the way of repeatable data that can be thrown out. It's why Netflix had to invent a film grain effect. So the movie is compressed with no film grain, and then a filter is applied when it gets played back. It's a decent compromise but doesn't apply to 4K Blu-ray releases, only streamed movies. The remaster could be the only version anyone is allowed to see I have an extensive collection of DVDs and HD Blu-ray movies that I consider the versions that are worth keeping. If the original movie was not meant to have HDR and requires upscaling to hit 4K, then I might as well just let my TV or Blu-ray player do the upscaling based on that source, which is untouched by AI. The thing is, at least no one can come and mess with my discs and change the content. When it comes to streaming services like Disney, you're only likely to have access to that terrible AI-upscaled 4K version, and even when you "buy" a movie digitally, that's what you're going to get. Even the 1080p stream version will only be a downscaled stream of the butchered 4K master. I hate that I need to carefully check how a 4K movie was mastered before spending any money on it, but that's the world we live in now.

item.title: 4 "smart" home gadgets that don't need Wi-Fi or an app
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 2.18
I have a home filled with devices connected to my router, but I'm not fully convinced that these have made my home smarter. In fact, many of my favorite purchases, those I can recommend with an unequivocal yes, don't require an app at all. A night light that stays on when the power goes out It also doubles as a flashlight If there is one cheap upgrade you can make to your home that will absolutely improve your quality of life, it's this. Get a night light that stays on when you lose power. You'll never find yourself stranded in pitch dark. These night lights also serve as flashlights when you unplug them from the wall. I have a house filled with portable power stations I can use to turn the lights back on, but I need the flashlight to help me see our breaker panel in the first place! My phone is typically the most convenient light, but I don't always have it on me. Meanwhile, these night lights are practically shouting "Look at me!" I purchased several GE 4-in-1 Power Failure LED Night Lights from Amazon, and they were my favorite purchase of 2025. Mine relies on AA batteries, but there is a variant with a built-in battery you can switch to instead. Hot water dispenser Enjoy drinks without waiting for water to boil As an avid tea drinker, I loved my electric kettle. I also resigned it to the donate pile as soon as I was sent a Waterdrop M6CG countertop hot water dispenser. Owning one of these things is like having a Keurig without being limited to overpriced, wasteful K-Cups. Put your mug under the dispenser, choose the temperature, and walk away. When you come back, your tea will have steeped. Yet while the countertop hot water dispenser instantly displaced my kettle, I didn't use it for long. As a homeowner, I have the option for a built-in hot water dispenser instead. Waterdrop's K6 instant hot water dispenser now sits next to my kitchen faucet, and it's my favorite kitchen upgrade so far. Unlike the countertop version, it doesn't need to be manually refilled. It also offers more precise temperature controls. It may not have the attractiveness of a smart kettle, but I can still fill a teapot with instant hot water when I want to serve tea the traditional way. Samsung Music Frame A Bluetooth speaker that I want in every room of the house I have ambient music playing all throughout the day. It helps wake me up in the morning as I start to get my kids ready for school. It helps me concentrate as I write. Nothing complements ambient music, music that's intended to blend into the background, quite like a Bluetooth speaker that is just as non-intrusive. The Samsung Music Frame is that speaker. Samsung's picture frame shares its name with the Frame TV, but these are very different products. While the TV has an always-on matte display and comes with Tizen OS, the Music Frame is a traditional picture frame that happens to double as a Bluetooth speaker. It's up to you to supply a paper photo or pay extra for a custom canvas. If you funnel the power cord through the wall as I have, the only tell is the frame's thickness, which is bulkier than the other frames on my wall. The Music Frame technically integrates with Samsung SmartThings, the company's smart home platform, but you don't need to download that app at all to use the Frame as a speaker. Just plug it in, pair it, and start listening to sound that is surprisingly rich. The Music Frame isn't new, so while it remains pricey, you may be able to find one refurbished and heavily discounted, as I did. A battery-powered fan Airflow wherever you need it My home has central air conditioning, but if I have a choice between cranking up the AC and turning up a nearby fan, I'd rather feel air blowing against my skin. Yet even with ceiling fans in nearly every room, some areas still don't get the air. That is why SwitchBot's Circulator Floor Fan isn't a gimmick — it's actually one of my favorite additions to my home this past year. I love this fan so much that, even after being sent a free review sample, I very quickly purchased another one of my own. Like all SwitchBot products, this fan can connect to a SwitchBot hub, be controlled by an app, and integrate with all sorts of automations. That's not the best thing about it. What I love most is the fact that it's simply an attractive-looking battery-powered fan that's easy to pick up and move wherever I want it to be without having to drag around a cord or look for an outlet. I can now float a fan in the middle of our living room without introducing a tripping hazard. The built-in light also provides just enough ambiance to help me navigate spaces at night. The product functions just fine as a portable fan, without requiring an app for setup. Skipping the app makes a smart home more resilient I enjoy my share of smart home automations. It's nice having certain lights come on automatically in the evening and turn off in the morning. I like having ceiling fans that turn on and off based on whether I'm in the room. But these fail when my smart home hub loses power or the internet goes down. The products above are always useful, no matter what my networking is doing.

item.title: 5 ways my Bambu Lab 3D printer has paid for itself this year
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 2.05
When I bought my 3D printer, I didn’t have any great expectations of value for money—but it definitely feels like my Bambu Lab P2S has paid for itself. I’m not just talking about my bank account, either—there are some other pleasing upsides to 3D printer ownership. My new Switch 2 grips are great At a fraction of the price of the retail equivalent The last thing I printed, two days ago, was a set of grips for the Nintendo Switch 2. My console has sat largely unused for the past couple of months, with a backlog of games piling up that I’ve been meaning to play. One of the biggest upsides to the Switch is its portable nature, but I’ve always found it a bit cramped for longer play sessions and games that demand a bit more in terms of dexterity. Instead of buying a set of $60 grips that I wasn’t even sure would fit my hands properly, I spent about $1 on filament to print my own. The result is transformational. Not only have I literally saved $59 plus postage, but I feel like I can properly make use of the console for the first time in its oh-so-cozy portable form factor. So far, all I’ve done with this opportunity is become horribly addicted to Balatro again, but I no longer think twice about hand cramps before reaching for the console. The convenience of 3D-printed fixes shouldn’t be overlooked It’s not always about the money saved Money is one thing, but time and effort are another. I 3D-printed some custom wall plugs to fix a broken awning winch a few weeks ago, and by doing that I was able to avoid buying several different sizes of plugs and having to drive an hour round-trip. I fixed the problem before I’d even made it back from the store. The hardest part is remembering that many household fixes can be solved with a printer. You can 3D-print all sorts of helpful items, from door shims to spare parts. With parametric models, you don’t even need to design your own prints. If you do take the time to develop the skill, you’ll be able to make almost anything. I’ve greatly expanded my camera lens and filter options Adapters ahoy Camera lenses are expensive, and over the years I’ve collected quite a few of them. I don’t take photos quite like I used to, but I’ve managed to rekindle the hobby a bit over the last year with my 3D printer’s ability to create adapters. By far the most exciting are those that allow me to adapt my Sony mirrorless for use with other lenses. This allows me to use Canon, Nikon, and some of the weirder 35mm-era lenses I’ve collected on a completely different camera system, without autofocus. Add to this the camera’s ability to create fine threads for use on filter adapters and manipulate the way light enters the lens for fun bokeh shapes, and I’ve managed to get a lot of value out of a few grams of filament. A hidden AirTag mount might save my bike And my fake trackers aren’t bad either Item finders like AirTags can’t stop your stuff from being stolen, but they can help greatly in its recovery. The only problem is that you need to find somewhere convincing to hide an AirTag so that it’s not immediately disabled and thrown away. While looking at 3D-printed AirTag holders, I discovered a bicycle saddle AirTag mount that fits to the underside of a saddle neatly out of view. This is just one of many options, with others like decoy reflectors, bottle cage mounts, and AirTag holders for hiding the item finder in suspension forks and cranks. I’m in the process of buying a new bike, and I’m wary of bike theft. An AirTag mount like this—many of which don’t even exist at retail—delivers a bit of security that money can’t necessarily buy. On top of this, I’ve also made a few decoy item trackers to deter thieves. I’m starting to think differently about solutions and prints My eyes have been opened I’m a firm believer that if you enjoy something, you shouldn’t feel bad spending money on it. That is to say, a hobby can “pay” for itself in pure enjoyment, fun, and inspiration. 3D printing can become something of a hobby, particularly if you’re fond of functional prints that can level-up your power tools or fix your messy desk. There’s also an endless number of projects to take on, from printing your own speakers to creating your own smart home accessories. I have a long list of things I want to make and items I’ll eventually need to print, saved for a rainy day. I also have a new outlet for my intrigue and boredom, plus a means of experiencing what genius ideas other people have come up with. Yes, I’m cognizant of the waste involved in producing plastic items at home, but this skepticism is what makes me print things I know won’t immediately make their way into the recycling. Considering a 3D printer? Learn why print quality is one of the last things you should be concerned about.

item.title: Universal USB-C docks are convenient, but old-school docking stations were actually better
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 2.03
My first laptops were usually office hand-me-down machines and one I remember most fondly was a Pentium 133 system that was pretty thin and light for its time. The coolest thing it came with was a docking station, but this wasn't what you'd think of as a laptop dock today. It was a device molded to fit the entire laptop, with a proprietary connector that ensured the peripherals in the dock, such as hard drives and CD-ROM drives, performed the same as any internal drive. All you had to do was come home, press the laptop into the dock until you heard a click. Now, I dock my Windows laptop using a USB-C dock that would work with almost any computer using a modern USB-C port. On a technical level, it's a superior solution and far more flexible, but I still think model-specific docks have a few things going for them. Old laptop docks were designed as part of the computer Fits like a glove Being built specifically for a given laptop or family of laptop computers is probably the thing I liked the most about old-school laptop docks. They were designed from the ground up to work with a specific laptop body, and so the designers could use that as a way to elevate the experience. That was often literally true, since some docks lifted the laptop, acting as a monitor riser and sometimes letting you type at a more comfortable angle. The idea wasn't necessary that you would always use an external display, so many of these docks helped make the laptop easier to use even if you didn't have an external monitor or other peripherals. While a single USB cable that connects everything and sometimes even charges your laptop is impressive, it just doesn't have the same cohesiveness. Proprietary connectors offered predictable performance It takes the "U" out of USB I've written before about how USB-C is a real mess of a standard and that's a major issue for docks. There are so many variables involved that if you take a random mix of dock, cable, and laptop, you actually have no real way of knowing what performance or capabilities you'll get when it's all plugged in without looking up spec sheets. This is especially true if your dock is also charging your laptop via USB-C, since whether the laptop gets as much power as it needs depends on the stars aligning just right. With proprietary docks, you're using the dedicated power supply designed for that laptop and dock combo. So not only do you have one less thing to plug in, you also know that your laptop is charging at the speed it should, and receiving exactly as much power as it needs. Modern USB-C docks turn one fast connection into several compromises Bottlenecks galore Even if you have a fast USB4 or Thunderbolt connection on your laptop, its total bandwidth is finite. All the devices connected to that port share that bandwidth, and the more things you plug in, the less bandwidth there is to go around. One advantage of proprietary docs is that all the peripherals don't share the same set of wires. If you look at something like the Dell E-Port docking station, you'll see the proprietary connector has numerous wires in parallel. So each set of ports gets a direct line to the bus and the controller it needs without having to share with other types of port. A USB-C plug cannot replace a proper docking mechanism It's a little flimsy, to be honest One of my biggest gripes with modern "universal" docks is that they're risky and fragile. It is stupidly easy to accidentally break off a USB-C plug in its port, and I have never liked having a dongle dangling. The best compromise I've found so far is using this attachable USB-C dock with my MacBook. It's connected using both USB-C ports and a dummy headphone jack. So that makes it pretty secure and stable. It also has proper power passthrough and is a little less annoying to connect than a typical dongle-style dock. Of course, this also gives up some of the flexibility of these USB-C docks, since this only works on MacBooks that have a very specific port layout. Still, I feel it's the best of both worlds at this point, giving me some of the advantages of old docking stations, while benefiting from the full bandwidth of two ports, therefore compromising less. Universal docks are more convenient—but less dependable I can't argue that modern USB-C docks that will work with any laptop sporting the same connection standard are amazing and convenient devices, but it does put the onus of making sure everything works on you as the customer. It's obviously more convenient to have a single docked setup where anyone with a modern laptop can plug in and get it all up and running in seconds, but the reality is that when you plug a modern universal dock into your laptop, you don't actually know that everything will work correctly, run at the best speeds, or in some cases even work at all.

item.title: I ditched store-bought organizers for these 4 3D prints I use every single day
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 2.01
Like most people, I've printed mostly decorative items and novelties since starting this hobby. I like an articulated dragon or a cool figure as much as the next person, but I honestly haven't unlocked that much true utility from these machines. That, of course, is entirely my fault. We've all seen the amazing things people can do with 3D printers when they have the talent and time, which I both lack, but there are actually a few 3D prints that I genuinely use every day, because they're better than the store-bought alternatives. The Bookshark Bookmark by blecheimer It's nothing to be scared of This might be one of the simplest things I've ever printed, but the Bookshark bookmark is also one of the most ingenious because of it. I am a voracious reader, and I have been all my life. I also tend to read half a dozen books at once, and I have plenty of anthologies where I might go a few weeks or months between short stories. In other words, I need a lot of bookmarks to keep track of my reading. I first printed out some Booksharks because I thought they looked cool. There's a little stopper under the shark fin part, so when your book is closed, it looks like a shark swimming in the ocean. However, as I started using these, I quickly stopped using all my store-bought bookmarks. Booksharks are just so small, easy, and reliable to use that I never reach for anything else. They also use very little material, and on a modern printer you can knock one out in a minute or two, or even a whole plate full of them. I like using multicolor filament so that my Booksharks are all different colors, but I guess you could deliberately print them in sets of colors for a color-coded system. Strong Locking Cable Clip by neoyarus Those cables aren't going anywhere I've tried a lot of 3D-printed cable management solutions over the years. Some have worked better than others, but in the end, I've actually settled on this brilliant locking cable clip. The print-in-place hinge is already impressive enough, but neoyarus has really thought this one through. There are 16 sizes, supporting one to sixteen cables. There are four different mounting options, and the clip at the end really is easy to open and close. I have a little trolley with my handheld gaming consoles, VR headset, and other miscellaneous gadgets to charge, and using some double-sided tape to attach one of these clips to the back has been a godsend to stop my charging cables from flopping all over the place when I unplug my PlayStation Vita or Meta Quest 3. Under Desk Headphone Mount by Chickenface This one finally has me hooked I always seem to be drowning in headphones, so I've tried every reasonable store-bought headphone mount you can think of. I've tried the ones that have a suction cup for your desk, magnetic ones that stick to your desk's legs, and, of course, the type that slips over your desk's edge. I always accidentally knock that last type off the desk at some point, so I'm not a fan. Chickenface has taken a previous design and remixed it into a very elegant under-desk headphone hook. There's a variant with and without a screw hole. You can use adhesive to attach the former, but I personally don't trust that. All I needed was a short wood screw and a screwdriver that fit through the bottom guide hole, and I had the hook fitted in less than 30 seconds with a rock-solid attachment. If you have a desk with existing screws that are in the right place, you can even just remove the screw and replace it with the hook in between. The screw holes are countersunk, so you probably don't need a longer screw in most cases. Print in place BAG CLIPS by Shadow_Flash1234 It just tastes better when fresh I used to use clothing pegs to keep open bags closed, to prevent things from getting stale or bugs from getting in. Then I saw people 3D-printing bag clips, and that seemed like a potentially better solution. The thing is, most of the designs I tried either break too easily, or they do a much worse job of keeping the bag closed than a spring-loaded peg. Shadow_Flash1234's BAG CLIP design has none of those issues. It has a built-in clip and is under tension when it's closed. The little clips do eventually break after repeated openings, but they are fast and cheap to print, and good for long-term use for things you don't need often, like flour bags. It's the simple things that work best I've tried lots of supposedly helpful gadgets that have just too many moving parts, or ask for too much of typical filament.

item.title: Rokid wants anyone to build AI agents for its smart glasses
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 5.53
What you need to know - Rokid's AIUI Studio is a browser-based platform that lets anyone build spatial AI apps for Rokid Glasses, with no coding experience or dev kit required. - Developers can describe an idea, while the AI-native workflow helps turn it into a working app. - The built-in smart glasses simulator lets developers create and test projects before getting physical hardware involved. Rokid is making it easier to build apps for its AI glasses, and you won't need a coding background or even to own a pair of the glasses. The company has launched AIUI Studio globally at IFA Berlin 2026, giving developers a browser-based platform for creating and publishing spatial AI applications. Much of the development process takes place via an AI-native workflow in AIUI Studio. You can say what you want to build in plain language, and the platform can take that idea and build an app without the traditional coding skills. It also offers a simulation of Rokid’s smart glasses, enabling developers to work on their projects without having to purchase the hardware. There’s still a reason to get the real hardware involved eventually, though. Rokid’s developer documentation advises testing agents in its Interactive Inview simulator before performing a final check on the actual glasses. For developers who want to have more control, Rokid pairs its AIUI Skills Library framework with AIUI Code assistance. The company says this helps creators make better use of the glasses’ hardware while also optimizing apps for less latency, less memory use, and less power consumption. The move is the latest as Rokid’s developer ecosystem continues to grow. The company says it now has some 35,000 registered developers and more than 500 agents available through its Agent Store. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android AIUI Studio is now available worldwide. If Rokid can take advantage of that growing developer base to create a steady stream of useful agents, its glasses might just become a platform that people actively build around. item.title: Android makes switching password managers much easier
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 5.14
What you need to know - You can now move passwords and passkeys directly between supported apps on Android without exporting sensitive data to an unencrypted file. - Your new password manager hands the process to Android, which detects compatible managers installed on your phone and coordinates the transfer. - Once authorized, Android moves the credentials between apps without requiring manual file handling. Android has always made it a pain to switch password managers. Moving passwords usually involved exporting your data into an unencrypted text file, and passkeys were pretty much stuck in place. Android is tackling both of those issues with a new transfer experience that makes moving your credentials much more secure and simple. In a blog post, Google said the new system lets you transfer passwords and passkeys directly between password managers, without first having to download a file. That eliminates one of the biggest security hassles of the old process, which was that sensitive credentials were sitting unprotected on your device for a while. Furthermore, passkeys weren’t transferable, so you had to manually recreate them across websites and apps. The process is built to be mostly out of your way. Start in your new password manager and select the option to import or copy credentials from another provider. The app then hands the job to Android, which knows which compatible password managers you have already installed on your phone and shows you where the data can come from. You are then sent back to the password manager you already use to select, review, and approve the transfer. Once approved, the passwords and passkeys move between the apps in just a few seconds. The feature is already available with Google Password Manager, 1Password, Bitwarden Password Manager, and Dashlane. Dashlane notes that CXP is compatible with devices running Android 10 or newer with the latest Play Services update. Bitwarden needs Android 14+ with Play services 26.21+. It is not merely a matter of convenience. Passkeys are more secure than passwords and resistant to phishing. Adoption has been stalled in part due to user concerns around vendor lock-in. CXP removes that barrier. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android Bitwarden says the creation of passkeys peaked this summer at over 500% compared to early 2024, with nearly half of all passkeys created in the past three months alone. Google says more partners are on the way. If you’ve been waiting to change password managers because of the hassle, that excuse just went out the window. Jay Bonggolto always keeps a nose for news. item.title: Google Photos could soon be built much deeper into Samsung Gallery
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 4.93
What you need to know - Samsung's OneDrive Gallery integration is ending soon, but Google Photos appears ready to take its place. - A new Gallery Cloud Sync service has appeared on the Galaxy Store with support for backing up to Google Photos. - Samsung hasn't announced the Google Photos integration yet, but it could start rolling out within weeks. Samsung has started laying the groundwork for what appears to be the replacement for its outgoing OneDrive integration, and unsurprisingly, it's Google Photos. Earlier this year, Samsung announced that users would no longer be able to use OneDrive to back up photos and videos directly through the Samsung Gallery app. Until now, Galaxy users have been able to automatically sync their Gallery photos and videos with OneDrive without needing to use another app or service. However, that partnership is coming to an end later this month. And now, Samsung appears to be preparing its replacement with none other than Google Photos. X user Sandeep Adap has spotted a new Samsung service called "Gallery Cloud Sync" on the Galaxy Store, which appears to be designed to take over from the existing Gallery OneDrive Sync integration. The app listing says Gallery Cloud Sync will safely back up your memories, including photos and videos, to "Google Cloud" so you can access them across your devices. The mention of Google Cloud might sound slightly confusing, but it appears Samsung is actually referring to Google Photos here. User That Josh Guy on X was able to preview the upcoming functionality, which isn't live just yet, and found that Samsung Gallery will offer an option to sync directly with Google. The Gallery settings will reportedly show your available Google storage, let you choose which albums to sync, and offer controls to sync over Wi-Fi or while roaming. This could be a big change if you currently rely on OneDrive for Samsung Gallery backups, since you'll likely need to switch to Google Photos. That said, the overall experience should remain pretty similar, with the sync controls still built directly into the Gallery app. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android The OneDrive sync option has already started disappearing from Samsung Gallery for some users and is expected to be discontinued completely later this month. Thankfully, Samsung's upcoming Google Photos integration looks like it could be an even more natural replacement. Samsung hasn't officially announced Galaxy Cloud Sync or started rolling out the Google Photos integration just yet. But with OneDrive support ending soon, we expect the new option to become available sometime later this month or in early October. item.title: Meta's next smart glasses could solve a big privacy concern by ditching the camera
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 4.75
What you need to know - Meta is reportedly developing Luna smart glasses without a camera, with a launch possible as soon as next month. - Luna will reportedly feature six microphones, six speakers, and a dedicated button for quickly accessing Meta AI. - Meta is also developing Phoenix AR glasses with virtual workspaces and movie screens, reportedly coming in 2027. Meta is reportedly preparing to enter a slightly different category of the smart glasses market with a new pair that doesn't have any cameras. Smart glasses have faced plenty of scrutiny over the past few months, and privacy has always been one of the biggest concerns surrounding models with built-in cameras. Meta has taken several steps recently to prevent users from tampering with the capture LED and secretly recording people, but the privacy concerns and perception around camera-equipped smart glasses still remain. Now, it looks like Meta is preparing an alternative for people who want smart glasses without the camera. According to a report from The Information, Meta is developing a new pair of camera-free smart glasses and could begin shipping them as soon as next month. The new model will reportedly be called Luna and could be unveiled at the Connect developer conference next week. The glasses are expected to be available in two designs, called Clubmaster and Burbank. While Luna won't have a camera, it will still pack plenty of hardware for accessing Meta AI. The glasses will reportedly feature six microphones and six speakers aimed at the user's ears. This will allow users to talk directly with Meta's AI chatbot without pulling out their phone. The glasses are also expected to retain a dedicated button on the side for quick access to Meta AI. Removing the camera will reportedly allow Meta to slim down Luna considerably. The new model is expected to look and feel much closer to a conventional pair of glasses, which could make them more appealing to people who don't necessarily want the bulk or privacy concerns that come with camera-equipped smart glasses. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android Luna isn't the only new pair of glasses Meta is reportedly working on, though. The company is also developing its own augmented reality glasses, reportedly called Phoenix. Meta is reportedly preparing a major demo of Phoenix that could show us a different way of video calling. The glasses will reportedly be capable of displaying virtual workspaces and large virtual movie screens. Phoenix is still further away, though, with the AR glasses currently expected to arrive sometime in 2027. Sanuj is a tech writer who loves exploring smartphones, tablets, and wearables. item.title: Triple launch: Boox debuts Note Air6 C and Palma 3 just in time for fall binge-reading
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 4.22
What you need to know - Boox launched three new ePaper tablets today (Sept 16), starting with the 10.3-inch HD color ePaper Note Air6 C. - The company is also expanding its Note series with the 8.5-inch Note Mini C and its next Palma, the Palma 3 with a redesigned premium frame. - The Note Air6 C is available now for $579, while the Mini C and Palma 3 are "coming soon," those will start at $579 and $339, respectively. Onyx Boox launched a trio of ePaper tablets today (Sept. 16), just in time for the chillier months. Each tablet features a built-in front light, capable of reading in any situation. This morning, Boox detailed its press release for the Note Air6 C, Palma 3, and the Note Mini C. Reading and writing are the hallmarks of these tablets, and we're beginning with the Boox Note Air6 C. "Available now," the Note Air6 C continues what Boox states is its "most popular series." Consumers will find a 10.3-inch HD color ePaper display with a 4nm octa-core processor and "Dual Tone" to adjust the screen's warm and cooler tones for a softer eye experience. The tactile writing experience is something Boox reiterates as a positive note from many Air C-series consumers. The Air6 C delivers that with a native Notes app with Outline, Tag, and Search tools. This Notes app features a "Dual Note" feature, letting consumers open two separate notes "horizontally or vertically." What's more, Boox states the tablet fully supports Android 16 and the Google Play Store. Reading is another major highlight for Boox tablets. The post states it delivers a "40% reduction in page turn speed compared to its predecessor," thanks to its BSR technology. Additionally, the tablet offers 6GB of RAM, 64GB of storage, and includes the Boox Pen3 stylus. The Boox Note Air6 C is available today for $579. The tablet will become available on Amazon soon. On the other hand, we have two more ePaper tablets that are "launching soon." The first is another addition to the Boox Note series: the Note Mini C. This smaller, 8.5-inch color ePaper display reportedly balances "portability and readability." Boox spoke highly of its one-handed use in its overview of the tablet. With the smaller size, Boox says it has kept its PDF legibility intact for users. The included InkSight Magnetic Active Stylus has been redesigned with a side button and a stronger magnetic connection. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android Boox made sure to provide the Note Mini C with the same front-light treatment. It states the tablet features "Dual-Tone" adjustable warm and cool tones. This should provide an easy-on-the-eye experience, especially when using the device for prolonged periods. BSR technology assists the Mini C's lag-free scrolling for documents and websites. Android 16 and access to the Play Store are included as well. Once the Mini C arrives, consumers can utilize its 6/64GB configuration and 3,150mAh battery. Boox states the Note Mini C will "launch soon" for $579 in the U.S., with Amazon availability to follow. The Palma series gets another If we're talking portability and the one-handed experience, it's hard not to mention Boox's Palma series. Luckily for consumers, the Palma 3 was announced this morning. The Palma 3 features a 6.1-inch ePaper display. Boox adds that it's improved the screen with "deeper blacks and higher contrast." However, the Palma 3's redesigned frame is also earning attention. According to the post, Boox integrated "fine stationary" tactility. It replaced the plastic body with anodized aluminum to emulate a more premium feel. The fiber-glass back panel reinforces that ambition of a premium ePaper tablet. The Palma 3 also features the "Dual Tone" front light tech for warm and cooler tones, alongside an Ambient Light Sensor. Boox says this sensor will adjust the device's brightness depending on your surroundings. Similar to the other two devices launched today, the Palma 3 features Android 16 and Google Play Store support. Other specs include 6GB of RAM and 128GB of storage. The 3,950mAh battery is said to provide "days of deep reading" on a single charge. The Boox Palma 3 will launch soon for $339. Nickolas is always excited about tech and getting his hands on it. item.title: Samsung might've started racing ahead to Android XR glasses with a color display
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 3.44
What you need to know - Rumors claim Samsung is developing a new pair of smart glasses, and has tapped Samsung Display for an in-lens color display. - The glasses would allegedly focus on displaying "text, notifications, icons, and more" on an extremely thin panel. - Samsung has its Intelligent Eyewear, which is supposedly coming out this fall, but those are mostly voice-focused with Google's Gemini and a camera. Samsung has barely dipped a toe into the world of smart glasses, and there's already a rumor that it wants to go bigger next time. This report from The Elec (Korean) claims Samsung might've started developing smart glasses with a color display (via 9to5Google). The publication cites its "industry sources" in saying Samsung has tapped Samsung Display to "create microdisplays" for a future pair of AI smart glasses. These rumors claim Samsung has a lot on its plate to prepare this product. Specifically, the post claims Samsung has a "technical challenge" to overcome: its FOV (field of view). The company is purportedly chasing a wide FOV for these glasses to accommodate the information users would see. What's more, Samsung is leaning on its Display side to create "ultra-small panels" of ~0.2 inches or smaller for the lenses. Samsung is allegedly focusing on displaying "text, notifications, icons, and navigation arrows" (machine-translated). It's still incredibly early to know for sure how Samsung's first color display smart glasses will arrive. However, the publication suggests the glasses could see a launch in the second half of 2027 or "early" in 2028. Got lenses? Samsung's getting serious. I don't think its Intelligent Eyewear are a bad start, though. It's starting simple. Useful, even. Everything is based on your voice. You still have a camera to take photos, and Gemini is there to help with hands-free assistance. To put a color display—a proper screen—would definitely take things up a notch. To me, I think this rumor is probably a little more eye-catching. We can't help but think about the Ray-Ban Display glasses from Meta. In fact, that's probably the kind of competition Samsung wants to get itself involved in. These glasses also feature the neural band. It makes it easier to control the display and content on your lenses with hand gestures. There's plenty of time still to see how Samsung manages this. Right now, we have (kind of) Samsung's "Intelligent Eyewear." These glasses are in partnership with Google, alongside designs from Warby Parker and Gentle Monster. These are Samsung's first smart glasses, but they lean more on the user's voice. Users can communicate with Gemini for navigation, order pickups, and photos. The glasses feature a camera and a microphone to get all of this done. Google reiterated its Samsung partnership during this summer's Unpacked. These glasses aren't out yet. During the original announcement this past spring, Samsung said we shouldn't expect to see them until "later this fall."
