The site’s main domain at nightmare-stresser.com has since been replaced with an FBI seizure notice. Back in 2022, federal agents previously seized the group’s other domain at nightmarestresser.com while charging six suspects behind dozens of DDoS-for-hire services. NightmareStresser had over 566,000 registered users, providing an easy way for anyone to launch a DDoS attack, according to a 2023 report from cybersecurity provider Searchlight Cyber. The site was charging between €25 to €19,999 for a variety of DDoS methods and intensities. NightmareStresser itself touted: “Backed by the most experienced minds in the DDoS industry, it now stands tall as the longest-running, most powerful, and most respected platform of its kind. For over 8 relentless years, NightmareStresser hasn’t gone down.” Although the site portrayed itself as offering stress-testing services, the FBI says NightmareStresser's actual customers were using the service "to facilitate attacks on victims in the District of Alaska and across the United States." The FBI’s takedown is part of Operation PowerOFF, an ongoing effort from international law enforcement to crack down on DDoS services. Still, it’s possible NightmareStresser could return with a new site. About Our Expert I've been a journalist for over 15 years. I got my start as a schools and cities reporter in Kansas City and joined PCMag in 2017, where I cover satellite internet services, cybersecurity, PC hardware, and more. I'm currently based in San Francisco, but previously spent over five years in China, covering the country's technology sector. Since 2020, I've covered the launch and explosive growth of SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet service, writing 600+ stories on availability and feature launches, but also the regulatory battles over the expansion of satellite constellations, fights with rival providers like AST SpaceMobile and Amazon, and the effort to expand into satellite-based mobile service. I've combed through FCC filings for the latest news and driven to remote corners of California to test Starlink's cellular service. I also cover cyber threats, from ransomware gangs to the emergence of AI-based malware. In 2024 and 2025, the FTC forced Avast to pay consumers $16.5 million for secretly harvesting and selling their personal information to third-party clients, as revealed in my joint investigation with Motherboard. I also cover the PC graphics card market. Pandemic-era shortages led me to camp out in front of a Best Buy to get an RTX 3000. I'm now following how the AI-driven memory shortage is impacting the entire consumer electronics market. I'm always eager to learn more, so please jump in the comments with feedback and send me tips.

item.title: Nvidia, Meta CEOs Argue Against Anthropic's AI Slowdown Plan
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 5.12
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang have both voiced their opinions on AI safety concerns. This weekend, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei advocated for government intervention to help companies simultaneously slow the development of self-improving AI models, ensuring each releases only safe-to-use technology. Jensen Huang spoke to CNBC on Tuesday, arguing directly against regulation for AI firms. Huang said, “The fact that we need new laws, new antitrust laws, or new regulations, so that these companies could do their fundamental engineering and do it properly before they release products, that is just completely unnecessary. We have plenty of laws. We have plenty of regulations that govern the reliability and the functionality of products.” Huang said safety is important in AI development, but the onus is on each company to ensure proper testing is conducted. He said, “We should create products and properly test them. And if they’re not ready to be released, just hold on to it and keep testing it and keep engineering until it’s ready.” Zuckerberg also disagrees with Amodei's message, taking to social media to say that while safety is important, it should be each company's responsibility. In a post on X, Zuckerberg said, “I believe the key to building a positive future for everyone is maintaining the right balance of power. This is within our power to do.” He confirmed Meta delayed its most recent Muse model for "several months" due to internal safety concerns. Zuckerberg said, “We didn't call for everyone else to do this before we would. We just did it as part of our day-to-day work because it was clearly the right thing for people and for us. I'm proud of the security foundations we've built.” He also suggested that Meta's rivals should engage more independent evaluators and advisors to ensure they follow safe development practices. He said Meta does this, and “other labs can just do this too.” He also hopes for an expansion of the third-party AI evaluator industry to make it easier for firms to ensure they're safely following rules. Zuckerberg and Huang were notably absent from the conversation in the first few days after Amodei's call to action was published. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, SpaceX's Elon Musk, and Google DeepMind co-founder Demis Hassabis have all spoken positively about Anthropic's suggestion of a collective three-prong approach to slow development. Anthropic's plan includes expanding third-party evaluators within each AI company, alongside a call for a set of safety standards developed in conjunction with the US government. He also believes the US government should enter into agreements with foreign countries to limit potentially dangerous use cases of AI. However, US President Donald Trump doesn't agree with Amodei's plan, arguing against regulation for what he calls the AI safety "hoax." Trump said over the weekend, “We could put guardrails. We can do this and that. But I think you have a lot of very negative forces that are...bringing up things that won’t happen." About Our Expert I’ve been a journalist for over a decade after getting my start in tech reporting back in 2013. I joined PCMag in 2025, where I cover the latest developments across the tech sphere, writing about the gadgets and services you use every day. Be sure to send me any tips you think PCMag would be interested in.

item.title: Shark PowerDetect UV Reveal Review: Stellar Carpet Suction Meets Subpar Mopping
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.80
The Shark PowerDetect UV Reveal is a hybrid robot vacuum and mop with serious strengths and some drawbacks. It handled stubborn carpet debris effortlessly and navigated tricky floor plans without bumping into toys. Yet it struggled to pick up all pet hair and fell short on mopping, smearing messes across the floor. If you have a pet-free home with mostly carpeted flooring, it’s worth considering, but its $1,299 price puts it above more well-rounded premium models. The Ecovacs Deebot X8 Pro Omni ($1,099.99) remains our Editors' Choice thanks to its lower price, similar vacuum performance, and stellar mop design. The Shark PowerDetect UV Reveal has an understated design with just enough accents to avoid appearing bland. It isn't overly large, but it’s not quite small enough to squeeze under most furniture. The front of the disc-shaped Shark PowerDetect UV Reveal robot holds its namesake feature. In an indent on the bumper, alongside a 3D RGB sensor and an UltraRange Camera, is its UV module, which uses ultraviolet light to detect invisible stains needing extra attention. The top features a raised, mostly square tower with rounded edges that houses a 360 LiDAR module for navigation. At the front of the top is a hidden touch control panel with buttons that light up when the robot is working. The water droplet button starts a mopping cycle, while the icon with curved spokes on a wheel starts a vacuuming cycle. Press and hold both the vacuum and mop buttons together to start a whole-home combo clean. Between them is a home icon with a power symbol in the middle; press this button to send the robot back to its dock, or hold it to turn the cleaner on/off. A red icon will appear if there's an error, and a blue Wi-Fi icon illuminates during setup. Press the lever at the back of the top to release a section containing the dustbin, detachable mop pad, and water tank. The mop is a flat trapezoid with rounded edges that runs the width of the body. During operation, the hypersonic mopping process vibrates the pad 100 times per minute. The bottom of the robot also features a central, rotating brush roll that alternates curved bristles and plastic fins. Flanking the brush roll are large retractable wheels, which can independently raise to help the vacuum get unstuck when it encounters obstacles. A separate, small wheel behind the mop can extend to lift the back of the robot, and thus its mop, when traversing carpets. The front of the bottom has an omnidirectional caster wheel and a side brush with three straight prongs. Edge sensors line the perimeter. You won’t have to flip the vacuum over or access its dustbin often, as the base station empties the robot's dustbin into a canister that can store up to 60 days' worth of debris while reducing foul smells with a replaceable air freshener. This bagless compartment pulls free from the base station by pressing a lever hidden in an indent on the right side. Once free, the bottom flips open when you press a separate orange button, and the opening is wide enough that dirt never got stuck when I was emptying the bin in testing. Just make sure you’re emptying it over a waste can with a large mouth so it encircles the entire reservoir. Under a lid on top of the base sit the clean and dirty water reservoirs, which should allow up to 30 days of maintenance-free mopping with normal use. There's no separate compartment for cleaning solution, as on some other robot floor cleaners, but it comes with a 12-ounce bottle that you pour into the clean reservoir. Note that the lids on the reservoirs aren’t attached. I almost dumped dirty water all over myself because I was expecting the lid to flip open, and it came off entirely. To prevent the carpet from getting wet, the base station can remove the robot's mop pad for dry runs. During combined runs, the robot will vacuum carpeted areas first without the mop attached, then return to the base to pick up the mop before targeting rooms with hard floors. After a cleaning run, the base washes the mop with water heated to 185 degrees Fahrenheit and dries it with 175-degree air. I appreciate all the extras Shark includes with the PowerDetect UV Reveal. In addition to the aforementioned cleaning solution and air freshener, it comes with a replacement side brush. Unpacking everything takes a few minutes, as is typical for a bigger machine. Then, the setup is pretty quick. You’ll need to find a spot for the base station on a hard floor, near an outlet, with a strong Wi-Fi signal. The base needs a foot of clearance on each side and two feet of free space in front so the robot can move freely. Snap the front ramp into place, then insert the anti-odor cartridge, and fill the clean tank with tap water and cleaning solution. Finally, plug in the base, and you’ll see the front indicator light illuminate, indicating it’s powered on. Next, push the side brush into place until it clicks, then roll the robot into the base station and, within moments, it’ll power on with a jingle of chimes. From there, you’ll need to download the Shark Clean app (available for Android and iOS), create an account, and add a device. It’ll then walk you through connecting the robot to your Wi-Fi network, giving it a name, going through terms and conditions, and installing updates. Once the app is set, it prompts you to send the robot on a mapping run. In testing, the PowerDetect UV Reveal completed its exploratory trek of my 1,500-square-foot, two-bedroom apartment in 10 minutes and 55 seconds. The Ecovacs Deebot X8 only needed 7 minutes and 48 seconds to map my place, but the extra couple of minutes didn’t bother me. The vacuum was a little loud while mapping, as though its suction was engaged, and it emptied its dustbin afterward, even though it wasn't cleaning. The map's perimeter was oddly shaped, but it still looked good overall. The app then instructs you to send the robot on its first cleaning run to verify and complete the map and to discover the locations of area rugs and carpet. This process took roughly an hour. You can then manually merge, split, or rename rooms, or add no-ho zones to the map. When manually editing the map, I found it a bit fiddly to change the perimeter between rooms. Additionally, I couldn’t make the no-go zone small enough to block off just the litter box area in my office. Once the map is set in the app, a button below it starts a whole-home clean, and pulls up options to vacuum, mop, or vacuum and mop. You can choose from three vacuum suction levels, three water flow levels for mopping, and whether to enable UV Stain Detect. The app lets you select a spot on the map or specific rooms for targeted cleaning, but, oddly, only for a vacuum or mop run. You can’t start a combined run on a smaller selected area; it only applies to the whole floor plan. As another limitation, the app doesn’t let you save multiple maps, and overwrites older ones when you make a new one. Otherwise, the settings menu in the upper left lets you create a schedule and configure device options such as enabling Do Not Disturb times, changing button sounds, and turning on the Under Glow Lights, which illuminate when errors, stains, or particularly dirty areas are detected. From this menu, you can also connect the robot to Amazon and Google for voice control. After its two mapping runs, I started a whole-home combo run with the Shark PowerDetect UV Reveal. It finished in 105 minutes, with a couple of pit stops at the base station to empty the dirt, again taking longer than X8 (77 minutes) on this task, but it covered the floor thoroughly. It left its mop in its base station while vacuuming the throw rug in my bedroom, and my carpeted living room and office. After it retrieved the mop, it covered the rest of the rooms, including the remaining space in my bedroom. When traversing the same throw rug with the mop attached, it lifted its tail into the air like it was doing a downward-dog yoga pose, looking goofy in the process, but successfully avoiding any contact between the mop and the rug. After the run, my floors mostly looked good, with a few strands of cat hair left here and there. On subsequent runs, I’d occasionally find clumps of hair left near chair and table legs. The PowerDetect also sometimes struggles with cords. It ran over them on several runs, but mostly managed to untangle itself with its independently lifting wheels. I did have to rescue it once when it managed to get itself fully wrapped within a tangle of cords. Aside from cords, the PowerDetect excels at obstacle avoidance. I tested this by scattering cat toys of various shapes and sizes on the floor, and it found its way around all of them without bumping into or running over any. I test battery life by running whole-home cleaning cycles on the default power level until the robot stops and returns to the base station to charge. I consider 60 minutes the functional minimum for covering a small home, and 90 minutes a passing grade for medium- to large-sized spaces. The Shark PowerDetect UV Reveal lasted for 141 minutes. That’s an impressive result that beats the Deebot X8 (134 minutes) and most other premium models, but falls short of our all-time battery champ, the Ecovacs Deebot X11 (180 minutes). For measured vacuum testing, I assess performance on 100 square feet of carpet and hardwood, using two types of debris: rice (representing everyday debris) and sand (representing stubborn debris). I distribute a specific amount of debris onto a precleaned floor and weigh the robot's dustbin before and after each test run to determine how much it picked up. The PowerDetect picked up 46% of sand on the carpet, beating the X8 (37%) and other recent premium models, and falling only a few points short of the Dyson 360 Vis Nav, which earned the highest-ever score on the test at 53.6%. On hardwood, the PowerDetect picked up 97% of the rice, an excellent result on this relatively easy test. It effectively cleans along walls and avoids flinging dirt with its side brush. With sand on hardwood, it also avoided spreading the debris, but collected only 62.7%. The X8, for comparison, captured 90% of rice and 82.3% of sand on hardwood. The PowerDetect picked cleaned my carpeted test space in an average of 9 minutes and 41 seconds, and my hardwood space in 9 minutes and 8 seconds. While its cleaning time on carpet is similar to that of other recent high-end models, it proved particularly fast in my hardwood testing space, beating most competitors by a couple of minutes. The Shark PowerDetect UV Reveal struggled in my mopping stress test. For this test, I spread 0.25 ounces of raspberry jelly in a single area on my kitchen floor, and then send the robot on a combined cleaning run targeting the room. The PowerDetect clearly detected the stain. It stopped over it, let the mop scrub for a few seconds, then returned later in the cycle for an additional pass. With the extra attention, it managed to remove almost all residue from the initial stain area, but it spread some seeds and even a couple of globs of jelly to other nearby parts of the room. The whole kitchen floor felt a touch sticky to me afterward. The design of the flat, vibrating mop is the culprit. Roborock has used a similar mop design on its hybrid models for years, and the Saros 10 similarly struggled in this stress test. Newer designs, such as the self-refreshing roller mop on the Ecovacs Deebot X8 and X11, perform much better. Even spinning mop pads, like those on the Roborock Qrevo Curv, outperform a single vibrating pad. Final Thoughts Shark PowerDetect UV Reveal - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.5 - Poor: Do not buy this product - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. If your home is mostly carpeted and free of pets, the Shark PowerDetect UV Reveal delivers powerful suction and smart, hassle-free dock automation. However, its vibrating mop pad simply can't handle tough, sticky messes on hard floors, and it drops the ball on heavy pet shedding. Given its steep price tag, you'll get significantly better performance and value from our Editors' Choice winner, the Ecovacs Deebot X8 Pro Omni, which mops better, handles pet hair cleanly, and costs less. About Our Expert I’m PCMag’s senior writer covering smart home and wearable devices. I’ve been reporting on tech professionally for nearly a decade and have been obsessing about it for much longer than that. Prior to joining PCMag, I made educational videos for an electronics store called Abt Electronics in Illinois, and before that, I spent eight years covering the smart home market for CNET. I foster many flavors of nerdom in my personal life. I’m an avid board gamer and video gamer. I love fantasy football, which I view as a combination of role-playing games and sports. Plus, I can talk to you about craft beer for hours and am on a personal quest to have a flight of beer at each microbrewery in my home city of Chicago.

item.title: Duda Website Builder Review: Powerful, Flexible, and Packed With Features
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.75
Simplicity is Duda's selling point. We've tested many website builders for years, and this one lets you quickly and easily build attractive websites that look great on desktops, smartphones, and tablets. Despite high-end tiers that target professionals, Duda lets you create handsome sites even if you have little design or technical knowledge. Since our last review, Duda has also enhanced its AI tools. Featuring numerous templates, strong e-commerce tools, and a top-tier editor, the slick and powerful Duda is an Editors' Choice winner for website builders alongside Wix, which stands out for its fantastic free tier. Duda lacks a free tier, but you can sample the service using its 14-day free trial. It has three paid tiers that focus on collaborative websites. The first is Basic ($25 per month, $19 per month if billed annually), which lets a single user create one website. However, Basic limits your customer support contact method to email. Team is the next tier up ($39 per month, $29 per month if billed annually). It increases the maximum team size to three, adds chat and phone support, and lets visitors leave site comments. The Team tier is where Duda focuses on web agencies, software-as-a-service (SaaS), and web hosting services, with client billing and management options, as well as white-label analytics, included. In fact, the next tier is called Agency ($69 per month, $52 per month if billed annually). It lets you build up to four websites, rope in six team members, and build widgets to give your site unique capabilities. Beyond these main tiers, Duda offers a White Label tier ($199 per month, $149 per month if billed annually) with more enterprise customization. Duda also has a full-on custom option if you need managed services and 24/7 dedicated support, but you must contact the company for a quote. Each plan comes with unlimited storage and monthly data transfers. Although each paid tier is built for a certain number of sites, you can add more for an additional monthly fee. This fee depends on your subscription plan: $19 per site per month for the Basic tier and $17 per site per month for the other tiers. E-commerce also costs extra. The standard e-commerce add-on is $7 per month for a maximum of 100 products in your digital storefront. For an additional $20 per month, you can sell up to 2,500 products, sell on Amazon and eBay, and even create multilingual stores. The top-end e-commerce plan costs $45 per month and lets you sell unlimited products and leverage a Square point-of-sale system. All these costs add up, since they're added onto the base subscription price, and can threaten to push Duda out of the realm of the casual user. Wix's business plans start at $36 per month. To start a new site, you choose from more than 100 attractive, modern templates. There's a search bar if you're looking for a specific template, but Duda has many other sorting options. You can look by overall color or filter by categories, such as Online, Travel, Restaurant & Food, and Blog. Duda makes it simple to see everything it offers, unlike Squarespace and other website builders, which have questionnaires to help narrow the template hunt. After clicking a template thumbnail, you'll see a panel showing how the template looks on a phone or tablet. You can even see how the template looks on all three device types—desktop, smartphone, and tablet—at once. That's better than what many site builders do. Strikingly, for example, has just one preview. However, you can resize the browser window to see how it will look on smaller screens. Once you choose a template for your Duda site and start customizing, you can't easily switch templates later, as you can with Squarespace or Simvoly. You have to basically reset your site. That's because Duda sites aren't responsive in the strictest sense, though they fit the search engines' criteria for mobile presentation. This means they don't stretch and compress all elements as you resize the browser window. Duda uses the term responsive—not incorrectly—when describing sites it builds to mean that the presentation reformats based on whether you're viewing it in a desktop browser, tablet, or smartphone. Duda's approach means you get a lot more control over your site design and can tweak it to look different on mobile. If you want to completely rebuild your site, you can at least save some data (like images and store content) so you don't need to start from scratch with a new template. You can also manually tweak the JavaScript. Duda also has Flex templates, which are advanced editing options that let you create fully responsive sites. As a newer feature, though, it offers just a handful of templates. You can add Flex sections to traditional Duda templates, giving you more freedom to arrange elements within those sections of your site. You can even restrict Flex editing to certain team members. You build your site using the selected template, which is pre-populated with dummy content. You can pull images and other content directly from an existing site or Facebook page. For more on getting started building your site, read our primer on how to create a website. We started with the DigiStore template. The site builder interface features an intuitive left sidebar with tools for managing and designing your site. These let you customize your theme colors, text, and navigation, as well as add and manage pages and site settings from choices on the left panel. An arrow lets you collapse this sidebar for a helpful, full-page view. Also helpful are the Undo and Redo icons that work no matter what you're doing on the site. Ctrl-Z works, too. Furthermore, you can always get help by clicking a chat bubble icon at the bottom right—very handy. The basic page elements—images, text boxes, buttons, dividers—appear when you click the Widgets button. You may find this a bit confusing, as widgets are typically third-party goodies rather than basic site elements. You drag the elements onto your web page, as with Weebly and other competitors. Aside from Flex sections, you can only drop elements in allowed areas, but it's not hard to add columns or change spacing to customize the layout to your taste. In fact, we love how you can choose Add Row or Add Column right from a page's Row button, which appears when you hover over any section. Third-party items, such as Disqus and Facebook comment modules, are included in the Widgets group, but Duda lacks a large catalog of third-party integrations like those found in Wix. Duda has continued to update its limited App Store with a handful of new selections, such as SimplyBook.me and Zuppler for Restaurants. However, using a web builder like Bluehost WonderSuite connects you to the much more expansive WordPress plug-in ecosystem. Upon launching Duda, you see the latest service updates, including new apps, templates, and features. Duda also integrates with services such as OpenTable, PayPal, vCita, and Yelp. For example, its integration with Yext embeds structured schema data into your website, making it easier for other sites to machine-read it. This helps search engines parse your site. The service makes it a breeze to incorporate social sharing buttons, including Facebook Likes, comments, and albums; a Twitter/X feed; and a WordPress feed. When we added the Click-to-Call feature to our test site, it merely displayed our number, which smartphones display as a link that opens the phone dialer. Duda's editor works well thanks to its clean, consistent layout. Along the top is an ever-present toolbar that lets you switch pages, undo your last edit, save your work, preview your site, publish your site, and view your site in three different screen sizes. The toolbar also grants access to your Dashboard page, from which you can manage all your existing Duda sites, start new ones, and connect them to a personal domain. There's an option to purchase a new domain name through Google Domains or Hover, and Duda offers specific integrated help for using a custom domain obtained from the major domain name registrars. If you don't choose a custom domain, Duda assigns your site a URL (you can pick your own prefix if it's not already taken). If you've built pages but aren't ready to publish them, you can save your edits for later publication. Duda lets you schedule overall site publication at a specific date and time, as Weebly does. Whenever you hover over an item on your site, you see a button with relevant edit options. It also supports right-clicking, which gives you a context-sensitive menu for each element. This provides an easy way to edit, align, or remove content. You can move elements around the page and resize them, though, as with most mobile-friendly site builders, your choices of where to move items are limited. For a paragraph object, the context menu lets you pull content from another site, edit the text, format it, and even hide it for selected device types. Clicking a page navigation link in the site designer takes you to that page on your site; you don't have to select it from a page menu as in some other site builders, though there's also a dropdown menu for switching among your pages. The Manage Pages panel is simple and clear, with SEO and navigation options available under a gear icon. It also lets you import images and site info from an existing site. To add a new page to a site, you simply tap the +New page button. There's a selection of page types to choose from, including Blank, URL, About, Contact, Photo Gallery, List, and Complex Page. Pages can be password-protected via the Settings menu. Hovering over a page type's thumbnail shows its layout on the three device sizes. Duda also has a very serviceable blogging tool. This lets you save and preview posts that you can format and add images to taste. Every option dialog for every Duda site element includes a Settings tab that lets you edit spacing in pixels, the CSS code, and—for premium accounts—the actual HTML code for the element. The service lets you use Secure Sockets Layer certificates (SSL), so site visitors see HTTPS in the browser address bar. Most modern browsers make HTTPS connections by default; this level of security is especially important with the arrival of GDPR. Duda offers all the tools you need to stay compliant with privacy regulations for your European visitors. You can enable a cookie notification, implement a privacy policy, require opt-in consent for contact forms, and provide a way to delete personal data. In the end, building a site with Duda is a pleasure: The interface is mostly quick, unlike some builders that take a few seconds to load modules. As with most such services, moving objects around can be finicky, but Duda got us the results we wanted. To add images to your site, you can use the included stock photography, drag and drop photos from computer folders, or import images from online sources, such as Dropbox, Facebook, Flickr, or Instagram. The included stock photography selection has improved since our last test, turning up plenty of clothing rack shots when we searched for "thrift shop," for example. You can even enter an image's URL or perform a web image search to find the picture you want. Uploading multiple images at once? Not a problem, whether it's a whole folder or multiple selected images within it. You can crop, resize, and even open an embedded image editor for some online photo editing and effects. In testing, we added a clickable link and tooltip, and changed the Alt text in the image-editing dialog. If you need more control, a gear icon gives access to CSS and HTML code. There are many photo gallery options, including image size, frame style, spacing, and animation. We also like that once you add an associated Facebook page, any public images from that page appear in the Duda images manager. You can also connect an Instagram account, so your photo gallery can pull images from there. Duda offers separate site-builder views for desktop, smartphone, and tablet designs. Our test Duda site looked as good and felt just as comfortable to navigate on an iPhone as it did in a PC web browser. A cool option lets you hide any image on a device of your choice—desktop, tablet, or phone. Some content doesn't work well in the smaller formats, so this is a valuable option. The other side of mobile development is the ability to actually build or edit your site on a mobile device. Duda doesn't offer a mobile app for site building, unlike Weebly. Instead, it offers a mobile web version of the site builder. This features a touch-friendly design with a menu bar for adding and editing widgets. This also lets you add photos to your site right from the tablet. Duda has a suite of business-focused AI features meant to enhance your site-building experience. The AI SEO Assistant can generate relevant meta tags for your pages, and you can grant permission for team members to adjust tone and translate text with the AI Content Assistant. Duda's AI tools can also generate text and entire sites based on prompts. You can even pay extra to make your site more visible to AI platforms like ChatGPT and Gemini, with that subscription starting at $19 per month. These AI features feel targeted toward professionals rather than hobbyists, which makes sense for the service. Still, we recommend against using AI tools to build websites due to the many downsides. With Duda, you can add buttons that link to your Facebook, Twitter, and other social media accounts. As with Weebly, Duda offers many monochrome or color buttons in different sizes. An older-style Share bar also lets you add buttons, but these aren't customizable in the way the other buttons are, offering no choice of button designs or even which social networks are included. You're better off sticking with the Social Icons option. You can also include an on-page Twitter feed, a Facebook Like button, and Facebook comments. Duda includes a full sales system, with shopping carts and checkout pages like those you get with Squarespace, Weebly, and Wix. You can also plug PayPal buy buttons into any site page, add printable coupons for site visitors, and create customer memberships. Any Duda user can add a 10-page web store to their sites, assuming they've paid for the e-commerce add-on. The process is slick, clear, and guided. When you add a store under the e-commerce section, Duda builds a new page for your site with a demo catalog, and it displays a Help box explaining how to set it up. A tooltip tour explains your store page, shopping cart, search, and store management features. There's a separate Store Control Panel page where you add products and configure shipping and payment options. Credit card transactions automatically use SSL security. Another well-designed wizard takes you through the store setup process. Adding images and formatting text is easy, as is assigning categories and SKU numbers to your products. You can also change the localization to support non-US currencies. Shipping options are integrated with UPS and FedEx, or you can set custom rates. FirstData, PayPal, and Stripe are the available payment processing options. You can import product lists in CSV, LiteCommerce, and XCart formats. Finally, Duda supports selling digital downloads (which the company calls "e-goods"), but the maximum size varies depending on your e-commerce add-on. Standard allows up to 100 MB file sizes, Advanced goes up to 1GB, and Unlimited boosts that limit to 10GB. Duda has a few customer support options that largely depend on your service level. In other words, the more you pay, the better your support experience will be. As stated earlier, Basic only lets you email the support squad, while Agency adds screen share and web chat to communication options. More impressive in the Agency tier is the priority support. At this tier, contacting support first brings you to a bot that takes your questions and tries to funnel you toward an answer in Duda's Knowledge Base. If that doesn't suffice, you can "Get in Touch," which connects you with a live agent. In our test, it took less than 30 seconds to reach an agent, and we received answers to our questions 20 seconds later. Duda can also connect you with verified partners called Duda Experts to give you even more insightful advice on how to improve your site. The directory lists the services experts provide, the regions they are from, their ratings, and their rates. Reliable website uptime is one of the most important aspects of a hosting service. If your site is down, clients or customers will be unable to find you or access your products or services. Fortunately, Duda displays its uptime on its site, and the results are basically perfect. In short, Duda is stable and dependable. Final Thoughts Duda Website Builder - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.5 - Poor: Do not buy this product - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. Duda is a highly capable and user-friendly website-building service, offering many impressive features, especially in the realm of custom enterprise software for teams. It should be among your top considerations if you prioritize a site's look and functionality on mobile devices. Wix, another top pick, offers more integration with third-party services, a solid editor, automatic site creation, and a free tier. However, Duda has site traffic statistics that provide more details, and its editor is one of the best we've tested, especially for agencies. All this earns Duda our enthusiastic recommendation and an Editors' Choice award. STILL ON THE FENCE? About Our Expert My PCMag career began in 2013 as an intern. Now, I'm a senior writer, using the skills I acquired at Northwestern University to write about dating apps, meal kits, programming software, website builders, video streaming services, and video games. I was previously a senior editor at Geek.com and have written for The A.V. Club, Kotaku, and Paste Magazine. I'm the author of the gaming history book Video Game of the Year: A Year-by-Year Guide to the Best, Boldest, and Most Bizarre Games from Every Year Since 1977, and the reason everything you know about Street Sharks is a lie.

item.title: Amazon Is Fixing a Fire TV Bug That Stopped Users Sideloading Apps
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.65
If you’re upset that your Fire TV Stick no longer lets you download third-party apps, there’s good news. Amazon has said that the recent disruption is due to a software bug, and a fix will be applied automatically to eligible devices this week. “There was a bug in a recent Fire TV Settings update that caused the “Install unknown apps” list to appear incomplete or empty on some Fire TV devices,” Amazon told AFTV News. “We have identified the cause and a fix will roll out in an upcoming Fire TV Settings update, installed automatically on affected devices over the coming week.” The statement was provided last week, so the fix should arrive on all compatible Fire TV sticks by the end of this week. However, there are a couple of things to consider here. First, the fix may only apply to older Fire TV Sticks running Fire OS. The newest Fire TV 4K Select runs on Linux-based Vega OS, and Amazon blocked sideloading on this device earlier this year for security reasons. Second, fixing the bug that broke third-party app installs doesn’t necessarily mean Amazon will allow apps that facilitate piracy. The company made its stance on piracy very clear in a statement to The Athletic last year. “Piracy is illegal… We’ll now block apps identified as providing access to pirated content, including those downloaded from outside our app store,” it said. Some recent comments on Reddit suggest Amazon’s systems have been good at blocking piracy apps so far. Therefore, even if sideloading returns to Fire TV sticks, you may only be able to use the feature for legit purposes, such as testing apps before launching them on the app store. Meanwhile, on all future Fire TV sticks running Vega OS, you may not be able to sideload apps at all. About Our Expert Jibin is a tech news writer based out of Ahmedabad, India. Previously, he served as the editor of iGeeksBlog and is a self-proclaimed tech enthusiast who loves breaking down complex information for a broader audience.

item.title: A Starlink Landline? VoIP Provider Ooma Taps Satellite Service for StarDial
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.59
As copper landlines disappear, a California company is trying to fill the gap by offering a home phone system that works with SpaceX’s Starlink satellite internet service, which is already popular in rural and remote areas in the US. Ooma supplies internet-connected telephone services, also known as VoIP. On Tuesday, it announced StarDial, a $129.99 bundle that includes a high-definition cordless home handset and a cellular base station for connecting to a home Starlink setup. The product may seem odd, given that you can already use all kinds of voice, messaging, and VoIP services with Starlink, like any other ISP. Still, Ooma views StarDial as an easy-to-use “home phone option” for US consumers who still want a landline and already use Starlink, which has over 2 million subscribers in the US. “StarDial gives Starlink users a simple way to add reliable home phone service to their internet connection at a time when traditional phone options are disappearing,” Ooma explains. “Telecommunications providers are retiring aging copper phone networks, while consumers in many rural and remote areas often face limited or unreliable cellular coverage.” This includes AT&T, which is working to retire most of its copper lines by 2029 and suing to remove them in California as well. Although many users have smartphones on a cellular carrier, Ooma notes that “Cell phones work well when you have a strong cellular signal, but many homes in rural areas experience dropped calls, weak reception, or dead zones indoors.” Thus, StarDial could act as a peripheral home phone for customers already signed up with Starlink, which uses orbiting satellites to receive broadband. Ooma says a buyer can set up the product in about 15 minutes; no need for professional installation. “Consumers simply connect StarDial to their Starlink’s Wi-Fi connection and pair the Ooma cordless handset with the StarDial base station." By default, the product can supply “unlimited nationwide calling at no extra charge beyond applicable taxes and fees,” along with address-based 911 service. Users can also pay an extra $9.99 per month for Ooma Premier, which includes unlimited calling to Canada and Mexico, along with call blocking, voicemail-to-email forwarding, and the ability to make calls over a second line. There’s also an option to port over an existing phone number to the service for a one-time fee of $39.99. Despite the Starlink connection, Ooma notes: “StarDial is not affiliated with or endorsed by SpaceX or Starlink.” It looks the same as Ooma’s other VoIP home phone systems, such as the Telo Air, which also costs $129.99. We’ve reached out to Ooma for details on how StarDial is different, and we’ll update the story if we hear back. UPDATE: Ooma told PCMag: "The underlying Ooma technology is the same as Telo Air. What's new with StarDial is that Ooma is specifically offering it as a home phone solution for Starlink users, particularly those in rural, remote and off-grid locations where cellular coverage can be limited and traditional phone options are disappearing." About Our Expert I've been a journalist for over 15 years. I got my start as a schools and cities reporter in Kansas City and joined PCMag in 2017, where I cover satellite internet services, cybersecurity, PC hardware, and more. I'm currently based in San Francisco, but previously spent over five years in China, covering the country's technology sector. Since 2020, I've covered the launch and explosive growth of SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet service, writing 600+ stories on availability and feature launches, but also the regulatory battles over the expansion of satellite constellations, fights with rival providers like AST SpaceMobile and Amazon, and the effort to expand into satellite-based mobile service. I've combed through FCC filings for the latest news and driven to remote corners of California to test Starlink's cellular service. I also cover cyber threats, from ransomware gangs to the emergence of AI-based malware. In 2024 and 2025, the FTC forced Avast to pay consumers $16.5 million for secretly harvesting and selling their personal information to third-party clients, as revealed in my joint investigation with Motherboard. I also cover the PC graphics card market. Pandemic-era shortages led me to camp out in front of a Best Buy to get an RTX 3000. I'm now following how the AI-driven memory shortage is impacting the entire consumer electronics market. I'm always eager to learn more, so please jump in the comments with feedback and send me tips.

item.title: Your Computer Might Demand Your Age Soon, No Matter Where You Live
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.31
Age verification laws have moved beyond social media and porn. Three US states have passed laws requiring operating systems to collect users' ages, and the EFF's Aaron Mackey says he expects Apple, Google, and Microsoft to mandate age verification nationwide. Congress is discussing a federal law to this end, too. Come 2027, you might even have to scan your face or upload a photo ID to prove you're a legal adult before you can use your computer. This new front in the age verification battle comes after more than two dozen states passed laws targeting adult websites like PornHub, and Utah started cracking down on VPNs. Major OS developers aren't pushing back, but the open-source community has been vocal about the risks to your online privacy and the future of the web. The California Ripple Effect: How One State Law Controls the Globe Starting in 2027, California's Digital Age Assurance Act will require operating systems, including Windows, macOS, Android, and ChromeOS, to ask users for their age during device setup and share an age range with apps. California's amended law now exempts Linux distributions, in a win for the open-source community. Depending on how future laws evolve, that process could eventually involve government IDs, credit cards, or biometric verification. Aaron Mackey, deputy legal director at the Electronic Frontier Foundation, warns the effects won't stop at California’s borders. Because tech companies rarely build separate operating systems for different states, he says these systems will likely be rolled out "for everyone who uses [operating systems], including the billions of folks outside of California." Colorado followed California by passing a similar law, and Illinois did as well. The three states are unlikely to remain alone for long. Similar bills are advancing in other states, while the proposed federal Parents Decide Act would, if passed, expand age verification at the operating-system level nationwide. At WWDC 2026, Apple discussed age-based content restrictions across apps and websites for child accounts, which are mandatory for users aged 13 and under. You might have to prove your age to avoid this requirement, too. Apple recently introduced mandatory age verification for new accounts in Texas, and more states are likely to follow. "The open-source community was rightly anxious about how they would ever comply with this," comments Mackey on the amendment. However, that isn't the end of the story. "At the end of the day, this sort of age-gating regime will go into effect in January," he says, pointing out the requirement still applies to macOS and Windows computers, as well as phones and tablets. He says Apple, Google, and Microsoft likely won't implement different age verification systems in each state, but rather a single national system for practicality. Privacy advocates, open-source developers, and lawmakers are now battling over a question that could reshape the future of computing: Should your computer know your age before you can use it? Here's what you need to know so far. Where You Live (or Don't) Matters: The 3 States Leading the Push As of this writing, three states have OS age verification laws: - California has the Digital Age Assurance Act (AB 1043), which takes effect on Jan. 1, 2027. It applies to closed-source operating systems such as macOS and Windows. California's law no longer applies to Linux and other open-source operating systems after AB-1856 passed in September, 2026. - Colorado has bill SB26-051, which takes effect on July 1, 2028. It exempts open-source operating systems, such as Linux. - Illinois has the Children's Online Social Media Safety Act (HB5511), which takes effect on Jan. 1, 2028. Illinois' law applies to Linux and other open-source operating systems, unlike the laws in California and Colorado. California’s law is the first and serves as a model for other states. It requires that operating systems ask for your age when you set them up. Your OS must then share an age bracket signal with the applications running on your computer. Applications will see one of the following age ranges: under 13, 13-16, 16-18, or over 18. Application developers are then “deemed to have actual knowledge of the age range of the user.” They would have a legal duty to comply with any laws requiring different treatment of minors and could not plead ignorance of the device user's age. An application might need to restrict access or features for users under 18, in accordance with other laws, including the federal Children's Online Privacy Protection Act of 1998 (COPPA), which requires online services to handle the personal information of users under the age of 13 differently. This could affect dating, gaming, and social media apps, for example. California’s law doesn’t affect websites. However, a proposed California law would extend the age signal to the web. Face Scans, Passports, or Honor System? How Age Verification Will Work Under California’s law, as written, your operating system must ask for your age during the device setup process. Your operating system will accept that age without requiring identification. Attestation—in other words, simply declaring your age—is sufficient proof. Nichole Rocha, a data privacy attorney who represents Children Now, a California-based organization that backs the law, tells me that California’s bill was designed to protect privacy. “There’s no requirement for the uploading of a government ID, and that was intentional on the part of the author, [California state assembly member] Buffy Wicks,” she says. “I think the bill strikes an appropriate balance. You see other states requiring the uploading of government IDs, and that’s incredibly invasive,” says Rocha. She argues that research shows parents set up devices for minors and will enter a child's age accurately at that time. “While the law on paper doesn’t require strict age verification, I think in practice compliance will look a lot more like age verification."
However, the EFF believes that operating system providers such as Apple, Google, and Microsoft will require more personal information. “While the law on paper doesn’t require strict age verification, I think in practice compliance will look a lot more like age verification,” Mackey says. He points out that there are fines and legal consequences if minors bypass age checks, and that companies will want to prevent minors from lying. “That involves more invasive forms of age verification that adult websites implement,” he says. That could mean providing a credit card, a facial scan, or a government ID during OS setup to verify that an adult was involved in the process. Microsoft's age verification system will cover both unverified and verified ages, with the latter requiring a facial scan or government document. Beyond California: The Federal Push to Track OS Users On the federal level, the Parents Decide Act, introduced in Congress in April, would require OS-level age checks in all states if it passes. Specifically, the proposed law says operating system providers must "require any user of the operating system to provide the date of birth of the user" to set up an account or use the OS. Adults would also have to provide their date of birth. The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) would also need to “issue regulations on how operating system providers can… verify the date of birth of a parent or legal guardian” if a minor is setting up a device. This could include government identification checks during device setup; implementation details would be up to the FTC. Similar language appears in other proposed bills. The Kids Online Safety Act, introduced in the Senate in 2025, would require the Secretary of Commerce to "conduct a study evaluating the most technologically feasible methods... to verify age at the device or operating system level." "I hope that by doing privacy-protective and nuanced legislation in California, we’re serving as a model for the rest of the states.”
Rocha doesn’t expect the federal government to take action. “Every year, things pop up in Congress that never get signed, right?” she says. “We just haven’t seen anything meaningful happen at the federal level in this space since the mid-1990s.” The EFF is concerned about the current legislative environment, however. "This is a trend we're seeing," says Mackey. "Lawmakers don't understand the technology, and they don't understand that these proposals are unpopular." Other states followed California and Colorado. As mentioned, Illinois legislators passed the Children’s Online Social Media Safety Act, HB5511. It requires the person setting up a device to declare only an age, without requiring proof of identity. “I hope that by doing privacy-protective and nuanced legislation in California, we’re serving as a model for the rest of the states,” says Rocha. Some states might require more personal identification. New York’s senate, for example, is discussing Bill 8102, which will require operating systems to determine user ages via “commercially reasonable age assurance methods.” Behind the Code: How Apps Will Silently Request Your Age Apps will get your age range from your operating system using an application programming interface (API). In other words, they’ll ask the operating system for your age range and get a response. Major operating system vendors are already implementing compliant APIs. Google offers the Play Age Signals API for Android apps on Google Play, while Apple offers the Declared Age Range API for iOS and macOS. Microsoft is adding a Windows Age API to Windows 11. The system software used by many Linux distributions now includes an age field for user accounts, too. Moving the Gatekeeper From Websites to Your Operating System The legislation discussed above moves age verification from the application or website layer to the device or operating system level. PornHub has urged Apple, Google, and Microsoft to implement OS-level age verification. With OS-level age verification, adult online services like PornHub would not need to confirm visitors' ages by collecting documentation themselves. Instead, the operating system would have that obligation. PornHub is already using Apple's iOS signals to verify visitors' ages in the UK. However, as mentioned, California law does not require the operating system to relay page signals from the web browser to a website. That’s surprising, given that age-verification laws in many states have targeted adult websites. Rocha says California’s lawmakers were trying to address the web in the original law, but “ran out of time.” California's Bill AB 1856 extended the age verification requirement to internet websites owned by application developers. For example, the law would apply to both Facebook's app and website. Web browser developers are already working on age-verification standards. Google’s Chromium and Apple’s Safari both support the Digital Credentials API to share government identification information with websites. If you save a driver's license or other government ID to Apple Wallet or Google Wallet on your phone, you can securely share your credentials with websites. Theoretically, you could use the same process to share an age you provided to your desktop operating system with a website, too. Why Open-Source Developers Are Fighting State Legislatures In addition to affecting Apple’s iOS and macOS, Google’s Android and ChromeOS, and Microsoft's Windows, some of these laws impact smaller open-source community operating systems, including Linux distributions. The open-source community is discussing age verification laws, and some projects have already commented publicly. GrapheneOS, a privacy-focused Android fork, has announced its intention to “remain usable by anyone around the world without requiring personal information, identification, or an account.” The project adds, “If GrapheneOS devices can't be sold in a region due to their regulations, so be it." “I think the open-source community is rightly very concerned about what’s happening here,” Mackey says of these laws. He points out that many open-source operating systems prioritize privacy and don’t want to collect user data or engage in surveillance. California now exempts operating systems distributed "under license terms that permit a recipient to copy, redistribute, and modify the software" after the passage of AB-1856. The EFF is pleased with this change, writing that "The bill is narrower now than it was before, and lawmakers clearly responded to concerns raised by EFF and the broader open-source community." It still takes issue with the concept of age-gating, however. Colorado's bill SB26-051, signed into law on June 4, 2026, exempts Linux distributions and other open-source software. Specifically, the law says it doesn't apply to "an operating system provider... that distributes an operating system... under license terms that permit a recipient to copy, redistribute, and modify the software." The Illinois age verification law, however, applies to Linux distributions and other open-source operating systems. Could VPNs Be Forced to Block Unverified Devices? California’s law doesn’t mention VPNs. However, under other laws or regulations, a VPN application might need to block access based on OS-level age signals. Or applications and websites might legally need to check the OS-level age signal to confirm user ages. A New Era of Hardware Tracking Although I spoke to lawyers for this piece, I’m not a lawyer. I’m a tech geek who’s been using computers and operating systems for decades. As far as I can see, there are two types of laws under discussion: those that ask for your age and those that require proof of your age. California’s law, as well as the laws passed in Colorado and Illinois, accept whatever you provide during device setup. This imposes additional legal requirements on operating system providers, including open-source communities, to design interfaces that collect users' ages. Rocha summarizes the California law’s approach: “We are going to try and protect as many children as possible in the most privacy-protecting way possible. And there will probably be some kids who get around the system, but the vast majority of kids will be protected by this.” Mackey is skeptical that you'll just be able to enter an age without any proof, however. He expects many companies will require more information to protect themselves from legal liability, despite good-faith exemptions in the amended bill. "I think it will be more invasive," he says. "We'll just have to see." “The open internet as we know it allows people to access information anonymously, privately, and securely. It’s in danger by lawmakers who have good intentions but are writing broad laws."
Legislation like the proposed bill in New York could require you to prove your age with a credit card, facial scan, government ID, or another method when setting up your device. A federal law could enforce this nationwide, depending on what the FTC requires. Future operating systems may require biometrics or identity document verification during device setup. I’m not a fan of either type of law. I don’t believe governments should require operating systems—especially small, open-source projects—to verify their users' personal information, or risk legal liability. I want privacy-centric operating systems that don’t collect any user data to continue existing. “The open internet as we know it allows people to access information anonymously, privately, and securely,” says Mackey. “It’s in danger by lawmakers who have good intentions but are writing broad laws.” Mackey doesn’t think these laws are inevitable, though. “My hope is that people are energized by this [debate] and recognize the opportunity that we can push back,” he says. About Our Expert I've been writing about technology for more than 15 years and using it in earnest for over twice as long. As a member of PCMag's software team, I focus on Windows coverage, but also write about other key desktop operating systems and system apps. (I used Windows 3.1 upon its release and have followed every subsequent release closely). Prior to joining PCMag, I wrote for How-To Geek starting in 2011, and my articles amassed over a billion page views. I went on to run the publication as editor-in-chief for four and a half years. I have also contributed to Computerworld, Fast Company, PCWorld, Reader's Digest, The New York Times, and many other outlets about everything from AI to PC hardware to Windows. I founded and ran my own direct-to-reader Windows-focused newsletters, Windows Intelligence and The Windows ReadMe, working in partnership with Thurrott.com.

item.title: Why Is the Internet Archive Blocking Users? Blame the Bots
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.25
Struggling to access the Internet Archive’s Wayback Machine? You may have been caught in the crossfire of an effort to stop web-scraping bots. The Internet Archive today published a blog post addressing user complaints about access issues with the Wayback Machine, which lets you travel back in time virtually to see how a web page looked over time. “We’ve heard you: ‘Fix the Wayback Machine!’” wrote Mark Graham, the Wayback Machine's director. “Here’s what’s going on. The Internet Archive’s Wayback Machine has been hit by waves of high-volume automated traffic, and we’ve put protections in place to keep the service running.” Unfortunately, those protections can sometimes ensnare real users. “If that’s happened to you, we’re sorry, and we appreciate your patience while we work to reduce the errors,” Graham added. Blocking can occur if you encounter a 429 error, an HTTP status code indicating that a user has sent too many requests in a given amount of time. “We’re getting better at telling abusive bots apart from the people who depend on the Wayback Machine every day. If you think you were blocked in error, email [email protected] with your operating system, browser, and IP address, and we’ll look into it,” Graham added. The San Francisco-based Internet Archive didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. So details about the abusive bots remain unclear. But the archive might be trying to crack down on web-scraping bots that gather data to train AI models. In 2023, the Internet Archive briefly went down after facing “tens of thousands of requests per second” from an AI company out to extract text data, according to the Nieman Journalism Lab. The AI-training bots have also triggered some news publishers to block the Internet Archive “out of concern that archived material could be accessed or reused by AI systems,” the library says. “Indeed, it has been suggested that we are victims, if you will, collateral damage caught up in the conflict between AI companies and publishers,” Graham said in a May podcast episode. About Our Expert I've been a journalist for over 15 years. I got my start as a schools and cities reporter in Kansas City and joined PCMag in 2017, where I cover satellite internet services, cybersecurity, PC hardware, and more. I'm currently based in San Francisco, but previously spent over five years in China, covering the country's technology sector. Since 2020, I've covered the launch and explosive growth of SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet service, writing 600+ stories on availability and feature launches, but also the regulatory battles over the expansion of satellite constellations, fights with rival providers like AST SpaceMobile and Amazon, and the effort to expand into satellite-based mobile service. I've combed through FCC filings for the latest news and driven to remote corners of California to test Starlink's cellular service. I also cover cyber threats, from ransomware gangs to the emergence of AI-based malware. In 2024 and 2025, the FTC forced Avast to pay consumers $16.5 million for secretly harvesting and selling their personal information to third-party clients, as revealed in my joint investigation with Motherboard. I also cover the PC graphics card market. Pandemic-era shortages led me to camp out in front of a Best Buy to get an RTX 3000.
