item.title: I Tested Canon's First Retro Camera, and It Proves Throwback Gear Doesn't Have to Be a Gimmick
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.24
I've been patiently waiting for Canon to hop on the nostalgia bandwagon and release a retro-inspired camera. A few of its competitors have turned back time with great results; the Nikon Z f and Fujifilm X100VI are obvious examples, both of which could be mistaken for a '70s or '80s film cam from a distance. Canon is joining the party with the EOS R8 Mark II (starting at $1,899), a retro-looking midrange full-frame camera that sits between entry-level and enthusiast-grade gear. Exterior aside, the Mark II is a refined version of the original R8; it adds 5-axis sensor stabilization and a larger image buffer, but is otherwise quite similar. That's not a detriment, as I praised the R8 for its excellent photos, fast autofocus, and 40fps capture when I reviewed it in 2023. I spent two weeks putting an early preproduction copy of the Mark II through its paces to see if Canon's retro experiment actually delivers in the field. Subtle Retro Style That Doesn't Overdo It In typical Canon fashion, its retro design approach is a little more conservative than that of other brands. The first thing I noticed is that the EOS R8 Mark II is an all-black body, while most mirrorless cameras with throwback designs are made in both a two-tone silver-and-black and a black finish. The silver bodies read a little more "old school" than all-black, but the R8 Mark II's textured leatherette does some heavy lifting in the visual department, covering the grip and rear thumb rest in contrast to the rest of the camera's matte black finish. Canon tells me that it looked back to the EOS T80, its first-ever autofocus SLR, when sketching up the R8 Mark II. It's not the obvious choice. I know I'm not alone in wanting to Canon to make a digital camera that looks like the AE-1, a '70s manual focus SLR with distinctly angled lines and a buzzsaw-style shutter speed dial, but the T80 has its charms. Its lines are more angular, a significant departure from Canon's typically rounded edges, but despite that change, the R8 Mark II still feels like a modern Canon. It fits comfortably in my hands, and the company's hallmark angled shutter release and vertical forward exposure dial are in line with other models in the R mirrorless series. Ditching Frustrating Vintage Dials for Modern Usability Some cameras that look to the past for design inspiration go all the way with film-camera controls like manual shutter and aperture dials. Discrete shutter and aperture controls can be intimidating to new users (for years, they were only available in bougie digital rangefinders from Leica), but they have made their way down to entry-level throwbacks like the Fujifilm X-T30 III. Canon opted to stick with a PASM Mode dial and two flexible exposure dials for the R8 Mark II, a scheme that's far more approachable for advanced amateurs who want to make the jump to full-frame and beginners stepping up from a smartphone. Set the Mode to Auto or Program (P) if you want the camera to do most of the work, Aperture (Av) if you want to adjust the f-stop to blur or sharpen backgrounds, and Shutter (Tv) to freeze or blur motion. It also has Flexible (Fv) control, an exposure mode that Canon's been pushing since it launched the basic EOS RP. It lets you switch between aperture and shutter priority with the press of a button, so you aren't locked into either. I've found it more confusing than helpful, but there's room for disagreement. The R8 Mark II also includes Scene (SCN) modes that adapt settings to different real-world scenarios, a real benefit for beginners. The controls are largely the same as those on the EOS RP and R8, though not identical. The On/Off/Video toggle switch is now on the right side, nestled alongside the rear exposure dial. The R8 Mark II also adds an eight-way thumbstick that doubles as a joystick, letting you move the active focus area and navigate menus. It makes the camera more versatile for wildlife, sports, and action photography, as you can more easily manually focus on what you want. The thumbstick is more responsive and comfortable to use versus the R8's four-way d-pad (which continues on in the Mark II as well). It also includes a beginner-friendly menu system called Creative Assist. Available exclusively in the Auto mode, it replaces the usual array of numerical ISO, f-stops, and shutter speeds with a touch menu that's written in layman's terms. It lets you select a color tone from a list of presets, take photos with a defocused background using a slider that goes from Blur to Sharp, and adjust scene brightness with another slider. It also lets you adjust color saturation, tint images (blue/orange and green/magenta sliders are included), or switch to monochrome with or without a color tint (blue, green, purple, or sepia). And for experts, all other modes use standard photo nomenclature—f-stops, shutter speeds, exposure values, and so on. The Lightest Full-Frame With Sensor Stabilization Ease of use is one thing, but the R8 Mark II is easy to carry, too. It weighs just about 1.2 pounds without a lens, and is available in a starter kit with the compact RF 24-50mm F4.5-6.3 IS STM if you want a zoom to match. Together, the two weigh just shy of 1.7 pounds. I didn't get a chance to try the kit lens, so I grabbed the 4.2-ounce RF 28mm F2.8 STM ($349.99) and took it on a few photo walks around town. It felt like carrying almost nothing. It's worth noting that the R8 Mark II's nearest direct competitor, the Nikon Z5II, is heavier at around 1.5 pounds. The EOS R8 Mark II earns a superlative as the lightest full-frame camera with a stabilized image sensor, a feature that's missing from both the RP and the original R8. Sensor stabilization is handy; I used it to take some long-exposure images without lugging a tripod around, and it also makes it easier to get posed portraits in dim light. The biggest challenge will be getting your subject to stay still for a photo. The slim, lightweight build doesn't come without drawbacks. The R8 Mark II keeps the same relatively small (0.70x), 2.4-million-dot EVF as the older R8. If you want a viewfinder upgrade, consider stepping up to the EOS R6 Mark II, the next model up in Canon's line. Its EVF shows a larger image (0.76x), is sharper (3.7 million dots), and, since the R6 Mark II uses the same 24.5MP image sensor and processor, its picture quality is indistinguishable. The chips aren't perfectly identical, however. Canon's Shogo Yamaguchi explains that the company always "fine-tunes the sensor to optimize for each camera," but it is clear that the R8 Mark II's photos are "effectively" the same as the R8 and R6 Mark II. Smart Subject Tracking That Keeps Up With the Action Canon is more bullish on its improvements to the R8 Mark II's autofocus system. It's tweaked the algorithms to deliver stickier subject tracking versus the original, and extended the buffer to hold 30% more Raw and 58% more JPGs in a burst, too. I'm not yet able to perform technical testing as I've only tried a pre-production version of the R8 Mark II, but those figures are in line with up to around 100 compressed Raw (C Raw), 50 Raw, or 140 JPGs when using the fastest 40fps continuous drive setting. Dialing the drive all the way to 40fps is serious overkill for non-professional sports and most wildlife scenarios; you're better off using the High (20fps) setting for those situations. The focus system has all of the same tricks you'll find in Canon's pricier cameras. It can identify and track different subject types and jump to focus on eyes and faces for people, pets, and wildlife. I tried the focus with my cat and the ultra-bright RF 50mm F1.2 lens, and the R8 Mark II reliably put the focus box on her eye. It also has precapture, a mode that continuously saves images to memory when the camera is focusing, and only starts writing photos to your card when you press the shutter all the way in. Precapture snags a half-second of action before you press the shutter, compensating for slow reaction times and making it easier to catch fleeting moments without filling up your memory card. Smooth 4K60 and Creator-Friendly Video Extras More and more creators are turning to mirrorless cameras for video and vlogs, and while the R8 Mark II isn't purpose-built for video like its EOS R6 V, it's still a heck of a good camera for movies. It records up to 4K60 at a 16:9 aspect ratio using the full width of the sensor, and the stabilized sensor avoids the jumpy, jittery look when recording handheld. The IBIS system is bolstered by a digital system that crops into the frame to deliver steady video even when handholding telephoto lenses. In my experience, the digital IS works very well. I recorded handheld video with an 800mm lens using the EOS R6 V and was astounded by the results. The R8 Mark II also includes a swing-out screen, so you can monitor the frame if you're using it to vlog from the studio or for self-recording, and it has both headphone and microphone connections. I think content creators will be happy with its feature set. Speaking of which, Canon is adding one cool video option—the R8 Mark II can "blur out" during a shot. With the press of a button, the R8 Mark II shifts the lens's focus from the subject to its nearest point. It's a good way to end a video, one with more visual interest than a basic fade to black. The feature, called Video Defocus, isn't mapped by default, but is easy enough to assign to a button in the camera menu. Preorders, Pricing, and How It Stacks Up Against Rivals The R8 Mark II looks like another excellent camera from Canon, and a solid choice for photographers and content creators who want the full-frame look and prefer a stylish, lightweight build. I've only had a chance to use a preproduction copy, but if Canon hadn't told me it was an early sample, I never would have guessed it. I didn't run into any noticeable bugs or quirks while I was trying it out; it feels fully baked to me. Canon is pricing the camera at $1,899 as a body-only unit, or $2,099 as a kit with the RF 24-50mm F4.5-6.3 IS STM lens. It's also selling an Extension Grip, an $89.99 baseplate that adds a little height to the body for photographers who want just a bit more camera to hold onto. Preorders are open today, and Canon expects to start shipping in late October. The price is competitive. After all, the Nikon Z5II goes for $1,849.95 as a body, while the slim Sony a7C II costs far more at $2,499.99. The R8 Mark II beats the Z5II on speed and is noticeably lighter and smaller, but the Z5II's larger, sharper viewfinder may be enough to pull some creators to its side of the fence. The Sony a7C II is as tiny as the R8 Mark II, and its 33MP sensor packs more pixels than the R8's 24MP chip, but like many Sony cameras, it is on the pricey side. Among the Canon line, the original R8 is still available for $1,649; it's very similar but doesn't have a stabilized sensor. Creators who want a larger camera and better viewfinder may want to step up to the R6 Mark II for $2,299. All are good tools for imaging and video, so pick the one that appeals to your sensibilities and best fits your budget when you're ready to make the jump to full-frame. About Our Expert Images, and the devices that capture them, are my focus. I've covered cameras at PCMag for the past 15 years, which has given me a front row seat for the changeover from DSLRs to mirrorless cameras, the smartphone camera revolution, and the emergence of drones for aerial imaging. I have extensive experience with every major mirrorless and SLR system, and am also comfortable using point-and-shoot and action cameras. As a Part 107 Certified drone pilot, I’m licensed to fly unmanned aircraft systems (UAS) for commercial and editorial purposes, and am knowledgeable about federal rules and regulations regarding drones.

item.title: Cricket Wireless Starts Offering 5G Home Broadband
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.18
AT&T’s Cricket Wireless is starting to use its own brand to offer a 5G home broadband service. The new service is called Cricket 5G Home Internet and can start as low as $45 per month for existing customers with the carrier who enroll into auto-pay. The company is touting “predictable pricing, no annual contracts” and an easy setup process, with download speeds ranging from 90 to 300 Mbps. Cricket’s home internet isn’t fiber, but what’s called fixed-wireless access (FWA), which has been growing in popularity across the US. The internet technology uses excess 5G network capacity to deliver broadband-like speeds to the customer’s home. In 2023, AT&T began offering its own solution in AT&T Internet Air to compete with rival offerings from T-Mobile and Verizon. It looks like AT&T is now expanding the 5G home broadband to Cricket Wireless. That said, Cricket Wireless has been spotted offering a variant of AT&T Internet Air as early as November 2024 at certain stores, according to Wave7 Research. "This has been covered and documented in every Wave7 prepaid report for the last 22 months," says the research firm's principal Jeff Moore. Today, Cricket Wireless is highlighting the internet offering as a way for customers to save money. According to our best mobile network rankings, Cricket Wireless offers “the best average price per line per month at just a few cents over $30.” Cricket added: “Customers increasingly want the convenience of having their wireless and home internet services with one provider, and Cricket's new bundle offers a simple, value-packed way to bring those connections together.” For new customers, the company is also offering the home 5G internet service along with a Cricket Wireless cellular plan as a bundle for $75 per month. As a standalone offering, Cricket 5G Home Internet costs $65 per month without auto-pay. Cricket 5G Home Internet offers unlimited data and uploads of between 8 to 30 Mbps. But you can expect a latency between 30 to 65 milliseconds, or what’s higher than the 9 millisecond average for home broadband, according to Speedtest.net parent Ookla. You can check out our review of AT&T Internet Air to get an idea of the service. For faster, gigabit speeds, Cricket has been offering "Quantum Fiber from AT&T" in select areas. Cricket 5G Home Internet isn’t available everywhere; interested users can check by visiting the company’s service map. Another caveat is that customers need to pay a one-time $49.99 fee for the gateway equipment to receive the 5G access at home. But set up takes less than 15 minutes, the company says. "In rare cases, if your usage is contributing to congestion on the network, Cricket will greatly reduce your speed for a min. of 30 min," the carrier also noted. "Cricket may temporarily slow data speeds if the network is busy." Editor's note: This story has been updated to note Wave7 Research previously spotted Cricket offering AT&T Internet Air back in 2024. About Our Expert I've been a journalist for over 15 years. I got my start as a schools and cities reporter in Kansas City and joined PCMag in 2017, where I cover satellite internet services, cybersecurity, PC hardware, and more. I'm currently based in San Francisco, but previously spent over five years in China, covering the country's technology sector. Since 2020, I've covered the launch and explosive growth of SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet service, writing 600+ stories on availability and feature launches, but also the regulatory battles over the expansion of satellite constellations, fights with rival providers like AST SpaceMobile and Amazon, and the effort to expand into satellite-based mobile service. I've combed through FCC filings for the latest news and driven to remote corners of California to test Starlink's cellular service. I also cover cyber threats, from ransomware gangs to the emergence of AI-based malware. In 2024 and 2025, the FTC forced Avast to pay consumers $16.5 million for secretly harvesting and selling their personal information to third-party clients, as revealed in my joint investigation with Motherboard. I also cover the PC graphics card market. Pandemic-era shortages led me to camp out in front of a Best Buy to get an RTX 3000. I'm now following how the AI-driven memory shortage is impacting the entire consumer electronics market. I'm always eager to learn more, so please jump in the comments with feedback and send me tips.

item.title: Think Payroll Software Costs Too Much? The Math Says Otherwise
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.11
Payroll is expensive, no matter how you slice it. Not only do you have to compensate your employees and contractors for their work, but the logistics and associated expenses can also take a serious bite out of your bank account. You might see manual payroll as a cost-saving move because it spares you the monthly payroll subscription. But managing your payroll using a combination of calendars, emails, paper forms, spreadsheets, and tax tables can actually end up costing you more. Here's how automating the process with payroll software can yield a significant return on investment (ROI). This article was made possible in part by OnPay. It was written and edited independently without partner oversight. Reclaim Your Time: Automate Repetitive Admin Payroll involves countless moving parts and is thus one of the most complex elements of your company’s accounting operations. If you're a payroll manager, you know how endless the list of excruciatingly time-consuming tasks can feel. You must: - Maintain detailed worker records - Collect information on hours worked - Calculate gross pay for employees, which can involve multiple pay types (such as salary or hourly, overtime, bonuses, and commissions) and types of PTO (such as sick pay, vacation pay, or other types) - Calculate net pay, subtracting deductions like income taxes (federal, state, and local) and benefit contributions, garnishments, and other required government payments - Prepare paper checks and direct deposits - Enter payroll data in accounting records - Communicate with benefits providers and government agencies - Stay current on HR compliance - Calculate and submit payroll taxes and filings - Prepare periodic reports and year-end 1099s and W2s Payroll software can eliminate these repetitive tasks. Once you enter information in these apps, it appears on every relevant page, even in HR-related sections. You can get through a payroll run much more quickly when you don't have to dig for details in multiple places. Reducing these labor costs can free up the administrator’s time for things that require deeper thought and help move the company forward. Empower Employees With Self-Service Portals Numerous studies have examined how long it takes to return to work after a distraction. Researchers at the University of California, Irvine, found that it can take as long as 23 minutes to "get back into a concentrated state after an interruption.” Payroll managers who employ manual systems are likely to face myriad questions from employees and contractors. If you have even half a dozen people working for you, those conversations add up to a ton of interruptions. You might have to dig for each answer, for example, which could take some time if data lives in multiple places. And then, you have to try to refocus your attention. Payroll software centralizes all your payroll information, so the payroll manager can find answers quickly. Moreover, workers are less likely to even ask questions when they can access their payroll data, such as historical pay stubs, updated time off balances, and withholding information, from dedicated mobile and web apps. Catch Costly Payroll Mistakes Before You Hit Send Every time a mistake pops up in your payroll system, someone has to investigate and correct it. This can be anything from an erroneous hourly rate to missing overtime to an inaccurate tax calculation. The last example is a critical error, especially if you have already submitted your tax payment and filing for the relevant period. But a small mistake in one employee’s pay amount can wreak havoc, too, since it affects your payroll taxes and reports. Finding and fixing any errors manually is simply a major pain. Payroll applications have error-trapping capabilities. When they detect a problem as you’re preparing a payroll run, they stop you and explain how to correct it. And if you’ve done all your payroll setup thoroughly and accurately, it’s highly unlikely that the software will make a mistake on payroll taxes, since it’s just a matter of calculating. Unlock Instant Labor Cost Reports Without the Math With manual payroll systems, you're lucky if you manage to complete your payroll runs accurately and on time, as well as submit payroll taxes and filings according to schedule. Running reports that can help you analyze your labor costs is a luxury you probably don’t have time to pursue. Payroll software comes with pre-designed reports that provide insight into this element of your budget. Some apps even offer sophisticated custom reports that let you target specific data. Either type of report is simple to spin up in minutes. Avoid IRS Penalties With Automated Tax Filings The value of having a payroll site to calculate and submit your payroll tax is immense. The IRS and other tax agencies take taxes and associated forms very seriously; they must be accurate and arrive on time. You are responsible for knowing when your filings are due. The IRS spells this out on its website and also notifies new businesses of their obligations. Companies in states that require an income tax will need to contact their state’s revenue department and register as part of the payroll software setup. Calculating and submitting your payroll taxes is as challenging as running a payroll. If you’re using a manual system, the process is time-consuming and error-prone. You have to keep track of different tax types, rates, wage limits, deadlines, deposit schedules, and forms. You must tally and submit all the calculations you make to withhold correct amounts for obligations, such as federal income tax, Social Security and Medicare, and federal unemployment tax (FUTA) on paychecks. If your company grows or takes on employees in other states, this critical task becomes even more complex. Payroll software does the heavy lifting by handling all the calculations. It can even submit your payroll taxes automatically, give you advance notice of when taxes are due, and provide guidance. Most, if not all, payroll software companies will pay any penalties you incur if their services make a mistake. The value proposition here is obvious. You save money by saving time, and you minimize the risk of penalties and interest for errors. Grow Your Team Without Doubling Your Workload What happens if you’re doing payroll manually, and the size of your workforce doubles? You guessed it, your payroll workload also doubles. You might even have to bring on a new employee to handle the expanded responsibilities. Payroll software might spare you the significant expense of hiring another worker. Automating payroll allows you to manage greater complexity without increasing your administrative workload at nearly the same rate. Seamless Software Integrations Save Time and Tech Your payroll data doesn’t exist in a vacuum. At the very least, you need to make it a part of your larger bookkeeping system. In a manual system, that requires a lot of duplicate data entry, which increases the chances of transposition errors. The best payroll applications automatically integrate with small business accounting software. You can even connect some to scheduling, point-of-sale (POS), and time-tracking apps. The benefit of integrations goes beyond improving your company’s ROI. They enable automation in areas that would be difficult or impossible with a manual system. The Real ROI: Spend Time Growing, Not Calculating A lot of the above reasons involve saving money by saving time. That’s certainly a quantifiable measurement you can use to calculate your company's ROI in adopting an automated payroll service. But it’s what that extra time affords that's difficult to measure (and arguable more important). If your company's leaders get to spend more time working on things that require skill and analysis, the business has a better chance of thriving. Instead of asking whether you can afford payroll software, you should instead think deeply about how much time and money your manual system is already costing you. Then, research what might be a good fit for your business, starting with our in-depth coverage. About Our Expert I write about money. I’ve been reviewing tax software and services as a freelancer for PCMag since 1993. Along the way, I took on reviews of other types of business and personal finance technology. Prior to that, I had spent a few years writing about productivity and entertainment applications for 8-bit personal computers (my first one was a Commodore VIC-20) as a member of the editorial staff at Compute! After working at Lawson Associates, now Lawson Software, I switched my focus to accounting but learned that personal computer applications were more progressive and interesting to cover than mainframe solutions. So I served as editor of a monthly newsletter that provided support for accountants who were just starting to use PCs. I still ghostwrite monthly how-to columns for accounting professionals. From there, I went on to write articles and reviews for numerous business and financial publications, including Barron’s and Kiplinger’s Personal Finance Magazine.

item.title: Which Claude Do You Use? Cowork and Design Move Into One Simple Interface
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.10
Anthropic’s Claude interface is unnecessarily complicated: Cowork, Chat, and Design are available in different places, but an imminent update will make it easier to use. Soon, Claude itself will automatically determine the best next step in response to a prompt. Anthropic says, "Claude can now figure out what a task needs, so what Cowork and Design can do is available from any conversation, with the context, skills, and connectors you already have." This change comes after Anthropic found users were frustrated by the separation and often unsure which tool to use. Some projects started through Cowork weren't available in its other tools, and vice versa. Combining into a single interface will also give you easier access to Claude's creative tools, including the existing Design option and new Docs and Slides features. Docs allows you to make text documents using Claude models to generate the prose, while Slides makes presentations. Claude will draft each slide for you, and you can present them directly from the app or download them as a PDF or PowerPoint file. Claude Design launched earlier this year and focuses on visual work, such as one-pagers, graphics, or prototype documents. Claude Design, Docs, and Slides all remain in beta and will be available through a new Output button under the prompt box. This will also house Artifacts, Anthropic's shareable tools created by other users. These changes will first appear for Pro and Max subscribers, with their rollout set for the coming weeks across desktop, mobile, and the web. Free users will be able to access the updated platform at a later date. The same applies to those on Team plans and Enterprise logins, although an exact rollout window remains unclear. About Our Expert I’ve been a journalist for over a decade after getting my start in tech reporting back in 2013. I joined PCMag in 2025, where I cover the latest developments across the tech sphere, writing about the gadgets and services you use every day. Be sure to send me any tips you think PCMag would be interested in.

item.title: Meta One Bundles Instagram, Facebook, WhatsApp Subscriptions for $8 a Month
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.90
Throughout 2026, Meta has experimented with paid-for subscriptions for its most passionate Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp users, launching Plus versions of each social network. Now, you can get an all-in-one package, along with expanded Meta AI access to use with its new Muse model. The Meta One subscription plan gives you access to Facebook Plus, Instagram Plus, and WhatsApp Plus, as well as increased usage for Meta AI tools. The Core bundle starts at $7.99 per month, a $3 saving compared with buying each service separately. Instagram Plus gives you exclusive access to custom fonts, notifications when select people view your Story, previews of direct messages, and more. Meanwhile, Facebook Plus gives you extra super reactions for posts and expanded customization options for Messenger, while WhatsApp Plus gives you extra app themes, premium stickers, custom ringtones, and more. Meta says its all-encompassing package includes more than 50 features you don't get with its free service. Increased Meta AI access is said to expand the number of photos and videos you can create with the tools, although Meta has yet to detail exactly what the usage limits are. A top-tier option for personal use, called Premium, costs $19.99 a month. Meta says it includes “Everything in Core, with the most room to create content with Meta AI and across our family of apps." It also plans to introduce exclusive features for other services, including its Edits video-editing tool and its AI smart glasses. Meta has yet to detail exactly what those new features will be, and says to expect them to roll out "over time." Creators and businesses can also get a One membership, which includes enhanced profile information to highlight useful details, more prominent follow buttons on Reels, and the ability to set up automatic follow invitations across services. The cheapest Essential plan for businesses and creators costs $14.99 per month, while its Advanced package costs $49.99 per month. The top-tier Expert option starts at $149 a month and increases to $499 if you plan to scale usage across a large company.
