item.title: Meta May Launch a Pair of Camera-Free Smart Glasses Next Week
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 2.73
Amid growing privacy concerns, Meta is set to launch a pair of camera-less smart glasses next week, reports The Information. Over the past couple of years, Meta has faced widespread scrutiny over its AI smart glasses’ ability to record people without their consent or awareness. The situation has frustrated people so much that some are calling the wearable form factor “pervert glasses.” Smart glasses have also faced bans in courts and in select other public places. While the backlash continues, Meta may launch a pair of camera-free glasses at its Connect conference scheduled for Sept. 23 and 24, the report says. The rumored glasses are internally called Luna, and are expected to be available in two styles: Clubmaster and Burbank. Without the camera, Luna could simply function as glasses with a built-in AI assistant. According to The Information, the wearable will have six microphones, allowing users to speak to the Meta AI chatbot and the Muse AI agent. The glasses will also have a button for quick access to Meta AI and audio speakers similar to those in current models. Luna won’t be Meta’s first attempt at improving its glasses’ reputation. The company’s glasses have always featured an LED indicator to signal when a user is recording video or clicking a picture. Modders, however, found a way to tamper with the indicator, allowing wearers to record others by hiding it or even removing it entirely. To counter this workaround, Meta recently updated its software to block recording if the capture LED is modified or removed. Company-owned Instagram also began taking down creepy or harassing videos filmed using the Meta glasses. Despite these efforts, concerns around smart glasses remain. If Luna gets unveiled next week, Meta could begin shipping the glasses in October, the report adds. About Our Expert Jibin is a tech news writer based out of Ahmedabad, India. Previously, he served as the editor of iGeeksBlog and is a self-proclaimed tech enthusiast who loves breaking down complex information for a broader audience.

item.title: Trust in AI Eroded Significantly Over Past Year, Even Among Those Who Use It
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 2.73
If AI chatbots had feelings, a new Gallup poll might have them feeling nervous about how people see them. The survey finds that while more Americans are trying AI and think themselves at least somewhat versed in it compared with a year ago, they now trust AI less than they did in 2025. Specifically, the share of respondents who said they “always, often, or sometimes” use AI at school, work, or in their personal lives jumped from 39% to 51% from 2025 to 2026, and the share who rated themselves “very” or “somewhat” knowledgeable about AI rose from 60% to 68%. But familiarity did not breed contentment: The fraction of respondents who said they “fully” or “somewhat” trust AI to make fair and unbiased decisions slipped from 32% in 2025 to 28% in 2026. That erosion persisted even among respondents who said they use AI at least sometimes, with the share trusting AI at least somewhat falling from 46% to 43%. Among people who rarely or never use AI, it was more of a collapse, from an already-bad 23% to a woeful 12%, worse than the 17% job-approval rating for Congress in Gallup’s latest published polling. The survey did not ask about concerns that AI might lead to human extinction–a possibility many AI backers keep raising–but did cover the less disquieting possibility of economic damage. There, too, people feel increasingly uneasy. Gallup’s year-ago polling showed that 53% of respondents thought AI would yield more economic growth, while 24% said it would decrease; today, the numbers have almost flipped, with 45% expecting reduced economic growth and 36% forecasting a boost. A shrinking majority still sees AI increasing productivity, 52% versus 31% expecting it to decrease productivity. (Applied wisely, AI can help people work better, but management-prodded AI rollouts can also leave workplaces flooded by AI slop.) Large and growing majorities expect to see AI reduce the number of businesses (59% now think that will happen, with only 14% saying it will lead to more business) and the number of jobs (70% expect to see AI destroy more jobs than it creates, while only 9% have the opposite view). The anxiety surfaced in those last two figures should get the AI advocates like Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and Microsoft founder Bill Gates, who have predicted massive job disruption from this technology, to take a long look in the mirror. Or at least get an AI image generator to replicate that view for them. Gallup’s poll also asked people what they thought we should all do about this and found broad support for various forms of education and regulation. While only 45% of respondents approved teaching AI skills in core K-12 classes, far more backed education and training later in life: 66% endorsed on-the-job training programs and 72% favored boosting STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering, Mathematics) education. A full 79% of respondents endorsed having the government focus on setting safety and data-security rules even if they impede AI development. That’s a trade-off that President Trump keeps rejecting, but Gallup found relatively little partisan splits on most aspects of AI policy. The biggest approval gap involved whether the government should boost energy production for AI’s sake, a core element of Trump’s fossil-fuel-favoring “AI Action Plan”; 57% of Republicans backed that, but only 41% of Democrats did. As for who should write any such AI regulations, 60% said the US government should do so, 50% said companies should cooperate to develop shared rules, and only 17% backed letting individual companies create their own. Gallup respondents also wanted to see safety testing done outside of AI companies, with 75% saying independent experts should conduct these tests and 52% saying the government should run them. Gallup conducted this survey in partnership with the Special Competitive Studies Project, an Arlington, VA-based nonprofit think tank founded in 2021 by former Google CEO Eric Schmidt to advance American AI competitiveness. The Washington-based polling firm had 3,152 members of its Gallup Panel complete its web survey from June 2 to 23, meaning the survey was in the field too soon to capture any responses to the AI industry’s latest freakout over whether AI will kill us all. About Our Expert Rob Pegoraro writes about interesting problems and possibilities in computers, gadgets, apps, services, telecom, and other things that beep or blink. He’s covered such developments as the evolution of the cell phone from 1G to 5G, the fall and rise of Apple, Google’s growth from obscure Yahoo rival to verb status, and the transformation of social media from CompuServe forums to Facebook’s billions of users. Pegoraro has met most of the founders of the internet and once received a single-word email reply from Steve Jobs.

item.title: Why This Single iOS 27 Feature Turns the iPhone Duo Into a Pocket Laptop
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 2.31
Now that the initial dust has settled on Apple's historic iPhone Duo announcement, real-world utility takes the spotlight over hardware novelty. Never mind the device's physical engineering (which is impressive, admittedly)—the real conversation belongs to the software ecosystem. Thanks to the Duo, iOS 27 is introducing native, side-by-side split-screen multitasking to the iPhone, effectively giving us a pocket-sized laptop substitute. As someone who tests and reviews mobile operating systems, I’ve become frustrated with how Apple’s restrictive software bottlenecks its brilliant silicon. For me, this single OS upgrade is the killer feature that will transform the iPhone Duo from an expensive gimmick into a must-buy mobile productivity powerhouse. This is the pivot I’ve been waiting for. Breaking Nearly 20 Years of Limits Ever since the original iPhone launched in 2007, we've been trapped in a single-app vacuum. If you want to quote an article while writing an email, you have to exit the email app, jump into Safari to copy, exit, and return to email, and paste. It’s an archaic dance we’ve simply accepted because of the limitations of the underlying engine. Heck, even the iPad's Stage Manager implementation felt unoptimized and clunky when it first arrived. The adaptive version of iOS 27 on the iPhone Duo finally shatters that barrier. When you unfold the device to reveal its massive 7.6-inch inner canvas, you can run two completely independent applications side by side. Of course, Android power users are well within their rights to roll their eyes at this announcement. Devices like Samsung’s Galaxy Fold line have mastered split-screen app execution for generations now. What makes Apple’s multitasking unique isn't that it's first, but that it's deeply integrated. It leverages the Duo's canvas to slide background apps into fluid, hoverable stacks that feel less like a cramped mobile desktop and more like a natural extension of physical paper. That Drag-and-Drop Magic What has me most excited isn't just seeing two apps at once, but how they talk to each other. Much like the Visual Look Up AI that let me drag PNG elements across apps in previous updates, Apple’s new split-screen engine lets you grab an image or a block of text from a Safari web page on the left screen and slide your finger across the display's center seam to drop it directly into a Message, Note, or email on the right. To make this even more efficient, iOS 27 lets you lock your favorite app combinations together into "App Pairs." If you regularly check Slack while monitoring your Calendar, you can save that pairing to your Home Screen and launch both apps perfectly arranged with a single tap. Like a Computer in Your Pocket I’ve argued before that the iPhone hardware is ready for heavy lifting, but the software has actively stood in the way. Math Notes is a superb tool, but it has always felt cramped on a standard, narrow iOS screen. This new multitasking framework shifts the Duo's value proposition. You aren't paying $2,000 or more for a smartphone with a slightly larger screen and some neat party tricks. You’re paying for the freedom to leave your laptop at home with multi-window workflow management functionality right in your pocket. It’s the exact moment the iPhone stops feeling like a phone and starts acting like a true computer. The Pencil Synergy: Better Than a Keyboard? What truly cements this split-screen layout for me is how it handles the newly added Apple Pencil integration. As mentioned, using intricate software like Math Notes on a cramped iPhone screen felt like fighting a spreadsheet on a tiny shard of glass, forcing an absurd level of precision that killed any creative momentum. On the Duo's expanded screen real estate, however, the combination of native multitasking and stylus support changes the equation. I can keep a Safari research tab or a video open on the left screen while using the Pencil to handwrite formulas or sketch ideas directly in the right pane. It brings the fluid, notebook-style workflow that I've praised on iPadOS straight to a pocketable device. Multitaskers, Enter the Fold There is no doubt that the iPhone Duo is a luxury, starting at $1,999 for the baseline 256GB model all the way up to $3,199 for 2TB. But if you're eager to change how you use your phone on a daily basis, preorders go live on Friday, Oct. 16, with the phone officially hitting store shelves on Friday, Oct. 23. The standard iOS 27 update officially drops on Monday, Sept. 14. Although slab iPhones, like the new iPhone 18 Pro, won't get this desktop-class split-screen framework, the sheer power of this multitasking engine has me convinced that the future of Apple's mobile platform is unfolding right before our eyes. About Our Expert In 2014, I began my career at PCMag as a freelancer. That blossomed into a full-time position in 2021, and I now review email marketing apps, mobile operating systems, web hosting services, streaming music platforms, and video games as a senior writer. I'm a graduate of Hunter College, a hard-core gamer, and an Apple enthusiast.

item.title: Never Trust Facebook: 3 Ways to Protect Your Privacy When Using Meta AI
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 2.29
I use a variety of AI chatbots in my personal and professional lives, including Meta AI. Though not as popular as ChatGPT or Gemini, Meta AI pops up on Facebook, Messenger, Instagram, and WhatsApp, as well as on its own dedicated website and app. The problem here is that Meta has a poor track record of respecting and protecting your personal information, so periodic security reviews should extend to Meta AI, too. That’s not a simple task since Meta AI surfaces in so many places, but it is possible. As just a few examples, you can delete or reset your chat history, limit third-party access and tracking, use Incognito Chat mode in WhatsApp and the Meta AI app, and request that your account and data be excluded from AI training. Here’s how I was able to better secure my privacy with Meta AI. 1. Delete Your Meta AI Chats If you'd like to remove your chats so that they can no longer be seen or used by Meta, you can delete individual prompts. On the website, hover over the chat you wish to remove, select the ellipsis icon, and click Delete. In the mobile app, tap the two-line icon at the top to open the sidebar, then press and hold the chat you wish to remove, then tap Delete. To delete all your chats, log into the Meta AI website, click your account name at the bottom of the left sidebar, then select Settings > Data & privacy > Manage your information. Select Delete all chats and media > Delete all chats and media > Delete all to remove all past chats. To do the same from the iOS or Android app, select the two-line icon in the upper left and then tap the Settings gear icon at the bottom. Swipe down to the App settings section and tap Data & privacy > Manage your information to delete all your chats and media. 2. Control Share Settings By default, your conversations with Meta AI remain private. If you decide to share any of your prompts publicly on social media, the company could suggest them on other platforms such as Facebook and Instagram. To disable this feature, open Settings > Data & privacy > Suggesting your prompts on other apps (Suggesting your vibes on other apps in the mobile app) and then disable the switches for Facebook and Instagram. In the app, you'll also have the Mentions option, where you can control who is able to mention you and link to your Meta account in their comments. If the option is set to Everyone, change it to People you follow or Don’t allow mentions. 3. Ask to Be Removed From AI Training By default, Meta uses your AI chats and other information (including third-party data) to train its models. Unlike most other AI services, you can’t simply opt out of this training. Instead, you must send a special request to Meta asking that certain third-party data not be used for AI training. And Meta makes the process as difficult as possible. This type of request focuses on personal details such as your name, home address, phone number, or email address. The data in question can be available from the internet, third parties, or through products and services created by outside developers using Meta AI’s API. Browse to the page called Data Subject Rights for Third Party Information Used for AI at Meta. Here, choose your country and include your name and email address. You then must provide any prompts you sent to Meta AI that resulted in your personal information appearing in a response. You'll also need to provide a screenshot of the response. Once you've sent in the form, you'll need to wait to see if Meta approves your request. About Our Expert I've been working for PCMag since early 2016 writing tutorials, how-to pieces, and other articles on consumer technology. Beyond PCMag, I've written news stories and tutorials for a variety of other websites and publications, including CNET, ZDNet, TechRepublic, Macworld, PC World, Time, US News & World Report, and AARP Magazine. I spent seven years writing breaking news for CNET as one of the site’s East Coast reporters. I've also written two books for Wiley & Sons—Windows 8: Five Minutes at a Time and Teach Yourself Visually LinkedIn. I've used Windows, Office, and other Microsoft products for years so I'm well versed in that world. I also know the Mac quite well. I'm always working with iOS, iPadOS, watchOS, and Android on my various mobile devices. And these days, I write a lot about AI, so that's become another key area for me. My wife always jokes about all the tech products we have around the house, but I manage to put them to good use for my articles. I like Lenovo computers, so I own a couple of Lenovo desktops and several laptops. I have three MacBooks and a Mac mini. For my mobile life and work, I use an iPhone 16 Pro, iPad Pro, and iPad mini as well as an Apple Watch. But since I write about Android, I own several Android phones and tablets. Like any tech person, I have a cabinet full of cables, wires, and assorted mysterious gadgets. And when it's time to take a break from writing, I have an old Xbox 360 and Nintendo Wii, both of which I use for exercise and fitness games.

item.title: Google just fixed 42 Chrome security flaws. Update now
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 5.92
In summary: - PCWorld reports that Google has patched 42 security vulnerabilities in Chrome, with three classified as critical risks affecting Windows, macOS, Linux, Android, and iOS users. - Many of the fixes address use-after-free memory flaws, and while none have been exploited yet, the risks are serious enough to warrant immediate action. - Users should update Chrome now via the About Google Chrome menu to stay protected. In the new versions of Chrome 153.0.8010.47/48 for Windows and macOS, and 153.0.8010.47 for Linux, Google has fixed more than 40 security vulnerabilities, some of which are critical. According to Google, none of the patched vulnerabilities have been exploited in attacks yet. In the Chrome Releases blog post, Srinivas Sista lists 42 vulnerabilities that have been fixed. While Google discovered 26 of the vulnerabilities internally, another 16 were identified by external security researchers. Google has so far awarded them $2,500 in bounties. Three vulnerabilities are classified as critical, including two use-after-free (UAF) flaws in the Internals and Workers components. A further 28 vulnerabilities are classified as high risk, and the rest are classified as medium risk minus one that’s low risk. Again, the most common type is the use-after-free vulnerability, with 12 instances. Chrome usually updates automatically when a new version is available. You can manually check for updates via Help → About Google Chrome. Chrome 154 is due to be released as early as next week. Google has also released Chrome for Android 153.0.8010.47 and Chrome for iOS 154.0.8037.41 this week. The Android version addresses the same vulnerabilities as the desktop versions. The Extended Stable Channel for Windows and macOS now includes Chromium version 152.0.7977.130. Tip: Whether you keep your browser up to date, you need proper antivirus protections if you want your PC to remain secure and private. Check out our picks for the best antivirus software for Windows as well as best VPN services to stay ahead of security problems.

item.title: This hidden VLC feature lets you stream thousands of free TV channels
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 5.00
Most people know VLC as the little orange traffic cone that can play just about any video file you throw at it. But it can also stream video and audio straight from the internet. This feature is called “Open Network Stream,” and you’ll find it under Media > Open Network Stream in the VLC Player app. You can also press Ctrl + N to jump straight there. Paste in a supported stream URL then click Play and VLC will start streaming the content. The best way I’ve found to use this is with IPTV. The open-source IPTV-org project on GitHub keeps a massive collection of publicly available, legal TV streams from around the world. Its playlists include thousands of channels covering news, sports, entertainment, music, local TV, and more. Sam Singleton To give it a try, copy IPTV-org’s main playlist URL, paste the link into the network stream in VLC, and click Play. VLC will load the playlist, and begin streaming. You can then browse the available channels under Toggle Playlist. If you aren’t interested in the full list, then you can download individual playlists from the IPTV Github sorted by country, language, region, and category instead. Not every channel is going to work all the time though. Streams can go offline, move to a new address, or be restricted in certain regions. Still, it’s a pretty neat way to stream content for free from all over the world. For more fun and helpful tips, tricks, website and app recommendations, be sure to subscribe to our PCWorld Try This newsletter.

item.title: MyPDFTools review: A handy free PDF toolkit with some rough edges
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 4.37
At a glance Expert's Rating Pros - 36 free browser-based PDF tools - Clean, intuitive interface - Strong performance on routine PDF tasks - No account or software installation required Cons - Editing tools are limited - PDF-to-Word conversion can lose formatting and layout - OCR supports only English and files up to 30 pages - Limited transparency about who operates the service Our Verdict MyPDFTools is a convenient free option for quick, low-stakes PDF tasks, with a broad set of tools that generally handle the basics well. But its limited editing, uneven conversion results, and lack of operator transparency make it less suitable for demanding or sensitive work. Price When Reviewed This value will show the geolocated pricing text for product undefined Best Pricing Today Price When Reviewed Free Best Prices Today: MyPDFTools Billed as “Every PDF tool you need,” MyPDFTools gathers 36 PDF utilities in a single browser-based interface. The appeal is you can run only the utility you need when you need it without having to invest in a full-featured PDF editor like Acrobat or Nitro PDF. That formula works well for many everyday PDF tasks. But some of the more demanding tasks are where MyPDFTools starts to show its limitations. Read on to learn more, then see our roundup of the best PDF editors for comparison. MyPDFTools features and pricing MyPDFTools has a clean, intuitive layout. The utilities appear as tiles in the main window and in a left sidebar grouped into six categories: Convert Documents, Organize, Edit & Sign, Optimize, Convert Images, and Security. The sidebar remains after you open a tool, making it easy to move between jobs, while search boxes offer another route to find what you need. Michael Ansaldo/Foundry Nearly every tool works the same way: Upload your document, choose your settings, and download the processed file. An optional account adds an activity history, and the interface is available in 33 languages. All 36 tools are currently free, though OCR is marked “Free for now,” so that could change. Editing and signing PDFs The Edit & Sign category contains tools for editing and signing documents, redacting text, and “flattening” PDFs—locking in filled form values and removing their interactivity. All four worked in my tests, though the Edit tool offers far less than its name suggests. You’re able to place new text and images over a page but cannot change existing text or add annotations such as highlights, drawings, shapes, or comments. Added text can be resized, but there are no font or color choices. The other three tools worked as advertised. Redaction lets you drag boxes over material you want removed. The site says it converts each affected page to an image while leaving untouched pages alone; in my download, the covered text could no longer be selected or extracted. Because the entire affected page is rasterized, its remaining text also loses searchability and screen-reader accessibility. Michael Ansaldo/Foundry To sign a document, you choose the page and location, then draw or type a signature or upload one. Width and height controls are provided to adjust its size. The result is a visible signature stamp, not a certificate-backed digital signature. Organizing and protecting PDFs MyPDFTools handled routine page management well across several test documents. Merge and split preserved the page order, while rotate, delete, reorder, and crop all worked as expected. I also tested a three-page interactive form with text fields, drop-down menus, checkboxes, and radio buttons; its controls remained intact after splitting, merging, and reordering. Watermarks and page numbers also appeared where they should. To use the password protection utility, you simply upload a PDF, enter a desired password, and download the encrypted copy. My test file used AES-256 encryption and wouldn’t open without the password. Unlock PDF removed the protection with the correct password and returned a clear error when I entered the wrong one. Michael Ansaldo/Foundry Conversion and OCR performance MyPDFTools offers 14 conversion options, including conversions to and from Microsoft Office formats, plus text, RTF, and HTML to PDF. Word-to-PDF worked well in my testing. A three-page document came back as a clean, readable PDF with its pagination, spacing, emphasis, and colored text intact. It wasn’t an exact match, though. MyPDFTools substituted different fonts for the Microsoft fonts in the original. The file’s metadata indicates that the server uses LibreOffice for conversion. Converting a PDF to Word was more problematic. MyPDFTools preserved nearly all the text and the three-page division, but changed US Letter pages to A4 and replaced the original 12- and 13-point type with uniform 10-point Liberation Serif. Bold, italics, underlining, color, and highlighting disappeared. Each printed line also became a separate Word paragraph, making normal editing and text reflow cumbersome. In another test, the converter dropped an image and lost the original table formatting. Michael Ansaldo/Foundry OCR did much better. On a scanned document, it recognized names, dates, currency, identifiers, and percentages, then added a searchable text layer. The reading order wasn’t perfect and some stray text appeared, but the result was usable. OCR supports only English and files up to 30 pages. Privacy and trust concerns There’s also limited information about who runs the service. The site doesn’t name a company or provide an address, and contact is handled through a web form. The governing-law section of the terms contains what appears to be placeholder text—“These terms are governed by the laws of [Your State/Country]”—instead of identifying a jurisdiction. The homepage also says employees at several companies use the service, though it provides no supporting detail for those claims. None of this necessarily signals a problem, but it leaves users with less information to go on when deciding whether to upload sensitive documents Should you use MyPDFTools? MyPDFTools is easy to use and useful for simple, low-stakes work. Its tools cover many common needs without requiring payment or an account, which makes it a compelling option for quick PDF tasks. I would avoid it for detailed editing, faithful PDF-to-Office conversion, or sensitive material until those tools are improved and the site is clearer about who operates it and how uploaded files are handled.

item.title: Roborock Qrevo Edge 2 review: Slim and powerful (with caveats)
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 4.07
At a glance Expert's Rating Pros - Fits under low furniture - Side brush and swivel mop cleans corners and edges - Split main brush effectively reduces hair tangles - The docking station washes at up to 176 F and dries them at 131 F Cons - Thresholds over 0.8 inches are an obstacle - No cleaning solution tank Our Verdict The Roborock Qrevo Edge 2 is a great pick if you have low furniture and lots of edges to clean, but its limited threshold clearance and lack of automatic cleaning-solution dispensing keep it from being an all-around winner. Price at time of review This value will show the geolocated pricing text for product undefined Best Price Today Best Prices Today: Roborock Qrevo Edge 2 Robot vacuum cleaners with a slim design have (so far) been largely limited to expensive flagship models. The Roborock Qrevo Edge 2 brings this design to a much more affordable price. That said, Roborock still includes key convenience features like the extendable side brush, lifting mop pads, and a mostly self-cleaning dock. Our test shows just how the savings in chassis design, obstacle detection, and cleaning solution dispensing affect everyday use, as well as the advantages of the low profile design. Christoph Hoffmann Roborock Qrevo Edge 2: Design and build quality The robot measures 13.9 × 13.9 × 3.1 inches and weighs 9.9 pounds. Its low profile is particularly noteworthy. It matches the dimensions of Roborock’s top-of-the-line model, the Saros 20 Sonic, exactly and is significantly lower than several competitors: The DJI Romo P and Ecovacs Deebot X12 OmniCyclone are around 3.9 inches high, the Mova Z70 Ultra Roller Complete measures 3.8 inches with the sensor tower retracted, and the Roborock Qrevo Curv 2 Flow stands at 4.7 inches. Christoph Hoffmann This is made possible by RetractSense. The laser tower can be retracted into the body. A dToF sensor checks the available clearance height in advance. The tower retracts when approaching low furniture. To navigate underneath the furniture, the robot then uses, among other things, a vision module with a 100-degree field of view. Unlike the Saros 20 Sonic, the Qrevo Edge 2 does not have an adjustable chassis. Christoph Hoffmann At 13.4 inches wide, the station is comparatively slim, but at 20.5 inches high, it requires sufficient headroom. It is significantly narrower than the 17.3-inch-wide Saros station. At the top are two easily accessible tanks: one on the right holding 135 fluid ounces of fresh water and one on the left holding 118 fluid ounces of dirty water. Behind the front flap is the dust bag, which has a capacity of 91 fluid ounces. Christoph Hoffmann The wash basin in the base can be completely removed and rinsed out. This makes cleaning easier, as hair and lint tend to accumulate there over time. The build quality is in keeping with Roborock’s usual high standards. The flaps close flush, and there are very few gaps where dust can accumulate. The total weight of the robot and docking station is 28 pounds. Roborock Qrevo Edge 2: Specifications Roborock specifies a maximum of 25,000 pascals for the HyperForce suction system. To put this into perspective, the manufacturer quotes 36,000 Pa for the Saros 20 Sonic. Meanwhile, the DJI Romo P also achieves 25,000 Pa and the Qrevo Curv 2 Flow reaches 20,000 Pa. Ecovacs does not specify a value in pascals for the Deebot X12 OmniCyclone, instead quoting an airflow of 5.8 cubic feet per second. The Pascal figure alone says little about real-world performance. On hard floors and carpets, the brush design, brush contact, and airflow also influence the result. Mopping is carried out using two rotating pads at 200 rpm and eight newtons of contact pressure. According to the manufacturer, the DJI Romo P’s pads apply five newtons of pressure to the floor, while the Saros 20 Sonic’s vibrating mop applies 14 newtons. The mop roller on the Qrevo Curv 2 Flow operates at 15 newtons, while the Mova Z70 operates at 18 newtons at 800 rpm. The manufacturers’ specifications for contact pressure show significant differences; however, due to the different mopping systems, these cannot be directly translated into cleaning performance. Christoph Hoffmann For edge cleaning, Roborock combines the extendable FlexiArm Arc side brush with a swiveling mop module. This allows the robot to get closer to skirting boards and into corners. The split DuoDivide main brush helps prevent hair from becoming tangled. It guides hair towards the suction opening rather than allowing it to wrap around a continuous brush roller. Under the testing conditions, Roborock claims a zero percent tangling rate for hair up to 15.7 inches in length. The Omnidrehrad is also designed to make hair less likely to wrap round the axle. Christoph Hoffmann Reactive AI combines structured light with an RGB camera. According to Roborock, the system recognizes more than 280 types of objects. The Saros 20 Sonic’s side-facing VertiBeam light is missing, as is the StarSight solid-state LiDAR. DirTect technology distinguishes between dry and wet dirt. When encountering dust, the robot increases its suction power and does not mop. When encountering wet patches, it lifts the main brush. This ensures that less wet dirt gets into the brush. The battery has a capacity of 5,200 mAh and can be charged in less than four hours. Roborock states a runtime of up to 295 minutes in quiet mode. The Saros 20 Sonic and its sister model, the Qrevo Edge 2 Pro, each have a battery capacity of 6,400 mAh. The robot’s water tank holds just 2.3 fluid ounces. On larger mopping areas, this may require additional trips back to the station to refill, which extends the cleaning time. The dock washes the mops with water up to 175 F, dries them with air at 131 F, and largely cleans the wash basin itself. A dirt sensor can trigger additional wash cycles if necessary. According to the manufacturer, the dust bag should last up to 65 days without needing to be replaced under typical use. Christoph Hoffmann There is no separate tank for cleaning solution. Approved cleaning additives must be added manually to the fresh water. The Saros 20 Sonic dispenses cleaning solution automatically. The Qrevo Edge 2 Pro also has a dedicated compartment for this purpose. When purchasing, you should pay close attention to the model name. Within the Qrevo range, Roborock often sells model variants with very similar-sounding names (such as Edge, Edge Pro, Curv or Slim) simultaneously, some of which differ only by a single suffix in the name. The technical specifications – such as suction power, battery capacity, or cleaning solution tank – can sometimes differ significantly. The Qrevo Edge 2 supports Matter and can be integrated into smart home systems from Amazon, Apple, and Google. The voice assistant Hello Rocky responds even without an internet connection. Roborock Qrevo Edge 2: Setup The process follows the familiar Roborock procedure. Once the docking station has been set up, the access ramp is locked into place and the fresh water tank is filled. After installing the app and scanning the QR code under the top cover, the Qrevo Edge 2 will then pair with your smartphone via Bluetooth and connect to the Wi-Fi. If necessary, the app installs a firmware update. Our test unit was running version V02.15.44. The setup wizard guides you through the initial settings in detail. Here, you can set preferences for pets or carpets, configure Do Not Disturb mode, and enable map saving. For multi-story homes, multiple maps can be saved. The built-in voice assistant can also be activated. It responds to Hello Rocky and allows you to give basic cleaning commands without a smartphone. Christoph Hoffmann Quick mapping then begins. The robot scans the rooms as it passes through them, rather than covering every area in full. In our testing area, which is just under 753 square feet, this was completed in less than five minutes. The app then automatically divides the map into rooms and suggests suitable room names. It also marks recognized floor types on the map. Any errors can be corrected afterwards. Restricted zones, door thresholds, and furniture can also be added. Room names and boundaries can be adjusted later. The Roborock app remains one of the system’s strengths. Despite the high level of customization, cleaning modes, room cleaning, and no-go zones can be found without a lengthy search. Water flow can be adjusted in stages and configured independently of the suction power. The robot automatically detects carpets. Several cleaning strategies are available for this. Depending on the setting, it lifts the mops, navigates around carpets, or cleans them separately. The app offers a particularly wide range of options for carpets. The Qrevo Edge 2 can automatically return the mops to the docking station for carpet-only cleaning. If you set the robot to vacuum carpets first without the mops attached, you should monitor the first run and adjust the settings if necessary. Roborock Qrevo Edge 2: Performance Current robot vacuum cleaners differ significantly in terms of obstacle detection. In testing, Reactive AI usually recognized typical obstacles such as food bowls and dog toys lying around. Thin cables and very flat objects proved more challenging, however. Among the models we tested recently, the DJI Romo P, with its solid-state LiDAR and two fisheye cameras, delivered reliable obstacle detection. More problematic is the Qrevo Edge 2’s threshold-crossing capability, which is limited to 0.8 inches. A 0.8-inch threshold remains a common specification for traditional robot vacuum cleaners and is sufficient for flat transition profiles. However, modern top-of-the-range models can now handle significantly higher thresholds. Thresholds in older buildings or thick carpet edges can become a problem. In practical use, the Saros 20 Sonic, with its AdaptiLift chassis, can negotiate individual thresholds of up to two inches, while the Mova Z70 claims 1.9 inches. In our test, the Qrevo Edge 2 failed to negotiate a threshold just over 0.8 inches high between the bedroom and the hallway. Even manually entering the door threshold in the Roborock app failed to help. The robot then adjusted its approach angle and speed. Nevertheless, the edge remained insurmountable for the rigid chassis. Christoph Hoffmann Compared with the most recent models in this price range that we have tested, this limited climbing ability stands out as a negative point. For homes with higher thresholds, it’s a clear disadvantage. By contrast, the robot reliably recognized the runners on our cantilever chairs in the kitchen as obstacles. It stopped in front of the flat metal runners and navigated around them without getting stuck. The Qrevo Edge 2 lacks the Saros 20 Sonic’s side-facing VertiBeam light, which is designed to better detect low and narrow obstacles along walls. Thin cables should be removed before cleaning, especially those near walls. The pet functions proved useful in everyday use. If the robot approaches a pet, it stops the main brush and changes direction. It returns to blocked areas later. The design plays an important role in mopping performance. The two rotating pads, each with a force of eight newtons, pick up loosened dirt and are rinsed at the docking station at set intervals. Christoph Hoffmann In contrast, roller systems like the one on the Mova Z70 continuously rinse the roller with fresh water during cleaning. The Z70 uses twelve nozzles for this purpose and drains away dirty water immediately. In our test, this principle proved particularly effective against dried-on stains. The Qrevo Edge 2 operates on a different mopping principle. It achieves good results during routine cleaning. For dried-on residues, several passes or a higher water flow rate are required. On large surfaces, cleaning performance may diminish between two wash cycles as dirt gradually accumulates on the pads. The station’s dirt monitoring system can trigger additional mop wash cycles if necessary. This extends the cleaning time, but keeps the pads cleaner. The mop pads also absorb grease well and dry quickly after cleaning. The swiveling mop has an advantage around edges. With roller systems without a side extension, a wider uncleaned area can remain in tight corners or around furniture legs. The Qrevo Edge 2’s extendable mop reduces this gap and works close to the skirting board. In homes with lots of nooks and crannies, the good edge coverage is a distinct advantage of the Qrevo Edge 2. Christoph Hoffmann The robot lifts the mops off the floor when cleaning carpets. The system handles short-pile carpets easily. For high-pile carpets or those with long fringes, it is advisable to set up a no-go zone. In day-to-day use, the main tasks involve topping up the fresh water and emptying the dirty water tank. Occasionally, the wash basin and brushes also need cleaning, and the filters and sensors need checking. There is no dirty water tank inside the robot itself, and some of the loosened dirt remains in the pads until the next wash. Roborock Qrevo Edge 2: Conclusion The Qrevo Edge 2’s biggest strengths are its slim design and feature-packed cleaning station. Compared to the Saros 20 Sonic, it lacks the retractable chassis and VertiBeam. The the battery capacity is around 1,200 mAh smaller. The Edge 2 also does not have a separate cleaning solution tank. The cost savings relate primarily to the chassis, navigation, battery, and cleaning solution dispensing. For the mopping system, Roborock continues to rely on rotating pads rather than a roller. There are two key points to consider before purchasing. The maximum threshold height of 0.8 inches is on a par with many traditional robot vacuum cleaners. In homes with high door thresholds, the robot may reach its limits. With dried-on coffee and ketchup stains, the pads require more passes than the best roller systems. For homes with low furniture and lots of edges, the Qrevo Edge 2 is appealing, especially at its current price. In households with pet hair, the split main brush is an advantage. For large hard floors with dried-on kitchen grime, roller models such as the Qrevo Curv 2 Flow or Mova Z70 Ultra Roller Complete offer better performance. With high thresholds, a model with a lift mechanism is a must-have. Roborock Qrevo Edge 2: Tech specs - Robot dimensions: 13.9 × 13.9 × 3.1 in - Robot weight: 9.9 lbs - Dimensions of charging station: 13.4 × 19.2 × 20.5 in - Docking station weight: 18.1 lbs - Maximum suction power: 25,000 Pa HyperForce (manufacturer’s specification) - Rated power: 60 W - Mopping system: Two rotating pads, 200 rpm, 8 N contact pressure, swiveling, lifting mops, can be stored on the docking station - Edge cleaning: Extendable FlexiArm-Arc side brush and swiveling mopping module - Main brush: DuoDivide, split design. According to the manufacturer, 0 percent tangling rate with hair up to 40 cm in length - Navigation: RetractSense LiDAR, retractable, dToF sensor, vision module with 100-degree field of view - Obstacle detection: Reactive AI with structured light and RGB camera. According to the manufacturer, recognizes more than 280 object types - Dirt detection: DirTect, distinguishes between dry and wet dirt, main brush can be raised - Obstacle clearance: Up to 0.8 inches - Carpets: Detection, boost mode, mop lift, and mop storage - Fall sensors: 4 - Battery: 5,200 mAh, charging time under 4 hours, up to 295 minutes runtime in quiet mode (manufacturer’s specification) - Robot tank: 240 ml dust, 67 ml water, E11 filter - Docking station: 2,700 ml dust bag, 4,000 ml fresh water, 3,500 ml dirty water - Docking station functions: Mop washing with water up to 176 F, warm-air drying at 131 F, self-cleaning, automatic dust emptying, and removable wash basin. Dust bag lasts up to 65 days according to the manufacturer - Water flow: 30 settings, electronically controlled - Noise level: 63 dB in balanced mode - Smart Home: Matter, Alexa, Siri, Google Home, Hello Rocky voice assistant can be used offline - Contents: Robot, docking station, access ramp, power cable, mopping modules, and user manual. The set version also includes two mop heads and two dust bags - Warranty: 2 years

But not all deals are worth it, so we only highlight those offered by reputable providers that we’ve personally reviewed and recommend. We’ve also included some helpful answers to common questions about VPN shopping at the bottom of this article. Before you decide on a new VPN, be sure to check out our roundup of the best VPNs to help you choose the right service for your needs. Note: Tech deals come and go quickly, so it’s possible some of these VPN discounts will have expired before this article’s next update. Updated September 16, 2026 with the latest VPN deals and pricing. Best VPN deals - NordVPN, now $3.49 per month for 24 months + 3 free months (69% off at NordVPN) - ExpressVPN, now $2.99 per month for 24 months + 4 free months (80% off at ExpressVPN) - CyberGhost, now $1.99 per month for 24 months + 2 free months (88% off on CyberGhost) - Norton VPN, now $3.33 per month for 12 months (50% off on Norton) - Surfshark VPN, now $2.49 per month for 24 months + 3 free months (85% off at Surfshark) - Proton VPN, now $2.99 per month for 24 months (70% off at Proton VPN) - Private Internet Access, now $2.03 per month for 36 months + 3 free months (83% off at PIA) - PrivadoVPN, now $1.48 per month for 24 months + 3 free months (87% off at Privado VPN) - IPVanish VPN, now $2.49 per month for 24 months (83% off at IPVanish) Our Editors’ Choice and top overall VPN pick, NordVPN, is currently offering a good deal on its long-term 2-year plan for only $3.49 per month (69 percent off) and you get an extra three free months upon sign-up. Not only is Nord the most feature-rich VPN on the market, but it’s also the fastest we’ve ever tested. If you can swing it, upgrading to the Complete tier for $4.49 per month instead gives you a lot more for your money such as anti-malware, ad & tracker-blocking, scam protection, identity fraud monitoring, a password manager, and 1TB of cloud storage. ExpressVPN is also offering a great deal right now on all of its plans. While the Basic tier for $2.99 per month is the cheapest and gives you access to the outstanding VPN, I personally think the Advanced plan with ExpressVPN provides the better value. For just $1.50 more per month ($4.49/month) you get access to so much more: ad- and tracker-blocking, a password manager, Identity Defender services, and extra device connections, among other things. Finally, CyberGhost is running a Fall Special discount on its 2-year deal for only $1.99 per month with an additional two free months awarded after sign-up. This is the cheapest you’re likely to find a subscription to CyberGhost outside of larger holiday sales events. It’s a well-rounded VPN that is especially good for travelers thanks to its enormous server network. FAQ What is the best VPN deal? Right now, the 2-year plan for NordVPN‘s Complete tier is the best deal. For only $4.49 per month you’ll get access to the best VPN with the fastest speeds, excellent streaming compatibility, and top-notch privacy and security features. Included with this Plus tier are advanced protections such as a password manager and threat protection, plus 1TB of cloud storage. When’s the best time to shop for a VPN? Typically you’ll want to time your VPN shopping around a prominent sales period. The biggest sales periods are Black Friday/Cyber Monday in late November . The best sales often occur leading up to and during these two events and they are great times to snag a VPN subscription for cheap. Many VPN providers have even begun extending these deals past Cyber Monday and through to the end of the year. What should I look for in a VPN deal? There are a few things you should keep in mind when shopping for a good VPN deal. The first thing to consider is, of course, your budget. How much are you willing to spend each month? How much can you afford to drop on a longer-term plan with an upfront payment? You’ll also need to determine how long you intend to use the VPN. Do you just need it for a short trip? A few months? Or forever? The very best VPN deals are generally on longer-term plans for two or three years. After you decide on your budget and how long you’ll use the VPN, next you can start comparing features. Look at the number of servers and locations for each VPN. A good starting point is to look for services that have at least 1,000 servers and 30 or more country locations. The next thing to consider is VPN speed. This may be tricky to do since you aren’t likely to be able to test connection speeds without first paying to use the service. Reading reviews online will give you a general estimate. Look for reviews, like ours, that give you a relative average of connection speeds rather than direct Mbps speed comparisons for a more accurate picture. Finally, compare each VPN’s privacy protections. Does it have a no-logs policy? Has it undergone any independent audits of its servers? Where is the VPN company located? All of these are critical and you’ll want to go with a VPN that has clear and transparent data collection policies. What is a VPN? A VPN creates a secure tunnel between your PC and the internet. You connect to a VPN server, which can be located in the United States or a foreign country (like France or Japan). Your web traffic then goes through that server to make it appear as though you’re browsing from that server’s location and not from your actual location. When you’re using a VPN, it’s difficult for others to snoop on your web-browsing activity. Only you, the VPN service, and the website you’re visiting will know what you’re up to. A VPN can be a great solution to a variety of concerns, such as online privacy, anonymity, greater security on public Wi-Fi, and, of course, spoofing locations.

item.title: The used PC parts market is full of deals — and traps
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 2.76
Whenever the retail market loses its mind, we can always turn to the second-hand market for relief. It’s there with open arms to give us months-old and years-old hardware at great prices. Right? Well, not anymore. In 2026, the state of the used market is… less than ideal, to put it mildly. Prices are skyrocketing and AI images/videos make scams easier than ever to conduct. Buying used PC parts is a good way to save money this year, but it can be fraught with difficulty and danger. But it doesn’t have to be. If you’re careful, you can still find honest gamers and PC enthusiasts who are looking to offload old gear without gouging you. Here are some of my best tips and practices for safely buying used PC hardware and components in 2026. Know what you’re buying Technology can be frustratingly opaque and there are so many specs and numbers to know about: clock speeds, capacities, bandwidths, VRAM quantities, socket generations, chipsets. It’s confusing even for people who work with (and write about) this kind of hardware all the time. Before putting money down on anything, Google the name and model number. Ideally, get a SKU number to check the specific item you’re interested in. Is it current? Does that laptop have a decent graphics card or is it the base configuration? If it does have a GPU, is it the version with more or less VRAM? Is it overclockable? When you’ve decided to buy that specific component or device, make sure the seller confirms that it is what you think it is. Some devices and components can look nearly identical yet offer vastly different performance and features. If you buy the wrong one, you might find it doesn’t work with your existing hardware, so be doubly sure. Watch the phrasing There are enough second-hand parts on the market that you might as well skip over any that seem problematic. The language in the product listing can give you some red flags to watch out for. For example, skip anything that says “untested” unless you fancy repairing components yourself. Untested often means the seller can’t be bothered to confirm it’s working, but it could also mean they know there’s a problem and don’t want to be forthcoming about it. Roman Loyola/IDG “Open box” products can be incredible scores once in a blue moon, but often they’re returned products that original buyers didn’t like. Whatever it was, you probably won’t like it either. And even when the seller is honest, it’s better to skip any hardware that was used for cryptocurrency mining or hard overclocking, which will have put it through immense stress. Flashing the BIOS or upgrading the cooling can void warranties, so skip those as well. Trust your gut, not your excitement This is just good life advice in general, but when you’re buying hardware online, it’s important to trust your gut. If something about a listing feels off, if the deal seems too good to be true, if the seller is evasive when questioned… these are all signs to move on. Scammers often rely on FOMO (fear of missing out), limited-time offers, calls to urgency, and other high-pressure sales tactics to make you lower your guard and ignore your good sense. Don’t let your excitement at finding a cheap RAM kit blind you to the likelihood that you’re being taken for a ride by a cunning seller. Ask them the kinds of questions they should know the answers to if they were a genuine seller. How long have they had it? Why are they selling it? Did they use it for cryptocurrency mining or heavy overclocking? How’s the battery health? And when possible, ask for proof. See it to believe it A seller’s account status, reputation, and listing practices are all clues to how real the hardware is, but what you really want is to see the hardware with your own eyes. There are a few different ways you can do that: - See it in person: The ideal scenario is meeting the seller and getting to see the product with your own eyes. Even better, get them to run benchmarks to check for performance degradation. If you can’t see it working, at least get your hands on the hardware before handing over any money. - See it in a video: Video of the component in working condition is a great vote of confidence. However, it’s possible to fake these with AI and clever editing, so make sure the seller appears in the video and have them show an agreed-upon web page in it. The web page should have today’s date so you know it’s current. - See it in images: Images are increasingly easy to fake, but you can get around this by asking for multiple images from different angles, ideally containing some reference to the current date. Whatever proof you get, look for inconsistencies or weird artifacts or quirks that might suggest AI manipulation. If you get any sort of weird vibe about what you’re being shown, don’t buy it. Where you buy still matters Some online marketplaces have more hoops to jump through for sellers and offer more protection for buyers. eBay might be ancient but it’s quite buyer-friendly, with layers of security and clear reputational ratings for sellers. And if you get scammed, you’ll probably get your money back. T. Schneider/Shutterstock.com Meanwhile, Facebook Marketplace is easier for scammers, and traditional classified sites and apps are a complete Wild West. Focusing on platforms that have additional protections for buyers is a good way to avoid some of the most prolific scammers. This advice goes if you pick up the hardware in person, too. Have them meet you in a well-lit, public space, ideally with lots of other people around. Have a friend or family member go with you. Trust your gut. If the seller seems shifty, tries to argue over the previously agreed-upon price, or tries to move the deal somewhere else, just walk away. Buy with a credit card Bank transfers, cash, debit cards, cryptocurrency—they’re all convenient ways to buy, but those transactions can’t easily be reversed in case of a scam, at least not without jumping through serious hoops… and even then there’s no guarantee. If you use a credit card, you’ll have a much better chance of a successful chargeback if you’re scammed or you end up in a dispute with the seller. It gives you an extra layer of protection. Don’t pass it up. Record yourself opening it This is good advice for brand-new retail purchases of high-value items, too. There have been plenty of cases of graphics card sellers and manufacturers not honoring returns on bricked GPUs because they believe the buyer was at fault for the malfunctioning item. Make a recording of yourself opening the box, then clearly show off the item to the camera. Later, if you need to ask for a refund or return, you can prove what state it was in when it arrived in your hands. And if it was damaged in transit, or you ended up receiving the wrong item (or even a box full of rocks), you can prove it with your recording. Test it thoroughly ASAP If everything looks good with your new buy, confirm it with thorough testing. Install it, make sure it works with the latest drivers, run some benchmarks, play some games. If there’s any system instability, overly loud fan noise, or weaker-than-expected performance, consider asking for a refund. There’s no point in saving money on used if it leaves you with a lackluster experience. Do this right after getting the product, by the way. Don’t wait a week or more since you’ll need to move quick to secure your refund. Got storage? Wipe and reset If you’re buying a complete PC, laptop, or anything with storage on it, make sure to factory reset it—or better yet, securely erase the drive by zero-filling it. While it’s unlikely, if the previous owner had malware, the last thing you want to do is suffer that infection yourself. Clear the drive out and you can rest easy knowing there isn’t a nasty surprise waiting for you inside. Further reading: Want to build a gaming PC in 2026? Don’t

item.title: Best external SSDs for gaming: Portable performance drives for any budget
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 2.31
Maybe your gaming laptop doesn’t have enough storage. Or maybe you simply want to render your game library portable between systems. Rather than upgrade your internal storage — add a speedy external SSD. Not only will you have a lot more fast storage for your games, you can use it on any system you wish. But choosing the external SSD that’s right for your needs means sorting through a dizzying array of protocol and speed options. Making a poor choice might leave you feeling hard done by, either monetarily or performance-wise. Luckily for you, we’ve tested multitudes of the wee beasties and can offer recommendations guaranteed to improve your gaming experience. At a glance | | | | View Deal | | Show Pros & Cons Pros Cons Hide Pros & Cons | | | | | | | | View Deal | | Show Pros & Cons Pros Cons Hide Pros & Cons | | | | | | | | Check | | Show Pros & Cons Pros Cons Hide Pros & Cons | | | | | | | | Check on Amazon | | Show Pros & Cons Pros Cons Hide Pros & Cons | | | | | | | | Check on Amazon | | Show Pros & Cons Pros Cons Hide Pros & Cons | | | | | | | | View Deal | | Show Pros & Cons Pros Cons Hide Pros & Cons | | | | | | | | Check | | Show Pros & Cons Pros Cons Hide Pros & Cons | | | | PROMOTION Fortify your games and moments of glory Built for gamers and streamers, FireCuda X Vault offers massive capacity and convenient bus-powered single-cable connectivity. Vault’s striking design with customizable RGB illumination and Windows Dynamic Lighting keeps your vibe in check and syncs to your rig’s energy. Below we offer recommendations from 80Gbps down to 10Gbps; scroll below those to learn more about our evaluation process and what to look for when buying an external SSD for gaming. Note that SSD prices have risen considerably since our original reviews thanks to the AI / data center gold rush, and the recommendations below reflect that new reality. The older, linked reviews may not. We’ve also added a couple of enclosures to which you can add your own NVMe SSD, as the availability of many pre-populated SSDs is currently scattershot. Furthermore, an enclosure / DIY option is a way to save money in these time of inflated prices. Why you should trust PCWorld for external drive reviews and buying advice: PCWorld has been putting computer hardware through its paces for decades. Our external drive evaluations are thorough and rigorous, testing the limits of every product — from performance benchmarks to the practicalities of daily use. As consumers ourselves, we know what makes a product exceptional, or not. For more about our testing process, scroll to the bottom of this article. LaCie Rugged SSD Pro5 – Best 80Gbps external SSD for gaming Pros - Supports Thunderbolt 5 and USB4 - Impressive 80Gbps performance for creative pros - Rugged IP68-rated design - Longer than average five-year warranty Cons - Expensive - Requires 80Gbps Thunderbolt 5/USB4 port for full performance Who should buy the LaCie Rugged SSD Pro5? Anyone looking for top performance from an external SSD and who has the somewhat rare 80Gbps port to handle it, should shop the LaCie Rugged SSD Pro5. It’s not the fastest 80Gbps SSD I’ve tested, but it was close. Better, it’s available most of the time and its price hadn’t gone through the roof when I last checked. LaCie Rugged SSD Pro5: Further considerations The silicone-wrapped Rugged SSD Pro5 is beefed up to the tune of IP68 to ward off dust and liquids. It also features a full five-year warranty — two years longer than the norm for external SSDs. And while SSD components all come from the same sources, the LaCie (Seagate owned) name means something in the industry. Note that this drive was reviewed for sister publication Macworld, but by this same author and run through the same battery of tests I use for my PCWorld reviews. Adata SE920 – Best 40Gbps USB4 external SSD for gaming Pros - Fastest pre-populated 40Gbps SSD we’ve tested - Fan-cooled enclosure - Also fast on the Mac Cons - Pricier than USB 3.2×2 (20Gbps) Who should buy the Adata SE920? For those who still want stellar sustained throughput, but for less moolah than an 80Gbps SSD, the 40Gbps SE920 will get the job done and then some. Note, a 40Gbps USB4 external SSD isn’t for everyone. Your PC needs to support the USB4 or the Thunderbolt 3/4/5 spec in order to take advantage — and while cheaper than 80Gbps, it’s still not cheap. If you’re equipped to enter the club, the Adata SE920 EX will reward you with nearly 4GBps transfers, and at a slightly more affordable price than our previous pick for USB4, the OWC Express 1M2 — we’re talking $280 for a 1TB Adata SE920 versus $300 for the 1TB OWC drive. If you want a lot of capacity, the Adata SE920 EX ships with up to 4TB, though like all such-capacity SSDs, it’s currently in short supply and has become very expensive. Adata SE920: Further considerations In almost every benchmark, the SE920 EX beat the OWC Express 1M2, albeit by very small margins. It also comes with a nifty built-in fan, which is activated by sliding open the enclosure. This kept my drive noticeably free of heat during benchmark tests. The SE920 EX is also quite portable at around 4.1 inches long by 2.5-inches wide by 0.6-inches thick, and weighing 7 ounces — another advantage it has over the bulkier OWC Express 1M2 and others. Read our full SE920 External SSD review TerraMaster D1 SSD Plus – Best 40Gbps external SSD enclosure for gaming Pros - Second-fastest USB4 enclosure to date - Solid, thermally excellent design - Good-looking Cons - Bulky Who should buy the TerraMaster D1 SSD Plus? With the price of pre-populated 40Gbps SSDs rising due to the AI / data center memory arms race, buying a $110 (currently $70 on sale) 40Gbps enclosure such as the TerraMaster’s D1 SSD Plus, and then adding your own NVMe SSD is quite likely your most affordable external high-speed SSD option. TerraMaster D1 SSD Plus: Further considerations The TerraMaster D1 SSD Plus is bulky, and the style may not be everyone’s cup of tea, but the overtly-finned aluminum enclosure sheds the heat inherent with faster 40Gbps SSDs extremely well. When you populate the D1 SSD Plus, don’t overbuy with a PCIe 5.0 NVMe SSD, unless you want said SSD for use in something faster in the future. An affordable PCIe 4.0 model provides as much speed as the 40Gbps bus can handle. Note that TerraMaster also makes an 80Gbps enclosure, the D1 SSD Pro. Read our full TerraMaster D1 SSD Plus review PNY RP60 – Best 20Gbps external SSD for gaming Pros - Handsome, IP65-rated design (dust proof, water resistant) - Good 20Gbps performance - Nice flat Type-C USB ribbon cable Cons - USB port plug tether is difficult to reinsert. Who should buy the PNY RP60? If you tend to take your gaming drive everywhere, and/or you’re not the most careful person with hardware, a ruggedized external SSD is a practical way to ward off accidental damage. The PNY RP60 offers more than just a rugged IP65-rated exterior that protects against dust and water droplets. It’s handsome and lightweight to boot, as well as an admirable performer, even besting one of the fastest 20Gbps drives I’ve tested — the Crucial X10 Pro — in a couple of our tests. PNY60: Further considerations A 20Gbps SSD is the sweet spot in the price/performance ratio for external SSDs. The only issue is that the USB 3.2×2 drives function at only 10Gbps or slower unless attached to a dedicated 20Gbps port. That applies to most USB4 and Thunderbolt ports as well. The RP60 is competitively priced at $130 and $270 for 1TB and 2TB, respectively. Note that these prices are significantly higher than when I first reviewed the RP60 due to the global NAND shortage. Read our full PNY RP60 20Gbps USB SSD review Asus TUF Gaming A2 – Best 20Gbps external SSD enclosure for gaming Pros - Very fast performer - Military-esque styling - Super-rugged IP68 rated - Affordable Cons - You need to provide the NVMe SSD - Requires a USB 3.2×2 port for 20Gbps performance Who should buy the Asus TUF Gaming A2? Many gamers build their own gaming rig, so why shouldn’t they roll their own external SSD with an affordable enclosure such as the $60 TUF Gaming A2? With the price of pre-populated external SSDs currently reaching for the stratosphere, it’s an especially attractive proposition for 2026. The TUF Gaming A2 is styled to appeal to gamers, especially fans of first-person, military-style shooters. It’s built like a tank, carries an IP68 rating, and is easy to open for installing your NVMe SSD. Asus TUF Gaming A2: Further considerations The TUF Gaming A2 allows you to leverage older NVMe SSDs. Even a PCIe 3.0 SSD is fast enough for the 20Gbps bus, if you find a deal. With those going the way of the Dodo, however, an affordable PCIe 4.0 model will do just fine. Read our full Asus TUF Gaming A2 review Corsair EX300U – Best 10Gbps external SSD for gaming Pros - Fastest 10Gbps SSD we’ve tested - Small profile - Magnetic attachement to metal surfaces Cons - Almost as pricey as 20Gbps SSDs currently Who should buy the Corsair EX300U? For those looking for an SSD that won’t break the bank, but is still “fast enough,” the EX300U is an appealing little magnetic square of a drive. That said, $130 and $245 for 2TB is almost as pricey as the 20Gbps PNY RP60 listed above. Formerly, the drive was $100 and $180 respectively at those two capacities. Scant savings aside, the EX300U is the fastest 10Gbps SSD I’ve tested to date, besting the Teamgroup X2 Max listed below by a small margin. And unlike the latter, you can stick it to a metal object like a PC case via the circular magnet on the back. Note that aluminum is not particularly magnetic, so this doesn’t work with most Macs. Corsair EX300U: Further considerations The warranty on the EX300U is three years, which is the usual for external SSDs, but the 250TBW (terabytes that can be written) per terabyte of capacity is a little stingy. At least Corsair provides a TBW rating — most vendors don’t for external SSDs. Still, the odds of anyone exceeding that TBW limit is rather low. Most of the time games are reading data, not writing it. Read our full Corsair EX300U review Teamgroup X2 Max — Best 10Gbps thumb drive SSD for gaming Pros - Svelte thumb drive form factor - Fastest 10Gbps SSD we’ve tested - Dual Type-A/Type-C connectors Cons - End caps aren’t captive Who should buy the Teamgroup X2 Max? For those who want both fast 10Gbps performance, plus the super convenience of the thumb drive form factor and both Type-A and Type-C connectivity, it doesn’t get any better than the X2 Max. In fact, it’s the second-fastest 10Gbps SSD of any type that I’ve tested. Right behind the Corsair EX300U shown above. While it may not be sexy-looking in the gaming sense, pulling this out of your pocket when you sit down to game is the ultimate sandbag move. Let them laugh, they’ll never see you coming. Having both Type-A and Type-C connectors on board means never having to worry about what type of computer you’ll be using the X2 Max on, though having a thumb drive attached to your laptop can be a bit awkward if you’re lounging on the couch, etc. Teamgroup X2 Max: Further considerations While some gamers might scoff at “only” 10Gbps, that’s still plenty fast enough for loading games — and seek times are roughly the same as 80/40/20Gbps SSDs. Where you’ll lose out a bit compared to those faster models is in the time it takes saving games in the first place. Note that the 2TB X2 Max was on target for a 10Gbps SSD writing our 450GB file, never slowing appreciably or tragically as some do. The 1TB might not do quite as well. The current pricing of $210 for the 2TB model means you should weight this option against faster options for a little more cash, and/or creating your own external SSD using the enclosures listed above. A roll-your-own model, however, will never be this portable. Read our full Teamgroup X2 Max review Other notable external SSDs for gaming - Asus ROG Strix Aiolos: This 20Gbps NVMe enclosure offers RGB lighting and easy access to the internal M.2 slot. - Asus PA40SU: A good-performing single NVMe, USB4 drive enclosure that makes DIY storage easy, and looks nice in the process. - Glyph Atom EX20: Comes in a good-looking, protective silicon jacket while offering speedy 20Gbps performance. - Glyph Atom EX40: Sibling to the above, it has a similar sturdy exterior combined with USB4 compatibility and 40Gbps speed. - MSI DataMag 40Gbps: Not the fastest USB4 drive, but it’s got magnetic mounting. - Teamgroup PD20: A handsome, tough, and decently fast 20Gbps drive. - Crucial X10: A tiny, weatherproofed drive that can hold up to 8TB of storage. - Sandisk Extreme Pro SSD with USB4: A handsome design and relative affordability, but connection issues and comparably lackluster 40Gbps performance left us unamazed. - Addlink P21: Has a compelling combination of good performance and a striking design. - Corsair EX400U: On the slow side for a USB4 external SSD, but can sometimes be less expensive than the competition. - Seagate Game Drive SSD: Targeted at PS4/PS5 owners, this 10Gbps SSD is very fast for its class as well as attractively styled, complete with a Playstation logo, though it’s relatively pricey. - Lexar Armor 700: A 20Gbps drive that can withstand some abuse — perfect for the gamer on the go or the accident-prone. - Adata SD810: A solid 20Gbps drive, save for writing large amounts of data, where it slows down. How PCWorld tests external drives Drive tests currently utilize Windows 11 24H2, 64-bit running off of a PCIe 4.0 Samsung 990 Pro in an Asus Z890-Creator WiFi (PCIe 4.0/5.0) motherboard. The CPU is a Core Ultra i5 225 feeding/fed by two Crucial 64GB DDR5 5600MHz modules (128GB of memory total). Both 20Gbps USB and Thunderbolt 5 are integrated into the motherboard and Intel CPU/GPU graphics are used. Internal PCIe 5.0 SSDs involved in testing are mounted in an Asus Hyper M.2 x16 Gen5 adapter card sitting in a PCIe 5.0 slot. We run the CrystalDiskMark 8.04 (and 9), AS SSD 2, and ATTO 4 synthetic benchmarks (to keep article length down, we report only the first) to find the storage device’s potential performance. Then we run a series of 48GB transfer and 450GB write tests using Windows Explorer drag and drop to show what users will see during routine copy operations, as well as the far speedier FastCopy run as administrator to show what’s possible. A 25GBps two-SSD RAID 0 array on the aforementioned Asus Hyper M.2 x16 Gen5 is used as the second drive in our transfer tests. Formerly the 48GB tests were done with a RAM disk serving that purpose. Each test is performed on a NTFS-formatted and newly TRIM’d drive so the results are optimal. Note that in normal use, as a drive fills up, performance may decrease due to less NAND for secondary caching, as well as other factors. This issue has abated somewhat with the current crop of SSDs utilizing more mature controllers and far faster, late-generation NAND. Caveat: The performance numbers shown apply only to the drive we were shipped and to the capacity tested. SSD performance can and will vary by capacity due to more or fewer chips to shotgun reads/writes across and the amount of NAND available for secondary caching. Vendors also occasionally swap components. If you ever notice a large discrepancy between the performance you experience and that which we report, by all means, let us know. Note also that some of the SSDs in this roundup were tested using other equipment and methodologies, which you can read about in the standalone reviews. To learn more about our testing methodology see PCWorld’s article on how we test external SSDs. Who curated this article? Having started computing by flipping switches, Jon L. Jacobi has witnessed storage morph from punch cards and tape to solid state. He’s been using and testing HDDs, SATA SSDs, and NVMe SSDs for PCWorld for well over two decades. To paraphrase a well-known commercial, you might say he’s seen a thing or two. FAQ What is the best external SSD for gaming? At 80Gbps, the LaCie Rugged SSD Pro5 is our choice for absolute best performance. If speed is important, but you want to save a bit of coin, then the best 40Gbps external drive is the Adata SE920. For still-great 20Gbps performance, and a significant cost savings, consider the PNY RP60 and Crucial X10 Pro. Note that the Teamgroup X2 Max still offers good 10Gbps in a super-small form factor. What are the speeds of the various external interfaces and which one do you want? In descending order of performance the current external interfaces are: 80Gbps Thunderbolt 5/USB4, 40Gbps USB4/Thunderbolt 3 and 4, 20Gbps USB 3.2×2 (dedicated port required or it’s 10Gbps), 10GBps USB 3.2, then 5Gbps USB 3.x. For optimal gaming performance, we recommend 20Gbps or higher, though you can easily make do with 10Gbps. Note that currently, the real-world difference in performance between 40Gbps and 80Gbps is minimal. Also, the increase in power draw and heat produced as you climb the performance ladder from 10Gbps to 80Gbps is noticeable. Note that you’ll occasionally see mentions of 120Gbps Thunderbolt 5. 120Gbps is only available for downstream video, not storage or other applications. 80Gbps is the current top of the line. What causes an external SSD to fail? While mechanical hard drives are much more prone to failure than SSDs, it is still possible for an SSD to give up the ghost. Generally it’s the result of a controller failure, although that’s an increasingly rare occurrence; it’s also a relatively easy fix/reset for someone who knows the SSD’s internals such as a recovery service. SSDs will also eventually wear out, though this only precludes further writing to the unit. You can still read what’s on the drive, so it’s not the disaster a HDD failure can be. There were also instances in the ancient past of static electricity bricking Type-A connected SSDs upon insertion. Why does Windows say my external drive has less capacity than specified? This discrepancy is due to the difference between the binary and decimal number systems, their nomenclatures, and a Microsoft miscue. Your 2TB drive indeed has 2 trillion bytes of storage, and if you look at the byte count that Windows displays in a drive’s properties dialog, this should be what you see. This, in the International System of Units (SI/decimal), is 2 terabytes, or 2TB. Vendors use this system as consumers are far more familiar with base 10 than binary. However, Windows uses the newer International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC) binary multiples such as 2^10 (Kibibyte/KiB), 2^20 (Mebibyte/MiB), 2^30 (Gibibyte/Gib), etc. Binary multiples are larger than their decimal near-equivalents (one KiB is 1,024 bytes, one MiB is 1,048,576 bytes) so when Windows divides the total bytes by the IEC values you get something like 1.8TiB for a 2TB drive. Alas, Windows labels this as 1.8TB rather than 1.8TiB, misleading the user. Other reasons you might not see as much available storage in the properties tab are formatting or partitioning. The file system uses some storage for file location and size info, etc. Also, some drives come with a small partition containing software so the main partition will be smaller than the drive’s total capacity. How long will my external SSD last? SSDs don’t wear out or break mechanically like a hard drive, but their cells can only be written to so many times. SSDs generally have a TBW (terabytes that may be written) rating, but this is rarely provided by vendors for external SSDs. Hint: They may not use the same SSD inside throughout the product lifespan. Most internal M.2 NVMe TLC SSDs are rated for around 600TBW per terabyte, and QLC types for around 200TBW, though the type of NAND in use is also rarely provided by vendors. That’s a lot of data, and a lot of SSDs are rated well below what they might actually achieve. You can guesstimate by using a utility to see how much data you write to an SSD a day and then doing the math. External SSD warranties are generally between three and five years. As with all such things, it’s a financial risk formula calculated by the company. In this case based on expected NAND longevity and price. As is the TBW rating. Our best guess based on experience is perhaps a decade. However, certain models have had issues long before that — generally due to a flaw or failure in the bridge chip or controller. Exceeding a SSD’s rating does not affect the data stored on it. You can still read that data, you just can’t write more of it to the drive. Should you build your own external SSD with an enclosure and an NVMe SSD? Due to the current high price of NAND, buying an enclosure and populating it with an NVMe SSD is a more enticing proposition than ever before, and it has always appealed to PC builders. Note that even a PCIe 3.0 NVMe SSD will give you good performance in up to 20Gbps enclosures, though you’ll need at least a PCIe 4.0 model to get the most out of an 40/80Gbps enclosure.

item.title: My high-end PC was already fast. These 10 accessories transformed it
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 2.09
Whether you’re buying a high-end gaming desktop, a compact mini PC, or simply docking your laptop, those accessories you bought 5+ years ago might be showing their age—and even dragging you down. Believe me when I say that you’ll have a much better PC experience if you upgrade with a handful of accessories that most people overlook or underestimate. After I recently set up my own high-end gaming PC, I realized the blazing-fast GPU and CPU weren’t enough. For a truly elevated experience, I needed to ditch my outdated tech. Here are some next-level accessories and peripherals you should actually consider upgrading to, and why they’re worth every penny.
