That trend appears to have begun with Elon Musk, who invested earlier than most. By the time Elon Musk told a gathering of US governors that they needed to regulate AI right away, the SpaceX and Tesla CEO already had skin in the game. He’d already invested $38 million in OpenAI, as well as stakes in at least two other AI companies, and he’d publicly spoken about the dangers of AI for three years. In June 2014, he suggested AI research could produce a real-life Terminator, called AI “potentially more dangerous than nukes” that August, and suggested that working on AI was “summoning the demon” that October. In January 2015, he joined Stephen Hawking in signing an open letter asking for responsible AI research; Hawking had previously warned that the creation of AI might be the last thing humans ever do. “AI is a rare case where we need to be proactive about regulation instead of reactive. Because I think by the time we are reactive in AI regulation, it’s too late,” Musk told a gathering of US governors at the July 2017 National Governors Association summer meeting. In March 2018, he added: “AI is far more dangerous than nukes. So why do we have no regulatory oversight?” In the wake of Facebook’s Cambridge Analytica data scandal, the Meta founder suggested his company should be regulated — if it’s the “right” regulation. It was largely not about AI, but he did go there: Now that companies increasingly over the next five to 10 years, as AI tools get better and better, will be able to proactively determine what might be offensive content or violate some rules, what therefore is the responsibility and legal responsibility of companies to do that? Earlier in 2018, Microsoft began taking fire for working with ICE on facial recognition technologies, at a time many tech CEOs had condemned Donald Trump’s policy of separating children from parents who are arrested at the US border. While this form of AI isn’t quite the same as self-replicating intelligence, Microsoft president Brad Smith opened the door to voluntary regulation in a speech at the Brookings Institution, saying, “We believe it’s important for governments in 2019 to start adopting laws to regulate this technology. … We believe that the only way to protect against this race to the bottom is to build a floor of responsibility that supports healthy market competition. And a solid floor requires that we ensure that this technology, and the organizations that develop and use it, are governed by the rule of law.” “[T]here is no question in my mind that artificial intelligence needs to be regulated. It is too important not to,” wrote Pichai in an editorial for the Financial Times. “The only question is how to approach it.” “Companies such as ours cannot just build promising new technology and let market forces decide how it will be used,” he added. Like with Microsoft a year earlier, these comments emerged around fears about AI facial recognition specifically. In 2023, as generative AI fervor began to reshape the entire tech industry, scientists began suggesting that companies should slow down their research — or else. “If such a pause cannot be enacted quickly, governments should step in and institute a moratorium,” the letter, published by the nonprofit Future of Life Institute and signed by Musk, among others, reads. Two weeks later, Musk announced he’d created his own new AI company. Two years later, he would use DOGE to dismantle chunks of the federal workforce instead of helping to regulate anything. Brought before the US Senate for a series of AI hearings, Altman agreed that Congress should create a new agency to regulate artificial intelligence. “We believe that the benefits of the tools we have deployed so far vastly outweigh the risks,” he argued. “However, we think that regulatory intervention by governments will be critical to mitigate the risks of increasingly powerful models.” In another hearing on May 25th, Anthropic’s CEO warned US senators that AI could help create bioweapons. When OpenAI’s CEO was before Congress, we noted that the tone was friendly and they seemed to be trying to shape legislation together; here is an example of Microsoft trying to shape future regulation as well. One regulatory example: “New laws would require operators of these systems to build safety brakes into high-risk AI systems by design. The government would then ensure that operators test high-risk systems regularly to make certain that the system safety measures are effective.” “Mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority alongside other societal-scale risks such as pandemics and nuclear war.” While the 22-word statement doesn’t explicitly ask the government to step in, it’s hard to think world leaders wouldn’t raise their eyebrows even higher than before. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and then-Google DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis were among the cosigners. In a private Senate meeting, closed to the public and media, tech CEOs reportedly agreed that the AI industry needed regulation. One set of remarks was not so private: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said that “Congress should engage with AI to support innovation and safeguards.” “We think policymakers, academics, civil society, and industry should all work together to minimize the potential risks of this new technology, but also to maximize the potential benefits.” Between July 2023 and May 2024, tech companies signed a flurry of nonbinding agreements with governments that would supposedly keep them in check: - July 2023: Meta, Google, and OpenAI promise the White House they’ll develop AI responsibly - September 2023: More companies commit to the White House AI safety accord - November 2023: At UK’s AI Summit developers and govts agree on testing to help manage risks - May 2024: AI Seoul Summit: World leaders agree to launch network of safety institutes Also in September 2023: A book from Inflection AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman — who is now Microsoft’s AI chief — argued that governments should regulate. “This is a tough call and will make some people upset, but, all things considered, I think California should probably pass the SB 1047 AI safety bill,” Musk posted in August. Anthropic originally came out against it in July, as did OpenAI in August, but Anthropic changed its tune in September. California Gov. Gavin Newsom vetoed SB 1047, though, stating that “I do not believe this is the best approach to protecting the public from real threats posed by the technology.” “Governments should urgently take action on AI policy in the next eighteen months. The window for proactive risk prevention is closing fast,” Anthropic wrote in an open letter (bolding theirs). “It is critical over the next year that policymakers, the AI industry, safety advocates, civil society, and lawmakers work together to develop an effective regulatory framework,” the company added. The document begins by suggesting the UK stunted the development of its own automobile industry with regulation, while proposing “democratic AI” instead: “Rules and regulations for the development and use of AI should be based on the democratic values the country has always stood for.” In a guest essay for The New York Times, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei wrote: “Federal law does not compel us or any other A.I. company to be transparent about our models’ capabilities or to take any meaningful steps toward risk reduction. Some companies can simply choose not to.” The essay is against the Trump administration’s proposed 10-year moratorium on US states regulating AI. He wasn’t arguing for a slowdown, though, but rather a “national transparency standard” that “would help not only the public but also Congress understand how the technology is developing.” As California tried to regulate its AI giants again, Anthropic threw its support in early, and this one actually became law. It’s a transparency standard, like the one Anthropic was asking for, with safety reporting requirements and whistleblower protection. OpenAI lobbied against it. This summer, shit hit the fan. It became public that rogue AI agents can — and did — attack other companies. OpenAI said it hit the brakes in August, and on September 8th, a senior Anthropic safety researcher resigned in protest, declaring there’s a 10 percent chance AI could kill all humans by the end of the decade. Another Anthropic safety researcher agreed. Now, suddenly, the AI industry has seemingly agreed to slow down the pace of development. More: Is this a new call for regulation? From Anthropic’s CEO, it seems to be. In his essay “We Must Pace the Frontier,” Amodei writes that “The most effective method of pacing is via regulation that targets all US frontier AI companies, as that covers even those who are unwilling to cooperate voluntarily,” and he suggests governments might embed people inside AI companies to help prevent incidents. It’s not clear every AI company wants to go that far. “Where we will need the help of our government is for international coordination. But first we should do what we can ourselves,” OpenAI CEO Sam Altman writes. But Altman does say that he’ll commit to “independent evaluators with employee-like access” as well. Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg also doesn’t seem to be aligned. On September 15th, he posted that each company has its own individual responsibility to move at the right pace and that Meta is already doing so. He also prominently linked back to his manifesto from August, which contains this line: “Any policy that slows American model releases -- even by a month -- could add significant risk to American leadership while letting foreign models race ahead.” Regardless of what tech leaders are saying, regulation seems highly unlikely to come under the Trump administration, which has signaled it wants the industry barreling full speed ahead. Even if these companies don’t actually want the regulation they seem to be asking for, this is one of the loudest alarm bells they’ve sounded so far — and the world is watching.

item.title: Apple Has New Parental Controls for Your Kid’s iPhone. Here Are the 6 Settings to Know About.
item.description:
Source: Wirecutter Score: 5.61
Apple’s parental controls let you manage everything from screen time to what apps wind up on your kid’s iPhone. But the latest version of Apple’s iPhone software, iOS 27, refines those controls even further, making setup and management even easier while expanding what’s under your control. The same updated parental controls are built into iOS 27, iPadOS 27, and macOS 27, and you’ll need to upgrade to the latest versions across all your devices in your family to take full advantage of the new tools. I’ve been using parental controls for a few years to make sure my teenage daughter is accessing age-appropriate apps and not staring too long at a screen. I spent the summer testing the beta version of Apple’s updated iOS, and I have tips for parents looking to get the most out of it. How to set up a Child Account If you’re getting a new iPhone for your child, it’s simple to create a Child Account during setup — just follow the steps when prompted. But you can also create a Child Account from within the Settings app on your own iPhone. Tap Family on the main Settings screen, and on the subsequent screen, tap the Add Member button in the upper-right corner of the phone’s display. From there, it’s a matter of tapping Create Child Account and following the on-screen directions, which include setting up your child with email and Apple accounts if they don’t already have either. Apple’s streamlined setup tool now lets you decide which apps come installed on a child’s device. That includes essential apps such as Phone, Find My, Mail, and various study tools, or any of Apple’s built-in apps. You can also pick specific apps that you want included on the phone, guided by Apple-provided age ranges for what’s appropriate for teens versus younger kids. Over time you’ll be able to add more approved apps, as you deem appropriate. New parental-control features to know about If you’ve set up a Child Account before, many of the basics in Apple’s revamped software will seem familiar. But they offer some notable new features, plus changes that make existing controls easier to access. And if you’re setting up a kid’s iPhone for the first time, you’ll appreciate the guided setup process, which walks you through content and usage restrictions while leaving the final decisions up to you. Here’s what’s new: You can approve which websites kids can visit. The parental controls already included Ask to Buy, which sends parents an alert requesting permission before a child downloads a new app to their phone. The new Ask to Browse feature sends the same kind of text whenever your kid tries to visit a new website in Safari: You get a link so that you can give the site the once-over before deciding whether to approve the request. This feature is on by default for kids under 13, but you can also enable it in the accounts for any teenagers you’re managing by tapping their name in the Family section of the Settings app, selecting Apps & Websites followed by Restrictions, and then changing the Filtering settings under Websites. (This is also where you can adjust restrictions on app downloads.) You can better manage who kids talk to via apps such as Messages and FaceTime. Since last year, parents have had the ability to grant permission when kids want to add new contacts. The iOS 27, iPadOS 27, and macOS 27 updates add that capability to the Child Account setup process so that you can take control from the outset. For new contacts, your child asks for permission, in a process similar to that of Ask to Buy, and you can approve requests from your Apple device with a tap. Apple now blurs images and videos containing violence or gore. Apple already offered a Communication Safety feature that uses AI to recognize and blur nudity in video or photos received through text messages or FaceTime calls. The software update expands that capability to images with gore and violence, blocking kids from sending or receiving such messages. Communication Safety is turned on by default. You can set more specific Screen Time limits. Previously known as App Limits, the new Time Allowances help you better manage the kinds of apps your kids are spending their time using. Specifically, you’re prompted to set time limits in three app categories: Games, Entertainment, and Social Media. Though Apple lets you pick limits and even adjust categories to fit your preferences (such as if you wanted games to have more time, but social media to have less), it doesn’t leave you totally on your own. Apple now gives you recommended time allowances to start with that are based on your kid’s age and recommendations from experts. The Screen Time section is easier to use. It now emphasizes at-a-glance info on the apps your child is using the most, thanks to a redesigned screen that you see when you tap your child’s name in the Family section of Settings. One of the biggest changes introduced in the redesign comes in the form of three buttons near the top of the screen that provide more immediate control. The buttons allow you to pause device usage, permit unlimited use, or change the schedule of limits and allowances without having to dive deeper into the Time Allowances settings to make more permanent adjustments. I’ve been fortunate in that my daughter has accepted that my wife and I have the final say in how she uses her phone, and that the limits we’ve set are fairly reasonable. The parental-control changes that Apple just rolled out could help parents get more involved in setting limits early on. This article was edited by Signe Brewster and Caitlin McGarry. Meet your guide Philip Michaels Philip Michaels has been covering consumer tech since 1999, with a focus on smartphones and wireless carriers for the past decade-plus. In addition to Wirecutter, his work has appeared at Macworld, TechHive, Tom’s Guide, Six Colors, and Awful Announcing, among other publications. You can listen to him on podcasts hosted by The Incomparable Network. He publishes a weekly newsletter, is an avid cook and traveler, and has dabbled in acting and standup comedy. He lives in Alameda, California.

item.title: Need to Upgrade Your iPhone? Get Last Year's Model.
item.description:
Source: Wirecutter Score: 2.67
If you have an iPhone that you’re happy with, keep it. We don’t think you should upgrade just because Apple has released new phones. But if your current phone is running too slowly or is damaged, or if you’re simply ready for an upgrade and you want a new phone now, we still recommend last year’s Apple iPhone 17. It offers an almost Pro-like iPhone experience, with a bigger display and a higher refresh rate, excellent cameras, lengthy battery life, and a powerful processor. And as every phone in Apple’s lineup has gotten more expensive, the iPhone 17 remains a great phone for much less than a Pro model. Everything we recommend Top pick The iPhone 17 comes with features once reserved for Apple’s Pro models, including a bigger and brighter display with a 120 Hz refresh rate, a higher-resolution front-facing camera that takes better selfies, and long-lasting battery life. The Apple iPhone 17 is now a year old, but it’s still the best iPhone for most people. It has a big, bright 6.3-inch screen that supports Apple’s ProMotion display technology (up to 120 Hz) and an always-on display mode — two features previously exclusive to the iPhone Pro models. It also has a great camera system, with an 18-megapixel selfie camera and a 48-megapixel rear ultrawide camera. If you don’t need the intricate manual camera controls or the heavy-duty processor of the iPhone 18 Pro, this is the best iPhone for you. Upgrade pick Compared with its predecessor, the iPhone 18 Pro has a more powerful chip, longer battery life, and a new 48-megapixel camera lens with a variable aperture and some neat photography features. It’s also better at staying cool during intensive tasks. The Apple iPhone 18 Pro has the same design as last year’s iPhone 17 Pro, but with a few noteworthy upgrades. In addition to the powerful A20 Pro chip, it has an upgraded vapor-cooling system that better dissipates heat, a smaller Dynamic Island that supports up to three live activities, and slightly longer battery life. The standout feature, however, is the new variable aperture on the main camera lens, which allows you to capture better photos in both broad daylight and low light. Budget pick Apple’s most affordable iPhone isn’t the cheapest the company has ever made, but it offers long-lasting battery life and excellent performance. For better cameras, buy an iPhone 17. Although we wish the Apple iPhone 17e were cheaper, it offers an excellent value, providing a durable, 6.1-inch screen, solid performance, and lengthy battery life. It also supports MagSafe for easy wireless charging and attaching accessories. But its single rear camera lens could be better. When should you upgrade if you have an older iPhone? Our general philosophy about upgrading (as described by Wirecutter’s founder) is that if you’re happy with what you have, you don’t need the latest and greatest. Last year’s iPhone or the one before that (or even the one before that) should continue to serve you well. New phones tend to offer incremental upgrades — they’re not revolutionary products that change the experience. Apple still issues security updates to older devices, and iOS 27 still supports every iPhone from 2019 on, so even seven-year-old phones are getting new features. If you have an older phone that’s beginning to feel slower, you may want to check the battery’s health before you decide to replace it completely. Power-conservation features in modern iPhones can slow down phones whose batteries’ capacity is depleted. If the iOS Battery Health screen shows the status “Performance management applied” or “Battery health degraded,” having Apple replace the battery (which can cost up to $129 out of warranty) is a lot cheaper than buying a new phone. The best all-around package: iPhone 17 Top pick The iPhone 17 comes with features once reserved for Apple’s Pro models, including a bigger and brighter display with a 120 Hz refresh rate, a higher-resolution front-facing camera that takes better selfies, and long-lasting battery life. Apple’s affordable flagship, the iPhone 17, offers the best value in the iPhone lineup. Pro-level features, such as a 6.3-inch screen that supports an adaptive 120 Hz refresh rate for smoother scrolling, as well as an always-on display for viewing notifications and widgets at a glance, no longer require you to pay a premium price. The dual-lens camera setup on the back has a 48-megapixel ultrawide sensor for higher-quality photos, while the front camera has been upgraded to 18 megapixels with support for Center Stage and Dual Capture video mode (more on those later). The iPhone 17 also runs on Apple’s A19 chip, which delivers smooth performance and excellent battery life. If you have an older iPhone, you’re likely to appreciate the new features. It has a big, bright display with a high refresh rate. The iPhone 17 has a 6.3-inch OLED display, the same size as that of the iPhone 18 Pro. It’s an increase from the iPhone 16’s 6.1-inch screen; though that isn’t a major difference, we’ve always thought the standard iPhone model was a little too cramped in this era of giant phones. With a peak outdoor brightness of 3,000 nits, the iPhone 17’s screen is also brighter, up from 2,000 nits on its predecessor. This makes it easier to see even in direct sunlight. Apple’s base-model iPhone 17 also offers a lot of the same features that Apple previously reserved for the Pro iPhones. With ProMotion, the display’s maximum refresh rate has increased from 60 Hz to 120 Hz for smoother scrolling and graphics. It’s adaptive, which means it’ll kick in when you’re using the phone and then dip to 1 Hz when the phone is idle. The iPhone 17 also has an always-on display, so you can easily glance at the time, notifications, or widgets on your lock screen without having to tap to wake the phone each time. It has an upgraded front-facing camera with some useful selfie features. Apple has upgraded the front camera on the iPhone 17 from a 12-megapixel sensor to an 18-megapixel one, which results in higher-resolution images. In our tests, compared with images from previous models, selfies came out even more crisp — we could make out every detail (breakouts included) even in low-light images. The sensor is also now square and has a wider field of view. With the Center Stage feature, the front-facing camera’s field of view expands automatically to fit more people in the frame while you’re holding the phone vertically. This means you don’t have to manually rotate your phone for wider group shots using the front-facing camera. The feature works as advertised, too: I used it during a birthday party, where many selfies were taken, and whenever someone else stepped into the shot, it would quickly zoom out to fit them in. However, the muscle memory that people have built after years of rotating their phones to snap selfies with friends may take some time to fade. Center Stage also kicks in on video calls to keep you in frame while you’re moving around. I found this feature helpful while I was FaceTiming a friend from my desk, as I was able to move between using the iPhone and typing on my MacBook without having to manually adjust the phone each time. The iPhone 17 also introduces the Dual Capture video mode, which allows you to use the front and rear cameras simultaneously to capture more footage at once. Using Dual Capture on the iPhone 17 was both fun and simple in our tests. Once you enable the feature, the front camera’s video is in picture-in-picture mode, and the center of the screen shows what the rear camera records. It has an excellent ultrawide camera. The iPhone 17 has Apple’s Dual Fusion cameras. The name refers to the 48-megapixel main camera’s ability to double as a 12-megapixel telephoto camera, plus the 48-megapixel ultrawide camera’s ability to double as a 12-megapixel macro lens. The main sensor continues to deliver vibrant, sharp photos with strong dynamic range and little to no visible noise. But the iPhone 16 also has a 48-megapixel main sensor — the upgrade here is to the ultrawide lens. We compared the two and found a few differences: In our tests, the iPhone 17 consistently delivered colors that were more subdued and natural, with lower contrast, delivering more evenly lit, true-to-life images. It also proved to have better distortion control. The iPhone 16’s images, on the other hand, looked more saturated and appeared slightly more warped. Like last year’s version, the iPhone 17 uses a combination of software and hardware to shoot 2x optical-quality zoom, but it still delivered strong results that looked almost identical to what we got from the iPhone 17 Pro. It also has support for up to 10x digital zoom, but in this regard its images weren’t as sharp or clean as those from the Pro model; although the photos were somewhat usable, they exhibited a noticeable loss of details and blurriness. You also have the option to take full-resolution 24-megapixel images (the default) or to switch to 12 megapixels; the camera system switches to the latter when you’re taking photos with night mode, macro flash, or Portrait Lighting. The 24-megapixel option is better for capturing the most detail, while the 12-megapixel mode is ideal for capturing low-light images. Note, however, that images captured with the 24-megapixel option will occupy more space, so if you plan on using the iPhone 17 to take a lot of images, we recommend upgrading to the higher storage configuration. It’s plenty fast and powerful enough for most tasks. The iPhone 17 uses Apple’s A19 chip, which includes a 16-core neural engine, a six-core CPU, and a five-core GPU. And the iPhone 17’s performance is great, even a year later. Though we didn’t notice a huge difference coming from the iPhone 16, opening apps and switching between them did feel snappier. The higher refresh rate also allowed for a much smoother experience while we scrolled through social media and played a few rounds of Alto’s Odyssey. The iPhone 17 is more durable than past iPhone models. Apple introduced Ceramic Shield 2 with the iPhone 17 lineup. It’s the latest version of Apple’s proprietary glass, which the company claims has three times better scratch resistance than the previous version. Unlike the iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, and iPhone Air, the iPhone 17 doesn’t have the Ceramic Shield coating on the back, but it bears the same IP68 dust- and water-resistance rating as Apple’s more expensive phones. It has lengthy battery life compared with older iPhones. Apple claims that the iPhone 17 offers eight more hours of video playback in comparison with the iPhone 16, for a total of up to 30 hours. In our testing, the iPhone 17 lasted for longer than a day and a half of heavy usage on one charge. The extra battery life can be attributed to the addition of both ProMotion, which has an adaptive refresh rate that swaps between 120 Hz and 1 Hz, and the A19 chip, which is designed to be more power-efficient. And Apple claims that the iPhone 17 can charge up to 50% in 20 minutes on its 40W Dynamic Power Adapter with 60W Max. Using the Dynamic Power Adapter, we charged the iPhone 17 from 9% to 53% in about 25 minutes. The base model has more storage. It comes with 256 GB of storage, or 512 GB for a premium; both versions now cost an extra $100. Flaws but not dealbreakers It’s more expensive than it was at launch. When the iPhone 17 was released last year, it started at $800. But Apple just raised the starting price by $100, so the iPhone 17 now starts at $900 for the 256 GB model and $1,100 for the 512 GB version. You don’t get any additional features for that higher price, which is a result of the ongoing consumer electronics RAM shortage. It lacks a triple-camera system. Though Apple typically reserves triple cameras for the iPhone Pro models, it’s difficult not to criticize the company for including only two cameras on the iPhone 17, especially considering that the base models of both the Google Pixel 11 and the Samsung Galaxy S26 come with a main sensor, an ultrawide sensor, and a dedicated telephoto sensor. At this point, Apple seems to be falling behind the standards set by its Android-flagship competition. Center Stage selfies aren’t the perfect solution. Although it’s a nice feature to have on hand, taking selfies with Center Stage looks and feels awkward. Since it zooms out to capture everyone in the frame, it produces an ultrawide selfie that made our arms and torsos look really long. We preferred sticking to the standard method of rotating our phone and snapping a more cropped-in shot. The best cameras: iPhone 18 Pro Upgrade pick Compared with its predecessor, the iPhone 18 Pro has a more powerful chip, longer battery life, and a new 48-megapixel camera lens with a variable aperture and some neat photography features. It’s also better at staying cool during intensive tasks. The iPhone 18 Pro looks almost identical to the iPhone 17 Pro, with an aluminum chassis and a horizontal rear camera bump (also known as a “plateau”), but it’s available in more elegant colors. Apple also added other notable improvements, including an upgraded thermal system that better disperses heat and a faster, power-efficient chip, the A20 Pro, for heavy-duty gaming and video editing. As for the camera system, while the ultrawide-angle and telephoto lenses remain the same as those in its predecessor, the iPhone 18 Pro’s main camera lens now has a variable aperture and a few exclusive manual features that give you more control over your photos. If you want an iPhone that offers the most powerful processor, the highest-quality photos, and the longest battery life of all our picks, iPhone 18 Pro is worth the upgrade. But with such precise camera capabilities and a higher price compared with previous Pro models, it’s best suited for aspiring or professional photographers. The cameras are great — if you know how to use them. Like previous Pro iPhones, the iPhone 18 Pro has a triple-camera system that includes a 48-megapixel main camera, a 48-megapixel ultrawide camera, and a 48-megapixel telephoto lens (with 4x optical zoom and 8x optical-like zoom). But the iPhone 18 Pro’s main sensor is new, equipped with a variable aperture. Bear with me as I get technical here: The main lens has a built-in rotor mechanism that opens and closes depending on the f-stop. Whereas the iPhone 17 Pro’s main camera had a fixed, f/1.78 aperture, the new camera switches between f/1.48, f/1.8, f/2.8, and f/4. A wider aperture lets in more light, which is ideal for low-light environments, while a smaller aperture works better in daylight; a narrower aperture also allows for a longer depth of field. Apple also added manual control over shutter speed and white balance, plus a histogram for tracking whether your shot is properly exposed, all of which work well. If these terms mean nothing to you, the iPhone 18 Pro might be overkill. Though you can manually choose the aperture, the camera system also offers auto mode, which switches to the correct aperture based on the amount of light, the subjects in the scene, and motion. But I noticed that it didn’t always default to the best f-stop in certain lighting. When I tested the iPhone 18 Pro against the iPhone 17 Pro, I noticed that the new camera system applied a bit more skin smoothing, so subjects looked less sharp than in photos I took with its predecessor. This was intentional on Apple’s part, as it gives you more creative control and room to manually add grain or texture rather than applying those effects for you. But even on auto mode, the iPhone 18 Pro (like its predecessors) still delivers great shots. Whether in broad daylight or low light, my test images were vibrant and crisp, with rich contrast and sharp detail. But you’re likely to appreciate the manual camera features more if you’re a photographer with the background and knowledge to use them fully and get the most out of the device. If you don’t need any of these granular capabilities, I suggest opting for the iPhone 17. It has a powerful new chip and a better cooling system. The A20 Pro packs plenty of power, and the improved vapor-chamber system dissipates heat better. Like last year’s chipset, the A20 Pro offers a six-core CPU, but it also has a seven-core GPU (one extra core over that of last year’s A19 Pro) and an additional Neural Engine for powering AI-based tasks. It also now includes Apple’s new custom C2 chip to improve cellular quality. Apple claims that the A20 Pro delivers up to 20% faster CPU performance and up to 40% faster GPU performance than the A19 Pro. Though I didn’t notice a major change in performance, the iPhone 18 Pro felt slightly smoother and snappier than last year’s Pro model. It handled hours of social media scrolling, FaceTime calls, Siri AI interactions, and photo editing with ease. Like its predecessor, the iPhone 18 Pro remains the iPhone to get if you plan to use your phone for power-intensive, graphics-heavy tasks. It offers excellent battery life and fast wired charging. Apple claims that the iPhone 18 Pro gets up to 36 hours of video playback. In my testing, it lasted 30 hours on a single charge, which is comparable to what I experienced with the iPhone 17 Pro. You’re likely to notice a more significant improvement in battery life if you’re coming from an older model, such as an iPhone 13 Pro or iPhone 14 Pro. The iPhone 18 Pro supports slightly faster wired charging speeds than its predecessor. Using a 67 W charging brick, I charged the iPhone 18 Pro from 0% to 50% in about 16 minutes. It has a smaller Dynamic Island that supports up to three Live Activities. Like its predecessors, the iPhone 18 Pro has the same 6.3-inch OLED screen with support for ProMotion (Apple’s adaptive 120 Hz refresh rate) and an always-on display. The only noteworthy difference is the new, smaller Dynamic Island (the pill-shaped cutout at the top of the phone for quick access to app controls). By moving the Face ID camera directly behind the display, Apple shrank it by about 25%. The difference isn’t drastic — I noticed how much smaller it looked only when I placed this model next to the iPhone 17 Pro. But the change does make space for an additional Live Activity, and now, instead of two apps, you can see up to three there. For example, while out for a walk, I had the Fitness app, Google Maps, and Spotify running at the same time, which allowed me to access them all without having to manually find each app. It’s a minor addition, but a useful one, especially if you often track information across multiple apps at once (such as ride-share, sports scores, and delivery services). The iPhone 18 Pro comes with more storage. Last year, Apple increased the iPhone 17 Pro's base storage from 128 GB to 256 GB, but that model went up only to 1 TB. Now, with the iPhone 18 Pro, you also have the option to increase storage up to 2 TB, which matches the capacity of the Pro Max models. It’s not cheap, though: Upgrading to that configuration costs a whopping $2,400, which is $400 more than the iPhone 17 Pro Max with 2 TB. It’s available in beautiful color options with matching glass backs. The iPhone 18 Pro comes in three new colors: black, light blue, and burgundy, plus silver (also available last year on the iPhone 17 Pro). These color options are much more appealing than those of the iPhone 17 Pro lineup, which, aside from silver, was available only in blue or orange. The new light blue, called Glacier, is a great choice if you want a muted tone but still want a slight pop of color; the burgundy is a stunning deep red. This time, however, the new models also have color-matched glass backs. Last year’s iPhone Pro had a polarizing two-tone design — the worst of all was silver, which had a white square on the back. It’s nice to see that Apple brought back the sleek, monochromatic look of previous iPhone Pro models. Flaws but not dealbreakers The iPhone 18 Pro is more expensive than last year’s version. The iPhone 18 Pro now starts at $1,200 for the base 256 GB model, which is $100 more than last year’s iPhone 17 Pro. While this increase was expected, since Apple raised the price of its iPads and Macs in June because of ongoing RAM shortages, it’s still not ideal. It’s slightly heavier than the iPhone 17 Pro. Last year’s iPhone Pro design had a larger camera module, a bigger battery, and a thicker build than its predecessors, all of which added weight. The iPhone 18 Pro is even heavier — though it isn’t a drastic difference, it’s noticeable enough when you put a case on the phone. The exclusive Pro camera features can be tough to find. The iPhone 18 Pro’s new camera features — the variable aperture, histogram, shutter speed, and white balance — are buried within the Camera app’s menu, so you have to manually search through there to access them. In iOS 27, you can now edit the Camera Controls menu at the top of the viewfinder, so I added shortcuts to the lens aperture and shutter speed. But it would have been more useful if Apple had included those at the top by default. A more affordable option: iPhone 17e Budget pick Apple’s most affordable iPhone isn’t the cheapest the company has ever made, but it offers long-lasting battery life and excellent performance. For better cameras, buy an iPhone 17. At $700, the Apple iPhone 17e isn’t exactly cheap, but it is Apple’s most affordable iPhone, and it does everything you might need an iPhone to do. The iPhone 17e is an iterative update of the now-discontinued iPhone 16e, which itself replaced the popular iPhone SE (the last iPhone to have a home button). The 17e is similar to the 16e in most respects, though it now comes in pink (in addition to black and white) and offers MagSafe compatibility for magnetic wireless charging and attaching accessories such as wallets and PopSockets. It also runs on the same chip as the pricier iPhone 17. If you’re okay with a single rear camera that lacks the telephoto capabilities of more expensive iPhones’ cameras, it’s a perfectly fine phone. We just wish it were cheaper. The iPhone 17e delivers excellent battery life. While the most noticeable features of the 17e are its notched cutout for Face ID and its single camera lens, the real standout is its lengthy battery life. Its battery, combined with the power efficiency enabled by the company’s custom C1X modem (for connecting to the internet) and A19 chip, allowed the 17e to last 36 hours in our testing, even with extremely heavy usage. I charged it up to 100% on a Wednesday evening and then used it to scroll Instagram and get lost in looking at houses I can’t afford on Zillow until it was time to wind down for bed. The next day I toted the 17e along on a morning public-transit commute to a coffee meeting and then to the office, all the while responding to messages, navigating with Google Maps, and even using the phone as a mobile hotspot for another device. The phone finally died after a quick phone call midday on Friday. All of that is to say: If you’re upgrading from an older iPhone that you need to plug in well before bed, the 17e is a dramatic improvement. (The iPhone 17 lasts a bit longer than the 17e and charges up more quickly, but it also costs $200 more.) It supports MagSafe. The iPhone 16e lacked MagSafe compatibility, which seemed like a weird omission. Apple has rectified that with the 17e, which can now charge wirelessly on a magnetic Qi2 charging puck. You can also snap MagSafe accessories to the back, such as a wallet or a PopSocket (though Apple’s FineWoven MagSafe wallet tends to slide off the back of the company’s clear MagSafe case, so be careful). It can charge up quickly and wirelessly. Apple is all in with USB-C, and the iPhone 17e is equipped accordingly. Like its more expensive siblings, the 17e also supports fast wired charging, and in our testing it charged from completely dead to 46% in 30 minutes. It can also charge wirelessly with a MagSafe Qi2 charging puck at up to 15 W. (The 16e didn’t support MagSafe and could charge wirelessly only up to 7.5 W, so wireless charging didn’t make much sense for that phone.) The display is big, bright, and more durable. The 17e is almost all screen, with a 6.1-inch display and a minimal bezel with a notch cutout for the Face ID camera. The more expensive iPhone 17 gets much brighter than the 17e — to a max of 3,000 nits versus 1,200 nits on the 17e — but unless you often use your phone outside in direct sunlight, the 17e’s lower max brightness shouldn’t be a dealbreaker. The biggest upgrade to the 17e’s screen is the addition of Ceramic Shield 2, a coating that improves scratch resistance. If you’ve ever put your phone in your pocket next to a pair of keys and reckoned with the ensuing screen damage, you’ll appreciate the upgrade. The camera is perfectly fine, and it offers an improved portrait mode. With a lone 48-megapixel rear camera lens, the iPhone 17e isn’t for aspiring (let alone professional) photographers. But if you just need a camera that lets you quickly snap photos of your loved ones and pets, the 17e gets the job done. And with an improved portrait mode that blurs backgrounds more naturally and lets you readjust focus and depth of field after shooting, it’s an upgrade — albeit a minor one — over the 16e’s camera. If you want multiple lenses or more advanced image processing, turn to the iPhone 17. It looks more expensive than it is. The iPhone 17e, like the iPhone 17, has an aluminum frame with a matte-glass back, and it looks more like a modern iPhone than the SE did. It comes in white, black, or a pale pink, but you can add a case for a pop of color. It has the same chip as the more expensive iPhone 17. The 17e runs on Apple’s A19 processor, which means you get performance comparable to that of more expensive iPhones. The addition of A19 also means the 17e will be able to support future Apple software updates for years to come. It's future-proofed with Apple Intelligence and Siri AI support. Apple just rolled out a slew of new artificial-intelligence features in iOS 27, including a smarter version of Siri. The iPhone 17e gains all of those new features, which is a huge plus for a cheaper phone. Flaws but not dealbreakers It’s a little more expensive than we’d like. After the release of the iPhone 16e, we’ve come to accept that Apple’s entry-level iPhone won’t ever be as cheap as it was back in the day (to compare, the iPhone SE was $430). We still think it would be nice to be able to buy a new iPhone for under $500, though. And the 17e, like all of Apple’s other iPhones, got a $100 price increase in fall 2026 due to the ongoing RAM shortage, so it’s no longer the deal it once was. The single camera is fine, but other iPhones take better photos. The biggest differentiator across Apple’s phones is their cameras, and spending more allows you to capture better photos. The iPhone 17e has a single 48-megapixel rear camera lens, in contrast to the iPhone 17’s two lenses and the 17 Pro’s trio of lenses. It’s capable of switching between a standard angle and what Apple calls an optical-quality 2x telephoto, and the resulting images were good in our tests. It’s not capable of capturing clear, incredibly zoomed-in shots, so if that’s important to you, choose the iPhone 18 Pro instead. Other iPhones worth considering If you want a larger display and a bigger battery: The iPhone 18 Pro Max is almost identical to the iPhone 18 Pro, except for two key differences. First, it has a larger, 6.9-inch display. The bigger screen allows for a far more enjoyable viewing experience, especially if you use your phone for streaming content, reading ebooks, or editing photos. Second, it offers longer battery life — Apple promises up to 45 hours of video playback. Extra battery life is always a plus; I reached about 27 hours on a charge, but that was with continuous use while testing the device. However, with a starting price of $1,300, this model is $100 more than last year’s version. We prefer the iPhone 18 Pro, but if you truly want the bigger model, we suggest waiting until you find it on sale. What to look forward to In addition to the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max, Apple introduced its first-ever foldable iPhone: the iPhone Duo. It has a 5.4-inch cover display, a 7.6-inch main display (with the ability to multitask with two apps simultaneously), and a dual-camera setup on the back. It also has an IP68 rating, which means it offers full dust protection and water resistance. Like the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max, it runs on the A20 Pro processor and has a custom vapor chamber to help dissipate heat. The device won’t be available for purchase until October. The competition In addition to the iPhone 17 lineup, Apple also sells the $1,100 Apple iPhone Air, its thinnest iPhone ever. Although it represents a nice departure from the chunkier iPhones we’ve grown accustomed to, its slimmer profile makes some trade-offs. It offers a large, 6.5-inch display, but it has just a single rear camera lens, a single speaker, and a battery that barely lasted us 12 hours. Unless all you care about is the design, we think it’s too expensive for its lack of features. For details, read our full review. Apple no longer sells the iPhone 17 Pro and iPhone 17 Pro Max, our former upgrade picks, but you may still find remaining stock at third-party retailers or through your carrier. They have most of the same features as the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max, aside from a variable aperture and slightly shorter battery life. They remain great options, but we recommend waiting until they’re on sale. Apple still sells the Apple iPhone 16 but increased the price by $100 since last year. The now-$800 6.1-inch iPhone 16 has a smaller screen than the iPhone 17 and lacks support for ProMotion and an always-on display. The front-facing camera is 12 megapixels (in contrast to 18 megapixels on the iPhone 17) and lacks new features such as Center Stage and Dual Capture video. We suggest buying the iPhone 17 instead — its screen size is slightly larger than that of the iPhone 16, and it offers some display and camera upgrades you can’t get on the older phones.
